Around 1375 that workshop, associated with Abraham Cresques, produced a lavish atlas for the Aragonese crown covering the Mediterranean in nautical detail and the wider world in more speculative, decorated panels.

Its most striking image shows Mansa Musa of Mali enthroned south of the Sahara, holding a gold nugget, the first time a European map placed West Africa's wealth on record rather than leaving it blank. Elsewhere the atlas traces caravan routes toward Asia and includes one of the earliest drawn compass roses, blending genuine sailing knowledge with the legends still filling in what mapmakers had not seen.

Cats opened in London's West End in May 1981, setting Andrew Lloyd Webber's music to T. S. Eliot's light verse collection Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, a work never written with the stage in mind, staged with dancers in elaborate feline costumes and makeup on a junkyard set built to dwarf the actors.

The show had almost no conventional plot, built instead around a night of songs introducing rival cats competing to be chosen for rebirth. It ran in the West End for 21 years and on Broadway for 18, and for years held the record as the longest-running musical in both.

By 1853 Cayley was in his eightieth year and had never flown his own design himself. He is said to have ordered his coachman, John Appleby, into the glider instead, and Appleby was carried roughly 900 feet across Brompton Dale in Yorkshire before the craft came down. Family accounts say Appleby resigned on landing, unwilling to repeat the experience.

No independent witness account survives, so the story rests on family memory rather than contemporary report. What is not in doubt is the machine itself, a fixed wing with a boat-shaped body and a cruciform tail, built to Cayley's decades of aerodynamic notes. It remains the earliest known attempt to carry an adult in a heavier-than-air craft under any control at all.

The glider George Cayley launched at Brompton in 1804 was small enough to hold in both hands: a kite-shaped wing on a pole, with a movable tail and a weight slung beneath to fix the centre of gravity. Cayley had already worked out, on paper, that lift, drag, thrust and weight were separate forces to be balanced rather than one problem of flapping like a bird.

He had spent years testing whirling arms and paper kites before this model flew straight and steady across a room. The design fixed the layout every fixed-wing aircraft since has kept: a wing for lift, a tail for stability, a separate means of propulsion. Cayley published his reasoning in 1809 and 1810, decades before anyone built a machine large enough to carry a person.

HMS Challenger gave up most of her guns before she sailed, cleared for laboratories and winches instead. Over nearly four years from 1872 she covered almost 70,000 nautical miles, stopping to dredge the seabed and sound the depth at hundreds of stations across the Atlantic, Pacific and Southern Oceans.

Her soundings found the deepest water yet recorded, in the Pacific trench later named for the ship, and her trawls hauled up thousands of new species from depths once assumed to be lifeless. The fifty-volume report took nineteen years to finish and set the working method, systematic stations, stored samples, cross-checked instruments, that oceanography still runs on.

Tenochtitlan sat on an island in a saline lake, so drinking water had to be brought in from the springs at Chapultepec on the mainland. Aztec engineers built the aqueduct with two parallel channels, terracotta pipes set on a raised causeway, so one could be scoured and repaired while the other kept the city supplied.

Spanish chroniclers who saw the system after the 1521 conquest described it as one of the most impressive works in the city, comparable to Roman aqueducts they knew from home. Cutting the aqueduct during the siege of Tenochtitlan was one of Hernan Cortes's key tactics for forcing the city's surrender.

Prague's earlier stone bridge across the Vltava, the Judith Bridge, was badly damaged by flooding in 1342, leaving the city without a reliable crossing between its castle district and the old town. Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV, who had grown up partly in Prague and made it his imperial capital, ordered a new bridge and, according to tradition, laid its first stone himself on 9 July 1357.

Legend holds that Charles chose the date for its numerical symmetry, 1357 9, 7 5, 3, readable the same forwards and backwards. The bridge, likely designed by the architect Petr Parler, took decades to finish and carried Prague's main traffic for over five centuries before it was closed to vehicles and kept as the pedestrian landmark it is now.

Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV, who had studied in Paris and admired its university, founded one in his own capital of Prague in 1348, modelling it on the schools of Paris and Bologna and endowing it with faculties of theology, law, medicine and the arts.

It became the oldest university in Central Europe and drew students from across the region, though tensions between Czech and German factions within it grew sharp enough that a 1409 decree shifted control toward Czech masters, prompting many German scholars to leave and found a rival university at Leipzig.

The Paris Academy of Sciences ran a competition in 1738 asking entrants to explain the nature and propagation of fire. Emilie du Chatelet wrote her own essay in secret, working through the nights in her chateau at Cirey while Voltaire, with whom she shared the house and the subject, prepared a separate entry of his own.

Neither essay won the prize, but the judges thought both worth printing, and du Chatelet's argument that light and heat might share a common cause anticipated ideas later scientists took further. The Academy's decision to print her dissertation at its own expense made her the first woman to have a paper published under its name.

Chicago drew its drinking water from Lake Michigan while its river, thick with sewage and slaughterhouse waste, emptied into the same lake nearby. Under chief engineer Isham Randolph, the Sanitary District dug the 28 mile Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, deep enough to pull the river's current away from the lake and send it toward the Mississippi watershed instead.

The reversal, completed on 2 January 1900, was one of the largest earth moving projects attempted anywhere up to that point, and it worked as intended: the lake's drinking water supply stopped receiving the city's own sewage. Randolph later applied lessons from the project to his subsequent work on the Panama Canal.

In late 1978, farmers in Xiaogang village in Anhui province secretly agreed to divide collective land among individual households, each keeping what it grew beyond a quota owed to the state. The arrangement was illegal under the commune system introduced two decades earlier, one blamed for contributing to a famine that killed tens of millions between 1959 and 1961.

Deng Xiaoping's government tolerated the experiment rather than punishing it, and by the early 1980s the household responsibility system had spread nationwide with formal approval. Grain output rose sharply through the following years, and the reform is usually treated as the opening move of China's broader shift away from central planning.

Jonathan Schaeffer's team at the University of Alberta had been chasing this since 1989, building a program called Chinook that beat the human world champion Marion Tinsley in matches during the 1990s. Settling the game outright meant more than winning; it meant proving what happens if neither side ever slips.

In 2007 Schaeffer's group announced the proof: perfect play by both sides always ends in a draw. The work rested on an endgame database of 39 trillion positions, every configuration with ten or fewer pieces on the board, each traced forward to a certain result. It was the most complex popular game solved by computer until other games later broke the record.

Shirley Chisholm won New York's newly redrawn 12th congressional district in 1968, campaigning on the slogan 'unbought and unbossed' against the local Democratic machine, no Black woman having previously reached that chamber.

In office she pushed for expanded food stamp access and childcare funding, and in 1972 she ran for the Democratic presidential nomination, the first Black candidate and first woman to seek a major party's nomination for president. She won only a small number of delegates but said afterward that she ran to open the door for others rather than expecting to win outright.

A Chorus Line premiered on Broadway in July 1975, built from recorded workshop sessions in which real Broadway dancers spoke about their lives and reasons for pursuing the stage, then shaped by director Michael Bennett into a musical about seventeen dancers auditioning for eight spots in a chorus line.

Its bare stage, mirrored back wall and score by Marvin Hamlisch turned an unglamorous casting call into the show's entire drama. It ran for over six thousand performances, a Broadway record at the time, and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1976.

Whole blood clots within minutes once drawn, which had confined transfusion to a direct vein-to-vein link between donor and patient. In 1914, physicians working separately, including Belgian doctor Albert Hustin and Argentine physician Luis Agote, found that adding sodium citrate to donated blood kept it liquid without harming the recipient.

The discovery arrived just as the First World War began generating transfusion needs at a scale direct donor links could not meet. Citrated blood could be drawn ahead of casualties, kept for days, and carried to where it was needed, turning transfusion from a bedside procedure into something closer to a supply chain.

In 1983 Daniel Gorenstein announced that mathematicians had finally finished classifying every finite simple group, the indivisible building blocks from which all finite groups of symmetry are assembled, the way primes build the integers. The task had occupied dozens of researchers across roughly a hundred separate journal articles, together running past ten thousand pages.

The list settled into a small number of infinite families plus 26 stray exceptions called the sporadic groups, the largest of which, the Monster group, has more elements than atoms in a small planet. Gaps later turned up in the original argument and were not fully patched until the early 2000s, a reminder that a proof this sprawling could not be checked by any one person in the ordinary sense.

Jacqueline Cochran had already set more speed and altitude records than any other woman flying when Chuck Yeager, by then a friend, offered to help her break the sound barrier itself. She trained on a borrowed Canadian-built F-86 Sabre, with Yeager flying chase in another jet to confirm the instruments.

On 18 May 1953, over the Mojave Desert near Edwards Air Force Base, Cochran took the Sabre past Mach 1, averaging over 650 miles per hour and beating every man who had tried it before her that day. She was 47 at the time, having taught herself to fly less than two decades earlier after starting out as a beautician.

The Cocoanut Grove nightclub in Boston was licensed for around 460 people, but on the night of 28 November 1942 more than 800 patrons and staff were packed inside, many celebrating after a Boston College football game. A fire, reportedly starting near an artificial palm tree, spread rapidly through decorations and low ceilings.

Nearly 500 people died, many crushed against exit doors that were locked, hidden behind draperies or built to open inward rather than out. The disaster prompted sweeping changes to American fire codes, including requirements for revolving doors to be flanked by outward-swinging ones and for exits to be clearly marked and unobstructed.

Georg Cantor had asked in the 1870s whether there is an infinite set of numbers strictly larger than the integers but strictly smaller than the real numbers, the continuum hypothesis. Kurt Godel showed in 1940 that the standard axioms of set theory cannot disprove it. The other half of the question, whether those same axioms could prove it, sat open for over two decades.

Paul Cohen answered it in 1963 by inventing a technique called forcing, building alternative mathematical universes in which the axioms hold but the continuum hypothesis is false. Combined with Godel's result, this showed the hypothesis is independent: neither provable nor disprovable from the usual axioms of set theory. Cohen won the Fields Medal for the method, which mathematicians have since applied to many other unresolved questions.

Bessie Coleman could not find an American flight school willing to train a Black woman, so in 1920 she learned French and travelled to Paris, where the Federation Aeronautique Internationale accepted students regardless of race. She trained at the Caudron Brothers' school outside Le Crotoy.

She earned her international pilot's licence in June 1921, becoming the first Black woman, and reportedly the first Black American of either sex, to hold one. Back in the United States she made a living performing at air shows, refusing to fly at events that barred Black spectators, until she died in a crash during a 1926 rehearsal flight.

Work on Cologne Cathedral had stopped in the Middle Ages, leaving a half-built crane sitting on one unfinished tower for centuries as a visible symbol of the incomplete project. Building resumed in the nineteenth century using the original medieval plans, which had survived, and the cathedral was finally finished after more than six hundred years.

Its twin spires, at roughly 157 metres, made it briefly the tallest building on Earth. It was also the last church ever to hold that title: within a few years secular structures, first the Washington Monument and then steel-framed towers, took over the record for good.

Colossus began running at Bletchley Park in February 1944, built by the engineer Tommy Flowers to attack the Lorenz cipher used on high-level German teleprinter links, a machine far more complex than Enigma and used for messages between Hitler and his army commanders. It read paper tape at five thousand characters a second using nearly two thousand vacuum tubes.

Rather than decrypt a message outright, Colossus tested candidate wheel settings against intercepted traffic and flagged the ones statistically likely to be correct, work previously done by hand over days. It was the first programmable electronic digital computer, though its existence stayed secret until the 1970s, and most of the ten machines built were dismantled or destroyed after the war.

On the last night of 192 CE, Commodus's mistress Marcia poisoned his wine after learning she was on a list of people he planned to have killed. When he vomited it back up, the conspirators sent in his wrestling partner Narcissus, who strangled him in his bath rather than risk the poison failing twice.

Commodus had ruled since 180 and increasingly styled himself a gladiator and demigod rather than a statesman, alienating the Senate and his own household. His death ended the Antonine dynasty outright and opened the Year of the Five Emperors, a scramble for the throne resolved only by Septimius Severus a few years later.

Philips engineers unveiled the SL lamp in 1980, bending a fluorescent tube into a compact shape that could screw into a standard bulb socket in place of an incandescent. Earlier fluorescent tubes were long, straight and needed their own fittings, which had kept them out of ordinary table lamps despite using far less electricity than a filament bulb for the same brightness.

Folding the tube tightly enough to fit a household socket, while keeping the ballast that regulates the electrical current small enough to hide in the base, took years of development before Philips could sell one. Compact fluorescents used roughly a quarter of the power of an equivalent incandescent bulb and lasted many times longer, though their slow warm-up and mercury content later left them displaced by LED bulbs.

Qin Shi Huang's minister Li Si had ordered Confucian texts burned in 213 BC, so surviving copies had to be hidden. Tradition holds that Kong Fu, a descendant of Confucius and librarian in the family's home state of Lu, sealed a set of classics inside the walls of the Kong family house at Qufu rather than surrendering them.

The texts came to light generations later, in the second century BC, when Liu Yu, a Han prince granted the old Lu territory, began demolishing the house to expand his own palace and broke into the hidden cache. Among the recovered works was a version of the Book of Documents with sixteen more chapters than the version already in circulation, written in an archaic script scholars of the day struggled to read.

Harold Vanderbilt was three weeks into a cruise through the Panama Canal aboard the steamship Finland in October 1925 when he began reworking auction bridge with his fellow passengers. Auction bridge let a partnership score for tricks it merely won along the way, which Vanderbilt thought rewarded caution over daring.

His fix required a partnership to name its contract before play and score fully only for tricks bid and made, with a bonus for a slam and a penalty for falling short. He also introduced vulnerability, raising the stakes for a side already ahead in the rubber. The rules he wrote out on that voyage were published in 1927 and are still, largely unchanged, the rules of contract bridge.

Henri III ordered a proper lighthouse for the Gironde estuary in 1584, and the man he hired, Louis de Foix, built something closer to a royal chapel than a beacon. Construction dragged for 27 years through Henri's assassination and Henri IV's reign before the tower was finished in 1611, three storeys of columns and gargoyles standing on a rock the sea covered twice a day.

The light itself was a wood fire burning in the open on top, later replaced by coal and eventually a proper lamp and lens. Cordouan still stands at the mouth of the river below Bordeaux and is the oldest lighthouse still operating in France, a UNESCO World Heritage Site kept staffed largely because the tides that made it worth building make it hard to reach.

The tariffs Robert Peel abolished in 1846 had kept British grain prices high since 1815, protecting landowners at the cost of bread for everyone else. The Irish famine broke the argument for keeping them: with a harvest failing across the Atlantic, a duty on imported corn looked less like protection and more like a policy that starved people.

Peel split his own Conservative Party to pass the repeal, relying on opposition votes and losing the premiership within months. The decision became the founding text of British free trade policy for the rest of the century, and the vote itself is often read as the moment the party of landed interest lost control of it.

Ezra Cornell, who had made a fortune helping build the telegraph network, and Andrew Dickson White, a young state senator, founded a university in Ithaca, New York, in 1865, funded by Cornell's endowment and federal land-grant money.

Their founding principle, that any student could study any subject regardless of religion, race or background, was unusual for the period and set the school apart from denominational colleges. It became one of the original land-grant universities under the Morrill Act.

Paul Cornu built bicycles for a living and helicopters in his spare time. His machine had two large rotors mounted fore and aft of a light steel frame, driven by a single engine through belts, with no wing at all to provide lift by forward motion. On 13 November 1907, near Lisieux in Normandy, it lifted him a little over a metre off the ground and held him there for roughly twenty seconds.

Cornu's own journal is more cautious than the legend built around it, noting only that all four wheels cleared the ground. The craft had almost no lateral control and was never developed further; Cornu returned to bicycle repair. It remains the earliest instance of a rotor-lifted machine carrying a person clear of the ground under its own power.

Barbary corsairs from North Africa, guided to the remote Irish village of Baltimore by a captured Dutch sailor familiar with its layout, landed before dawn in June 1631. They moved house to house seizing nearly the entire sleeping population, an unusually far ranging raid for corsairs normally active closer to the Mediterranean.

Around a hundred villagers were carried off to be sold in the slave markets of Algiers, most never returning to Ireland. The raid left Baltimore largely abandoned for years afterward and became one of the best documented examples of Barbary slave raiding reaching as far as the British Isles.

Alan Guth, then a young physicist at SLAC, worked out in late 1979 that a peculiar state of the very early universe could have driven an episode of exponential expansion, stretching space by an enormous factor in a tiny fraction of a second. He published the idea in 1981, calling it inflation, after realising it solved puzzles the standard Big Bang model left unexplained.

Two of those puzzles were why the universe looks so uniform in every direction and why space appears geometrically flat rather than curved. Inflation explained both by proposing that any earlier irregularities were smoothed out and stretched beyond view during the burst of expansion. The theory remains unproven directly, but its predictions about the pattern of the cosmic microwave background have matched observation closely.

Shang dynasty China, around 1200 BCE, used cowrie shells gathered from the South China Sea and Indian Ocean as currency, strung on cords and counted in units rather than weighed like metal. Oracle bone inscriptions record shells given as gifts and payments, and burials of the period include hoards of them alongside bronze goods.

Shells could not be minted or divided, so China moved toward bronze cast into cowrie shapes and then toward standard round coinage within a few centuries. The character for money, bei, still carries the shell's pictograph, a trace of the system that later metal coinage replaced.

New York City had relied on wells and a few private companies for drinking water, none of it adequate for a city that had suffered cholera outbreaks and fires firefighters could not douse. The Croton Aqueduct solved that with 41 miles of masonry conduit, dropping only about 13 inches per mile so gravity alone carried water south to Manhattan.

Its opening in 1842 was marked by a five mile parade and fountains sent up in City Hall Park and Union Square, celebrated as proof the city could finally supply itself reliably. The aqueduct remained in service, later supplemented by a larger parallel tunnel, into the twentieth century.

Crypto AG, based in Zug, Switzerland, had sold cipher machines to governments worldwide since the 1950s, trading on Switzerland's neutrality to reassure buyers their secrets were safe from any single power. In June 1970 the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly bought the company for 5.75 million dollars through intermediaries, an arrangement the agencies code-named Thesaurus and later Rubicon.

For decades afterward the agencies quietly weakened the encryption sold to some 120 countries, letting Washington and Bonn read diplomatic and military traffic from Iran, Argentina and Libya. At its height Crypto AG's compromised machines supplied roughly 40 percent of the NSA's decrypted intelligence, an arrangement that stayed hidden until reporting by the Washington Post and German broadcaster ZDF exposed it in 2020.

Ctesibius worked in Alexandria as a barber before turning to mechanics, and little else of his life survives beyond the inventions later writers, chiefly Vitruvius, attribute to him. His water clock kept time by dripping water at a steady rate into a vessel that raised a float marking the hours, an old idea whose accuracy had always depended on the water source staying constant.

His improvement was a float valve in the supply tank: as the water level dropped, the float opened the inlet further, and as it rose, the float closed it down, holding the flow rate steady without anyone adjusting it by hand. Historians of engineering treat it as one of the earliest documented feedback control mechanisms, the same basic principle later used in cistern ballcocks and thermostats.

By the 1850s several scholars, Henry Rawlinson, Edward Hincks, Julius Oppert and the amateur Egyptologist William Fox Talbot, each claimed to have worked out how to read Akkadian cuneiform, largely from the trilingual Behistun inscription Rawlinson had copied off a cliff face in Persia. Each man's method was different enough that other scholars doubted whether any of them could really be trusted.

In 1857 the Royal Asiatic Society settled it with a blind test: all four were sent an unpublished Assyrian inscription and asked to translate it independently, sealing their results before comparing them. The four translations agreed closely enough on names, events and grammar that the society declared cuneiform genuinely decipherable, opening the entire written record of Mesopotamia to modern reading.

The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded jointly to Marie Curie, her husband Pierre, and Henri Becquerel for their work on radioactivity, a term Marie herself had coined. She was initially left off the nomination, and Pierre reportedly insisted the committee add her name before he would accept.

She won a second Nobel, in Chemistry, in 1911 for isolating radium and polonium, making her the first person of either sex to win in two different sciences. Her notebooks are still radioactive enough that researchers handling them today wear protective clothing, a detail that says as much about the material she worked with as any award.

Nicholas of Cusa was a German cardinal, not an astronomer, and his 1440 treatise On Learned Ignorance reasoned from theology rather than observation. He argued that because only God is truly infinite and unmoving, the universe itself can have no fixed centre and no outer boundary, so the Earth cannot occupy any privileged still point and the stars are not fixed lights but bodies like the sun.

He wrote a century before Copernicus put the sun at the centre of a working mathematical model, and Cusa's universe has no centre at all, which is a stranger and further claim. His reasoning was philosophical, not predictive, and made no astronomical measurements, but later writers who wanted intellectual cover for a moving Earth found his cardinal's authority useful to cite.

Built on the River Clyde and launched in November 1869, Cutty Sark was designed for one job: bringing the season's first tea home from China as fast as possible, since an early cargo commanded a premium price in London markets.

The timing worked against her. The Suez Canal opened that same year, favouring steamships that no longer needed to sail around Africa, and steam soon took over the tea trade anyway. She found a second life hauling wool from Australia instead, setting speed records on that route that steamships of her era could not match, and survives today in dry dock at Greenwich.

In 2000, the US Food and Drug Administration cleared the da Vinci Surgical System, letting a surgeon sit at a console some distance from the operating table and control instruments mounted on robotic arms inside the patient. The console translates the surgeon's hand movements into smaller, steadier motions at the tip of each tool.

The system gave surgeons a magnified three-dimensional view and instruments that could rotate further than a human wrist, useful in tight spaces such as the pelvis. It spread quickly into prostate, gynaecological and cardiac procedures, and da Vinci machines are now used in operating rooms across dozens of countries.

Two rival teams, the Supernova Cosmology Project and the High-Z Supernova Search, were both trying to measure how much the expansion of the universe was slowing down. They used Type Ia supernovae as standard candles, exploding stars bright enough and consistent enough to gauge distance across billions of light years, and in 1998 both groups found the same unexpected answer.

The supernovae were dimmer, meaning farther away, than a decelerating universe could explain. Expansion was speeding up. Cosmologists named the unknown driver dark energy, and later measurements put it at roughly 68 percent of the universe's total energy content. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for the finding.

A year earlier, at the first Grand Challenge in 2004, every entrant failed within the opening miles of a 150 mile Mojave Desert course, and the best car managed barely seven. DARPA doubled the prize to two million dollars and tried again in October 2005, and this time Stanford's Volkswagen Touareg, named Stanley, finished the route in just under seven hours with no driver or remote control.

Stanley used laser rangefinders, cameras and GPS to build a map of the terrain ahead and steer itself around rocks, cliffs and tunnels. Four other vehicles also completed the course that year, a jump from the previous year's total of zero, and much of the sensor and software approach carried directly into the driverless car projects that followed at Google and elsewhere.

Germany and Austria-Hungary set their clocks forward an hour on 30 April 1916, becoming the first states to enact nationwide daylight saving. The stated aim was fuel: an extra hour of evening light meant less coal burned for lamps and gas, at a time when the war had made both scarce.

Britain adopted its own version, British Summer Time, weeks later, and other European belligerents followed within the year. The United States held off until 1918, and even then only under wartime pressure, before repealing the federal law almost immediately after the armistice and leaving the choice to states and cities for decades.

Charles Deane patented his Smoke Helmet in 1823, a copper helmet with a flexible collar meant to let firemen breathe inside burning buildings, air pumped in through a hose by bellows. It sold poorly as firefighting gear, and Deane put the design aside for several years before returning to it with his brother John.

Around 1828 the brothers realised the same helmet, simply weighted and open at the neck, would let a man work underwater instead of in smoke, and they began marketing it as a diving helmet. Divers using it recovered cannon and cargo from wrecks within a couple of years, though the open design still let water in if the wearer tipped forward, a flaw Augustus Siebe's closed dress later solved.

The frigate USS Philadelphia had run aground off Tripoli in 1803 and been captured intact, giving Barbary corsairs a valuable warship and its crew as hostages. Stephen Decatur volunteered to destroy it rather than let it be repaired and used against the American navy.

In February 1804 he sailed a captured ketch, renamed Intrepid, into Tripoli harbour disguised as a merchant vessel, boarded the Philadelphia by surprise, and set it ablaze before escaping under fire. The raid cost no American lives and was widely admired at the time as a feat of nerve.

Two consecutive years of failed monsoon rains struck the Deccan plateau beginning in 1630, at the same time as Mughal armies were campaigning through the region against the Ahmadnagar sultanate, compounding a natural disaster with military disruption to trade and farming. Grain prices rose beyond what ordinary households could pay, and contemporary accounts describe roads and towns littered with the dead.

The Mughal court under Shah Jahan eventually ordered some relief measures, including free kitchens and tax remissions in the worst-affected districts, but they arrived too late to prevent mass mortality. Estimates for the dead run into the millions, making the Deccan famine one of the deadliest recorded disasters of the seventeenth century, and a lasting mark against the campaign that helped cause it.

The de Havilland Comet's prototype flew for the first time on 27 July 1949, a smooth, swept-winged airliner with four jet engines buried in its wing roots rather than hung beneath it. Jet propulsion had until then meant fighters; the Comet was designed from the outset to carry paying passengers at altitudes propeller airliners could not reach.

It entered commercial service with BOAC in 1952, cutting hours off routes like London to Johannesburg, and briefly made Britain the clear leader in jet air travel. That lead did not last: a series of catastrophic fuselage failures grounded the Comet within two years, caused by metal fatigue around square window frames that later, redesigned airliners would build around instead of repeat.

Deir el-Medina was the walled village housing the workmen who built and decorated the royal tombs across the Nile from Thebes, and its residents knew the Valley of the Kings' layout better than almost anyone else in Egypt. Around 1110 BCE, several of them were put on trial accused of breaking into royal and noble tombs and stripping them of gold and treasure.

Surviving trial papyri record confessions extracted under beating, describing how the men located tombs, broke through sealed doors and melted down gold objects to disguise them before selling the metal. The records are unusually detailed for ancient Egypt and give historians one of their clearest windows into how tomb robbery, a chronic problem across the pharaonic period, actually worked in practice.

Before 1976, sharing a secret code with someone meant meeting them first, or trusting a courier, because every cipher known assumed both sides already held the same key. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, working at Stanford, published a method by which two people could exchange numbers over an open, watched line and each arrive at the same secret, without ever transmitting the secret itself.

The trick relies on a one-way calculation: easy to compute forward, impractical to reverse. Diffie and Hellman credited discussions with Ralph Merkle, whose own related idea came slightly earlier but later. The scheme still runs, largely unchanged in principle, inside the handshake that opens a secure connection on the modern web every time a browser shows a padlock.

Dionysius Exiguus was not trying to invent a calendar. In 525 the Scythian monk, working in Rome, needed to extend an existing Easter table past its final year, and he disliked that the old one counted from the reign of the persecuting emperor Diocletian, so he restarted the count from the incarnation of Christ instead.

His table ran from what he called Anno Domini 532, and the numbering caught on far more slowly than the calculation did: England adopted it in the eighth century through Bede, and much of continental Europe not until the tenth. Dionysius never explained how he arrived at the birth year he chose, and modern scholars think it is wrong by several years.

Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House premiered in Copenhagen in December 1879, ending with its heroine Nora walking out on her husband and children after realising her marriage had treated her as a plaything rather than an equal. The closing sound of the front door slamming became one of the era's most argued-over stage moments.

Audiences and critics across Europe reacted with outrage at an ending that left a wife's departure unresolved and unpunished, and some productions altered it to have Nora stay. Ibsen refused to soften the play, which is now widely credited with helping establish realist drama built around ordinary domestic conflict rather than melodrama.

Tile games matching pips across paired ends had been played in China for centuries, evolving out of older dice and card traditions, before Italian traders and travellers carried a version of the game west around the turn of the eighteenth century. The European sets kept the Chinese logic, pairing tiles by their marked ends, but dropped the more elaborate Chinese rules built around specific tile combinations.

Italy and France took to the game first, carving early sets from animal bone or ivory backed with ebony, which is why players still call the tiles bones. From there dominoes spread into taverns and homes across the continent, becoming a fixture of European card- and tile-game culture that Chinese dominoes themselves never quite achieved outside East Asia.

Around 1480, Romans digging into the Oppian Hill broke through into buried, painted chambers, the surviving wing of Nero's Domus Aurea, sealed under later imperial baths since antiquity. Because the rooms were entered from above through holes rather than at ground level, visitors including Pinturicchio and later Raphael had themselves lowered on ropes by torchlight to study the walls.

The ceiling paintings mixed human figures with sphinxes, garlands and impossible hybrid creatures on a plain background, a style painters copied and named grottesche, or grotesque, after the grotte they thought they were in. Raphael reused the pattern in his Vatican loggias in the 1510s, and grotesque ornament from a buried Roman ceiling became a standard decorative vocabulary across European art.

A first cable across the Channel, laid in 1850, worked for barely a day before it broke, snagged either by a fishing boat's anchor or by chafing against rocks near Cape Gris-Nez. The single copper wire had only a coating of gutta percha for insulation and no protection at all against the sea floor.

The following year, engineer Thomas Crampton designed a heavier cable wrapped in iron wire armour, and on 13 November 1851 it carried the first message between England and France that actually stayed working. It remained in service, with repairs, until 1875, and its success set the pattern armoured cables would follow across the Atlantic and every other ocean telegraph line that came after.

Francis Drake returned to England in 1580 having completed a circumnavigation of the globe, loaded with plundered Spanish treasure from the Pacific coast of South America. Queen Elizabeth I, wary of provoking open war with Spain, initially kept a public distance from the voyage's obviously piratical proceeds.

In April 1581 she nonetheless boarded his ship, the Golden Hind, at Deptford and knighted him there in person, a deliberately public gesture of royal approval. The ceremony told Spain plainly that England intended to keep backing its privateers, and Drake's plunder alone reportedly covered the crown's entire annual debt.

Francis Drake, still a relatively junior privateer, led an attack on Nombre de Dios in 1572, the Panamanian port where Spanish silver mined in Peru was loaded for shipment to Europe. His initial raid on the town itself was beaten back after he was wounded, forcing a retreat before the treasure could be seized.

Drake stayed in the region for months afterward, working with escaped African slaves called Cimarrons who knew the interior, and eventually ambushed a mule train carrying silver across the isthmus. The campaign made his reputation and his fortune, and opened a sustained English assault on Spain's American treasure routes that lasted the rest of the century.

Cornelis Drebbel was a Dutch inventor working at the English court, and his diving boat was a wooden frame wrapped in greased leather with oars poking through leather-sealed holes. Around 1620 he took it under the Thames at a depth of roughly four metres, staying down for hours while two tubes with floating ends fed air from the surface. He built two more, each larger than the last.

The third carried sixteen people and, by most accounts, King James I among them on a test dive, making him the first monarch to travel underwater. Drebbel never worked out how to make the design useful for anything beyond demonstration, and the Royal Navy declined it. It would be more than a century before anyone built a submarine meant for actual combat.

In November 2019, thieves cut power to street lighting near Dresden's Royal Palace, smashed a window grille of the Historic Green Vault and used an axe to break display cases holding eighteenth century jewel sets before fleeing in a getaway car within minutes.

The stolen diamond and gemstone pieces, some worn by Saxon royalty, were valued at well over a hundred million euros. Several men were convicted in 2023, and prosecutors negotiated the return of most of the jewellery, though some pieces were damaged when gems were pried loose for easier resale.

Arabian herders brought the wild one-humped dromedary under domestication, an animal already adapted to extreme heat and long stretches without water, valuing it for milk, meat, wool and, crucially, transport across desert terrain no other pack animal could cross as efficiently.

The dromedary's domestication eventually opened trade routes across Arabia and into the Sahara that had previously been impassable for sustained commerce, laying groundwork for incense routes and, much later, trans-Saharan trade networks. Its two-humped cousin, the Bactrian camel, was domesticated separately in Central Asia.

The engineer Li Bing, governing the Qin province of Shu, built the Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min River around 256 BCE without constructing a dam to block the river's flow. Instead, an artificial levee split the river into an inner and outer channel, directing a controlled share of the water toward farmland.

The design let floodwater and silt pass through the outer channel while the inner channel fed the Chengdu plain, turning a flood-prone region into one of China's most productive agricultural areas. The system still functions on largely its original layout, irrigating farmland well over two thousand years after it was built.

Dutch shipwrights designed the fluyt around a single problem: crew wages ate into cargo profit. The result launched in 1595 was a bulky, pear shaped hull that needed few sailors to handle, since simplified rigging let a small crew manage sails that would otherwise have demanded far more hands.

Building it cheaply from standardised parts, largely of Baltic timber, kept the purchase price low too. The combination let Dutch merchants undercut rival shippers on freight rates across Europe, and the fluyt became the workhorse behind the Dutch Republic's dominance of bulk seaborne trade through the seventeenth century.

By around 800 BCE, engineers on the Iranian plateau were digging qanats, gently sloped tunnels that carried groundwater from an aquifer at the base of hills down to farmland, sometimes over many kilometres, entirely by gravity.

Because the water travelled underground, a qanat lost little to evaporation in the arid climate and needed no pumping. Vertical shafts sunk at intervals along the route let diggers remove excavated soil and maintain the tunnel, and the technique later spread from Persia across the Middle East, North Africa and parts of Central Asia.

Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest opened at London's St James's Theatre on 14 February 1895, its plot of two men each inventing a fictitious alter ego named Ernest to escape social obligations earning laughter through precisely balanced, epigram-heavy dialogue.

The premiere was a triumph, but within weeks Wilde's libel case against the Marquess of Queensberry collapsed and exposed evidence used to prosecute him for gross indecency. The play was pulled from the stage soon after his arrest, and Wilde's name was even removed from playbills while it briefly continued running.

Edinburgh had suffered a series of damaging fires in its cramped Old Town tenements when the city established a municipal fire brigade in 1824, appointing James Braidwood, then in his early twenties, as its first firemaster. Braidwood trained his men systematically, drilling them in using ladders and hoses together rather than relying on ad hoc volunteers.

His approach, treating firefighting as a disciplined, salaried profession rather than a sideline for insurance companies, was studied and copied by other British cities. Braidwood later moved to London to lead its fire brigade and was killed there in 1861 fighting a warehouse fire, but Edinburgh's brigade is generally credited as the first of its modern kind.

Edinburgh's town council secured a royal charter from James VI in 1582 and opened its doors to students the following year, funded partly through a bequest from a local bishop rather than by the crown or the church directly.

That municipal origin made it unusual: most older British universities had been founded by monarchs or religious orders, while Edinburgh's was established and run by the city itself, a model that shaped how it developed as a centre for medicine and the Enlightenment later on.

Edward had spent roughly a quarter century in exile in Normandy, sent there as a child when the Danish conquest of England displaced his father Aethelred's line. He returned in 1041 at the invitation of his half brother Harthacnut and succeeded him the following year, arriving with more Norman ties than English ones.

His piety earned him the name Confessor, and his signature project was a new church at Westminster, built in the Romanesque style he had seen in Normandy and consecrated only days before his death in January 1066. His childless death left the succession open, the dispute that produced the Norman Conquest within the year.

Llywelyn ap Gruffudd had ruled as Prince of Wales under a treaty with Edward I, but a rising led by his brother Dafydd in 1282 drew Edward into a war that ended with Llywelyn's death near Builth that December and Dafydd's execution the following year. With the native princely line broken, Edward moved to fix Wales's status permanently rather than leave it to another rebellion.

The Statute of Rhuddlan, issued in March 1284, divided the conquered principality into English-style counties and imposed English common law and administration, though it left some Welsh legal custom in place. Edward's son, born at Caernarfon Castle in 1284, was later made the first English Prince of Wales, a title the English crown has granted its heir ever since.

Edward II's reign had already survived one baronial revolt when his queen, Isabella of France, landed with an invasion force in 1326 backed by her lover Roger Mortimer. Edward's favourites were captured and executed, and by January 1327 Parliament, meeting without the king present, resolved that he had forfeited the crown through incompetence and had it settled on his fourteen-year-old son.

A delegation forced Edward to formally resign the throne at Kenilworth Castle rather than simply be removed by force, the first English king made to abdicate this way. He was moved between castles as a prisoner and died at Berkeley Castle that September, officially of natural causes, though contemporaries and later historians have never fully agreed on how he died.

When the French Capetian line died out in 1328, Edward III had as strong a bloodline claim as anyone, through his mother Isabella, daughter of Philip IV. French jurists invoked Salic law to bar inheritance through a woman and crowned Philip of Valois instead, a decision Edward accepted for a decade while more immediate quarrels over Gascony and Scotland occupied him.

In January 1340 Edward formally took the title King of France, quartering the French fleur de lis with the English lions on his royal arms and coinage. The claim gave legal shape to what became the Hundred Years War, and English monarchs kept the title, and the quartered arms, on paper for over four hundred years after any hope of the crown itself had gone.

Edward had been king for less than a year, uncrowned, when he told the government in November 1936 that he intended to marry Wallis Simpson, an American who was still finalising her second divorce. The Church of England he headed as king did not marry divorced people with a living former spouse, and his own ministers told him the marriage was incompatible with the crown.

He signed the instrument of abdication on 10 December 1936, the only British monarch ever to give up the throne voluntarily, and broadcast his reasons to the country the next evening. His brother Albert, who had never expected to reign and struggled with a stammer his whole life, took the throne as George VI within hours of the signing.

The only account of Eilmer's flight comes from the chronicler William of Malmesbury, writing more than a century later, who says the monk fitted wings to his hands and feet and launched himself from a tower of Malmesbury Abbey around 1010. William credits him with covering roughly 200 metres before landing hard.

Eilmer broke both legs in the fall and was lame for the rest of his life, and William records him blaming the crash on forgetting to give the wings a tail. He is said to have survived long enough to watch Halley's Comet pass in 1066 and to have recalled the omen from an earlier appearance, one of the details that makes the story, however thin its sourcing, stick in histories of early flight.

Elizabeth I's government consolidated decades of piecemeal local relief measures into a single statute in 1601, making each parish legally responsible for supporting its own poor through a compulsory local tax known as the poor rate. Overseers appointed in each parish decided who qualified for relief, distinguishing between those judged unable to work and those judged simply unwilling.

The law replaced the monastic almsgiving that had collapsed after Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries decades earlier, filling a gap that had left the destitute with no reliable support at all. Its parish-based structure remained the backbone of English poor relief for over two centuries, and versions of its logic, tying aid to local administration, echoed through relief policy across the British Empire long afterward.

Enheduanna held the office of high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur, a position her father Sargon of Akkad appears to have created for her to help bind the newly conquered Sumerian cities to Akkadian rule. Her surviving hymns to the goddess Inanna are preserved on cuneiform tablets copied for centuries after her death.

What sets her apart is that she names herself within the text, asking the goddess directly for help after being driven from her post during a political revolt. No earlier writer anywhere is known by name, which is why later Mesopotamian scribes kept copying her work long after the Akkadian empire that gave her the post had collapsed.

Arthur Scherbius patented his rotor cipher machine in 1918 and, through the firm Chiffriermaschinen AG, put a commercial version on the market in 1923 aimed at banks and businesses that wanted their correspondence unreadable to rivals. Sales to industry were modest; the machine was expensive and most firms had no real need for military-grade secrecy.

The German navy adopted a modified Enigma in 1926 and the army followed in 1928, eventually standardising it across the armed forces. That later military version, refined and re-wired through the 1930s, became the cipher that Polish, then British, codebreakers spent the Second World War working to defeat.

Before 1948, espresso machines used steam pressure alone, which topped out too low to do more than brew coffee quickly. Achille Gaggia, a Milanese bar owner, patented a spring-piston lever that a barista pulled by hand, forcing water through the grounds at far higher pressure than steam could manage on its own.

The higher pressure pulled oils out of the coffee that steam brewing left behind, and those oils emulsified into a thin reddish-brown foam on top of the shot. Gaggia marketed it as crema naturale, and bars advertised his machines as producing coffee with a cream that needed no milk. The lever design is why espresso, as a distinct drink, is usually dated from his machine rather than earlier steam models.

Etna began erupting on 11 March 1669 from a new set of fissures on its southern flank, and the resulting lava flow spent five weeks creeping toward Catania rather than the volcano's own summit. Residents hoped the medieval city walls would hold it back. On 30 April a stretch of wall roughly 57 metres long simply gave way, and the flow poured through into the streets.

The lava reached the sea over the following weeks, building a delta that pushed the coastline forward by around 800 metres and swallowed part of the harbour. It is remembered as Etna's largest recorded eruption, having buried farmland, several villages, and part of a major city, though contemporary accounts differ sharply on how many people actually died.

Henry VI founded a school beside Windsor Castle in 1440, intended to educate a fixed number of poor scholars without charge and prepare them for further study at King's College, Cambridge, which he founded the following year.

Henry's own reign ended in deposition and mental collapse, but his school outlasted him, becoming one of England's most prominent institutions and, over the centuries, the alma mater of a large share of the country's political leadership, prime ministers among them.

Somali piracy had grown from opportunistic coastal raids into an industry ransoming entire cargo ships, and by 2008 the frequency of hijackings off the Horn of Africa was disrupting a route carrying a large share of world trade.

The European Union responded that December with Operation Atalanta, its first ever joint naval mission, escorting World Food Programme shipments and merchant convoys through the Gulf of Aden. It marked the EU acting militarily as a bloc rather than through individual member navies.

Every plant, animal and fungus alive descends from a single merger deep in the Proterozoic: one microbe was engulfed by another, and instead of being digested it stayed, dividing alongside its host for billions of generations. That surviving guest became the mitochondrion, the organelle that still burns oxygen for fuel inside nearly every complex cell today.

The evidence is not a fossil but the cell's own machinery: mitochondria carry their own small loop of DNA, unrelated to the nucleus, and replicate independently within the cell that houses them. That mismatch is the fingerprint of two separate organisms folded into one, a single accident of failed digestion that made every subsequent large, complex organism possible.

The Ganj-i-Sawai was returning from Mecca loaded with pilgrims and treasure when Henry Every's small fleet caught it in the Arabian Sea in September 1695. Its escort had already fled, and after a battle in which the ship's own cannon burst, Every's crew boarded and held it for days.

The haul, reckoned at several hundred thousand pounds, made each sailor rich enough to vanish. It also enraged the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, who threatened the East India Company's trading posts until London launched the first worldwide manhunt for a criminal by name. Every was never caught.

Hunters on the Asian steppe began capturing wild raptors, such as falcons and eagles, and training them to hunt game cooperatively alongside people rather than simply competing for the same prey. The practice required patient handling to keep a wild predator calm enough to return to a handler after a kill.

Falconry spread from Central Asia westward into the Middle East and eventually Europe, carried along the same trade and migration routes as horses and other steppe innovations. It remains practised today largely unchanged in method, and is recognised by UNESCO as a living cultural tradition in dozens of countries.

Babylon's walls were reckoned among the strongest built anywhere in the ancient world, thick enough that a direct assault seemed pointless. Herodotus, writing over a century later, claimed Cyrus the Great's Persian army instead diverted the Euphrates river that ran through the city, lowering the water enough for soldiers to wade beneath the walls along the riverbed.

Babylonian sources instead describe the city's own priesthood and officials opening the gates to Cyrus, unhappy with their king Nabonidus, making the fall closer to a negotiated surrender than a stormed breach. Cyrus took the city in 539 BCE and later released the Jewish exiles held there, an act recorded on the Cyrus Cylinder.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network was set up by the United States Agency for International Development in 1985, in the aftermath of the Ethiopian famine that had killed hundreds of thousands and drawn global attention through television footage rather than official warning. Its purpose was to catch the next crisis in rainfall and crop data before it reached that stage.

Analysts combine satellite imagery of vegetation and rainfall with market prices and local reporting to flag districts moving toward food insecurity months in advance. The network now covers dozens of countries and issues classifications that international agencies, including the World Food Programme, use to decide where to send relief before a famine is formally declared.

An Irish scholar named Dicuil, writing around 825, recorded a report from a fellow monk that Irish hermits had lived on remote North Atlantic islands for nearly a hundred years before Norse settlers arrived. Archaeological finds of burnt barley grains on the Faroes, dated earlier than any known Norse presence, have since lent that written claim real support.

These monks were seeking solitude rather than land or trade, a pattern repeated across the Irish church's Atlantic outposts, from Iceland to smaller Scottish islands. Norse sagas later describe finding the Faroes empty of people, suggesting the monks left, rather than being displaced, once Viking ships began arriving in numbers.

Andrew Wiles presented a proof in June 1993, only for a referee, Nick Katz, to find a gap that summer while checking the argument line by line. Wiles spent another year trying to repair it, largely in secret, before enlisting a former student, Richard Taylor, to help close the hole using a technique the two developed together.

The corrected proof was published in 1995, finally resolving a claim Pierre de Fermat had scrawled in a book margin around 1637, saying he had a proof too long to fit there. Wiles worked toward it for roughly seven years, much of that time alone in his attic study, and the eventual proof drew on mathematics, elliptic curves and modular forms, that did not exist in Fermat's own lifetime.

Finland's parliament voted for independence on 6 December 1917, seven weeks after the Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd and with the empire that had ruled it since 1809 collapsing. Lenin's government recognised the new state on New Year's Eve, a rare instance of Soviet Russia conceding territory rather than fighting to keep it.

Recognition did not bring peace. Within two months Finland was fighting its own civil war between the socialist Reds and the conservative Whites under Carl Gustaf Mannerheim, a conflict that killed more Finns in a few months than the independence struggle itself and shaped the country's politics for a generation.

Claudius Amyand was operating on an eleven-year-old boy's hernia at St George's Hospital in London when he found the appendix inside the hernial sac, perforated by a swallowed pin. He removed it during the same operation, in 1735, decades before anyone understood appendicitis as a disease in its own right.

The boy survived, which was unusual for abdominal surgery of the period, done without anaesthesia or any grasp of infection. Amyand's own account of the case was published, but the operation was treated as a curious footnote rather than a method, and deliberate appendix removal for inflammation was not attempted again for well over a century.

Matthias Zurbriggen, a Swiss-Italian mountain guide hired for a British-led expedition, pushed ahead of his companions in the final stretch and reached Aconcagua's summit alone in January 1897. The mountain's extreme altitude, over 6,900 metres, and thin air rather than technical difficulty made it a serious test even without steep climbing involved.

His solitary final approach meant no one else was present to verify the summit at the moment of arrival, a detail that has occasionally drawn scrutiny but was never seriously disputed by the expedition's leader. The climb established Aconcagua as the highest peak yet climbed outside the Himalayas, a distinction it still holds among the Andes.

Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal reached Annapurna's summit on 3 June 1950, making it the first mountain over 8,000 metres ever climbed, and remarkably on the expedition's very first attempt at the peak. No supplemental oxygen was used, a decision that made the achievement more dangerous but has never been repeated as a first ascent of any other peak in that height class.

The descent nearly killed both men: caught by darkness, they spent a night in a crevasse, and Herzog lost his gloves in the process. He lost all his toes and most of his fingers to frostbite, and Lachenal lost his toes as well, injuries treated with amputations performed in camp without proper anaesthetic.

Archdeacon Hudson Stuck organised the 1913 expedition partly to give his young Alaska Native companion, Walter Harper, the chance to be first to the summit, hoping it would earn wider respect for native Alaskans. Harper reached the top of Denali on 7 June 1913, becoming the first person confirmed to stand on North America's highest peak, with Stuck, Harry Karstens and Robert Tatum following shortly after.

The party had set out from Nenana months earlier, hauling supplies by dog sled before the technical climb even began, and relied on caribou meat hunted by a fourteen-year-old base camp manager to stay fed. Stuck's own account of the climb, published soon afterward, became the standard record of the ascent for decades.

An Italian expedition led by Ardito Desio placed Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni within reach of K2's summit in July 1954, after weeks of establishing camps up the mountain's Abruzzi Spur. The two men reached the top late in the day, running low on oxygen after a support climber had reportedly moved the cylinders they needed higher up the mountain than planned.

K2 stands only slightly lower than Everest but is widely considered the more dangerous climb, owing to steeper, more exposed terrain and consistently worse weather. Disputes over exactly what happened with the oxygen supply on the final push simmered among the expedition's members for decades, souring what should have been a shared national triumph.

Hans Meyer, a German geographer, had failed on two previous attempts to reach Kilimanjaro's summit, once turned back by deep snow and ice on the crater rim. On his third expedition in 1889, with the Austrian mountaineer Ludwig Purtscheller, he finally cut steps into the summit ice cap and reached the highest point in Africa.

Meyer named the summit Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze after the German emperor, a colonial-era title the peak carried for decades before reverting to Uhuru Peak after Tanzanian independence. The climb required no technical rope work, but its combination of altitude, tropical glaciers and long approach through several distinct climate zones made it a serious undertaking for its time.

Edward Whymper had attempted the Matterhorn's summit repeatedly by its harder Italian ridge before switching to the Swiss side, where his party finally succeeded in July 1865. Reaching the top made the Matterhorn the last of the Alps' great peaks to fall, closing what mountaineers had called the golden age of Alpine climbing.

The triumph turned to disaster on the descent, when a rope broke and four of the seven climbers fell to their deaths on the glacier below. Whymper survived to become one of the era's most famous mountaineers, but the accident, investigated publicly in Britain, also brought the first serious scrutiny of the risks the new sport was taking.

A Geneva scientist named Horace-Benedict de Saussure had offered a cash prize for the first successful climb of Mont Blanc, hoping to have scientific readings taken at its summit. Jacques Balmat, a local crystal hunter, and the doctor Michel Paccard claimed it in August 1786, reaching the top of western Europe's highest mountain after a route-finding effort that had defeated earlier attempts.

Their success is usually credited as the opening act of mountaineering as a sport, distinct from the earlier, purely scientific or religious motives for climbing. Disputes over who led the final push and who deserved the greater credit persisted between the two men for years afterward, a rivalry that outlived the climb itself.

An American Alpine Club expedition, flown in and supported by US Navy aircraft, put the first climbers on Vinson Massif's summit in December 1966, reaching the highest point on the Antarctic continent. The mountain's remoteness, deep in an unsupported interior range, had kept it unclimbed decades after most other continental high points had already fallen.

Ten climbers eventually reached the summit across the same expedition, a comparatively generous success rate made possible by good weather and modern logistical support rather than by any easy technical route. Vinson has since become one of the Seven Summits sought by mountaineers aiming to climb the highest peak on every continent.

André Citroen sent five specially built half tracks, fitted with rubber Kegresse tracks instead of ordinary wheels at the rear, south from Touggourt in Algeria toward Timbuktu in December 1922. Radio reports of the vehicles' progress across roughly 3,600 kilometres of desert were followed closely back in France, turning the expedition into a national publicity event.

Led by Georges-Marie Haardt and the Sahara specialist Louis Audouin-Dubreuil, the convoy completed the crossing in early 1923, proving a motor vehicle could cross terrain long thought passable only by camel caravan. The success helped establish Citroen's reputation for engineering endurance and opened the way for later, longer expeditions across Asia using the same half track design.

Eileen Saxon was fifteen months old and had tetralogy of Fallot, a heart defect that left her lips and fingers permanently blue from lack of oxygen. On 29 November 1944 at Johns Hopkins, surgeon Alfred Blalock rerouted an artery to send more blood to her lungs, a procedure designed with cardiologist Helen Taussig and built in the laboratory by Vivien Thomas, who stood behind Blalock coaching him through it.

The shunt worked, and Eileen's colour visibly changed on the operating table, though she died a few months later of an unrelated complication. The operation proved the idea sound, and the Blalock-Taussig shunt became the first reliable surgical treatment for a class of heart defects previously considered untouchable.

Khan Asparuh led his Bulgars across the Danube into Byzantine territory in the late 670s, settling among Slavic tribes already living there. When Emperor Constantine IV marched an army to drive them out in 680, the Bulgars beat it, and Byzantium signed a treaty the following year recognising Asparuh's state south of the river.

That treaty is the conventional founding date of the First Bulgarian Empire, one of the few states of the period whose borders Byzantium formally accepted rather than merely tolerated. Asparuh's small warrior aristocracy gradually merged with the far more numerous Slavic population it ruled, a fusion that produced the Bulgarian language and identity that followed.

The outbreak is traced to Jessore, near Calcutta, in 1817, spreading along the rivers and roads that carried British troops and traders across the subcontinent. It reached as far as the Caspian Sea and southern China before receding around 1824, the first time cholera had travelled so widely from its long-standing home in the Ganges delta.

Medicine at the time had no idea the disease spread through contaminated water, so quarantine and troop movement restrictions did little to slow it. Five more pandemics followed over the rest of the century, the sixth still running into the 1920s, and the germ theory that finally explained transmission only emerged from John Snow's work on a later outbreak in London.

A distillery on Staten Island, then part of Dutch New Netherland, began converting Caribbean molasses into rum around 1664, one of the first operations of its kind in the colonies. It sat at the end of a supply chain that already ran from sugar plantations worked by enslaved labour in the West Indies to distillers in the northern colonies who turned the leftover molasses into a cheap, exportable spirit.

Boston had its own distillery within a few years, and by the mid-1700s New England alone held well over a hundred of them, importing millions of gallons of molasses annually. Rum became a currency of its own in the slave trade, exchanged on the West African coast for the enslaved people who then produced the next season's sugar and molasses.

Four open-cockpit Douglas World Cruisers left Seattle on 6 April 1924, each named for an American city, aiming to fly around the globe by island-hopping across oceans with no radio and no weather forecasting to rely on. The Seattle crashed into an Alaskan mountainside in fog within the first month; its crew survived and walked out.

The Boston went down in the North Atlantic between the Faroes and Iceland after engine failure and was lost under tow. Only Chicago and New Orleans finished the full route, landing back in Seattle on 28 September 1924 after 175 days and roughly 27,000 miles. It was the first aerial circumnavigation of the world, flown by aviators who had never crossed the Pacific before attempting it.

Newcastle upon Tyne hosted a gathering of pointers and setters judged against a written standard rather than simply admired informally, an event now generally regarded as the first organised conformation dog show. Entry was limited to sporting breeds used in the field, reflecting dog shows' early roots in hunting culture.

The format, judging dogs against a breed ideal rather than racing or working them, spread quickly across Britain and inspired the founding of dedicated dog show societies within the following decade. It set the template that formal kennel clubs would later codify with written breed standards.

In September 1998, a surgical team in Lyon led by Jean-Michel Dubernard grafted a donor hand onto Clint Hallam, a New Zealander who had lost his own in a circular saw accident. It was the world's first hand transplant, requiring immunosuppressant drugs to stop the body rejecting skin, bone, tendon and nerve, not one graft of a single tissue type.

Hallam struggled with the demanding drug regimen and reportedly stopped taking his medication, and at his own request the hand was surgically removed in 2001. The operation nonetheless established that a transplanted hand could be kept alive and partially functional, and later recipients elsewhere kept theirs for years.

Before insects had wings, they had to solve a simpler problem: breathing air instead of water. The earliest known specimens, tiny wingless relatives of today's silverfish, are preserved in Scottish chert alongside some of the first plants tough enough to grow on dry land, in one of the oldest ecosystems ever found intact.

Wings would not appear for tens of millions of years afterward, so these first insects crawled rather than flew, feeding on early plant tissue and fungal spores in damp soil. Their fossils are rare and fragmentary, but they mark land itself becoming survivable for animal life, opening ground that no backboned creature had yet reached.

The Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition set out to cross Antarctica overland from one coast to the other, a route no one had completed, using tracked vehicles rather than dog teams for most of the distance. Vivian Fuchs led the main crossing party while a separate team under Edmund Hillary, fresh from Everest, laid supply depots ahead of them from the opposite side.

Fuchs's team completed the roughly 3,500 kilometre crossing via the South Pole in 1958, meeting Hillary's support party partway and finishing a route first attempted, and abandoned, by Ernest Shackleton four decades earlier. The expedition relied heavily on aircraft and radio for resupply, tools unavailable to any of the earlier polar expeditions it was consciously completing.

A Norwegian whaling ship, the Antarctic, put a small party ashore on the Antarctic mainland in January 1895, seeking new whaling and sealing grounds rather than scientific glory. Among those who stepped onto the rock at Cape Adare was Carsten Borchgrevink, a young Norwegian-born schoolteacher working the ship as a hand.

The landing was disputed for years afterward, since a rival claimant said he had gone ashore first, but Borchgrevink's account became the accepted record and later launched his own expedition to overwinter at the same spot. The visit itself was brief, little more than an hour, yet it was the first confirmed human contact with Antarctic land rather than its surrounding ice and sea.

Scotland's Exchequer Rolls for 1494 record eight bolls of malt handed to a Friar John Cor at Lindores Abbey in Fife, wherewith to make aqua vitae, the Latin term for distilled spirit that later became the everyday word whisky. Eight bolls was enough grain to produce a substantial quantity of spirit, which suggests distilling was already an established practice at the abbey rather than an experiment being tried for the first time.

The entry survives only because royal exchequers kept careful accounts of grain issued from crown stores, not because anyone thought to record the birth of an industry. Distilling itself had reached Scotland earlier through monastic knowledge of alchemy and medicine, and Lindores Abbey's own claim rests on this single bookkeeping line rather than any surviving barrel or bottle.

Six American women scientists, working under a National Science Foundation programme that had only recently begun admitting women to Antarctic research, flew together to the South Pole in November 1969. They stepped off the aircraft as a group deliberately, so that no single one of them could be singled out afterward as the first woman to arrive.

The gesture answered years of official policy that had barred women from Antarctic stations on the grounds that facilities and logistics could not accommodate them. Their arrival opened the pole itself, and the wider American Antarctic programme, to women researchers on the same basis as men for the first time.

No federation sanctioned the 1886 match between Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort. The two men, both already considered the strongest players alive, simply agreed between themselves to play a title match, and history backdated the winner as the first official world champion because nobody else had a better claim to it.

The match ran across three American cities, New York, St Louis and New Orleans, with the venue changing partway through, an arrangement that would be unthinkable for a championship today. Steinitz won decisively after trailing early, and the result held up in retrospect largely because Steinitz's positional style, built on holding a defensible structure rather than chasing quick attacks, reshaped how top players thought about the game.

General Electric introduced its fluorescent tube commercially in 1938, after years of development work that drew on decades of prior research into gas discharge lighting. A current passed through mercury vapour inside the tube produces ultraviolet light, which a phosphor coating on the glass converts into visible light, a far more efficient path than heating a filament.

The tubes used far less electricity for the same brightness than incandescent bulbs and ran far cooler, which made them attractive for factories, offices and shops almost immediately. Wartime demand for cheap, durable lighting in aircraft plants and shipyards accelerated their adoption, and by the 1950s fluorescent tubes lit most commercial interiors in the United States.

The clipper Flying Cloud left New York in 1851 bound for San Francisco, a route that meant rounding the storm-battered tip of South America at Cape Horn rather than any shorter passage, since the Panama Canal did not yet exist.

Captained by Josiah Perkins Creesy and navigated by his wife Eleanor, who plotted the course, the ship completed the voyage in under ninety days, a mark that stood for over a century until a yacht finally beat it in 1989. Clippers like her were built purely for speed, sacrificing cargo space to carry sail area no older merchant hull could handle.

France built Fort Ticonderoga, originally named Fort Carillon, in 1755 at the narrow strip of land connecting Lake Champlain and Lake George in its North American colonies, a chokepoint controlling movement between French Canada and the British colonies to the south.

Its star-shaped design, typical of European military engineering of the period, let defenders cover every approach with overlapping fire. The fort changed hands repeatedly over the following decades, most famously seized by Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys in a surprise raid at the start of the American Revolutionary War in 1775.

Lady Denman, wife of the Governor-General, read out the new city's name in March 1913 before the foundation stones were even laid, having opened a sealed envelope prepared for the ceremony. The site sat on a sheep station chosen after years of rivalry between Sydney and Melbourne, neither of which the new federation would let host the capital outright.

The American architect Walter Burley Griffin had not yet won the design competition for the city's layout when the stones went in; his winning plan, with its lakes and radiating avenues, arrived the following year. Canberra grew slowly from paddock to planned capital, and Parliament did not sit there until 1927.

Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken announced their proof in 1976 at the University of Illinois, ending a conjecture that had frustrated mathematicians for over a century since it was first posed about colouring political maps. Their method narrowed the infinite variety of possible maps down to 1,936 unavoidable configurations, then checked each one for a valid four-colour solution.

Checking those configurations by hand was not realistic, so the pair ran roughly 1,200 hours of computer time to grind through them, an approach some mathematicians initially refused to accept as a proof at all because no person could verify every step. It held up under later scrutiny and was one of the first major theorems whose proof a human being could not fully check unaided.

France began building the Maginot Line in 1930, naming it for the war minister who pushed the project through parliament, a chain of underground forts, gun emplacements and bunkers running along its border with Germany. It was designed to prevent a repeat of the trench devastation France had suffered in the First World War.

The line's defences were formidable where they were built, but they stopped short of the Belgian border, leaving a gap French planners assumed was protected by the Ardennes forest. In 1940, German forces went around the line entirely through that forest, making the fortifications, however strong, irrelevant to how the invasion actually unfolded.
