France used a decades-old diplomatic slight, an Ottoman-appointed dey striking the French consul with a fly whisk, as pretext for an invasion in 1830. A French fleet landed troops near Algiers and defeated the dey's forces within weeks.

The dey surrendered the city, ending three centuries in which Barbary rulers there had taxed and preyed on Mediterranean shipping. France's occupation was meant as a punitive strike but became the start of a colonial presence in Algeria that lasted until 1962.

Benjamin Franklin had already written newspaper pieces in Philadelphia urging better precautions against fire when he helped organise the Union Fire Company in 1736, drawing on a volunteer model he had read about in Boston. Members agreed to keep leather buckets, bags and tools ready at home and to turn out together whenever a fire broke out anywhere in the city.

The company's roughly thirty founding members pledged to help fight fires regardless of whose property was burning, a departure from the more informal, self-interested firefighting common at the time. Other volunteer companies soon followed Franklin's example across Philadelphia, and the model spread through the American colonies over the following decades.

France's royal storehouse, the Garde-Meuble in Paris, held the crown jewels in a building whose security had grown lax amid the political upheaval of 1792, with revolutionary crowds and street fighting distracting the authorities meant to guard it. Over several nights in September, thieves broke in and made off with a large share of the collection.

The haul reportedly ran to thousands of gems, including major diamonds, some later recovered abroad and others never traced. The theft happened within weeks of the monarchy's formal abolition, and the jewels' fate became entangled afterward with the political chaos of the new republic rather than any single clean investigation.

France launched Gloire in 1859 with a wooden hull clad in iron plate up to 120 millimetres thick, a response to shell guns that had made unarmoured wooden warships far more vulnerable than they used to be after demonstrations earlier in the decade.

The armour meant no wooden battle fleet, however large, could now trade fire with her safely. Britain, which had built its naval dominance on wooden ships of the line, saw the threat immediately and answered within a year with HMS Warrior, starting an ironclad arms race that made every existing battle fleet in the world obsolete almost overnight.

Year one began retroactively from the day the monarchy fell, 22 September 1792, and months took names from weather and harvest rather than saints: Brumaire for fog, Thermidor for heat, Vendemiaire for the grape harvest. Each month held three ten-day decades instead of four weeks, so Sunday and its rest day disappeared along with the church calendar it replaced.

The decimal clock divided each day into ten hours of a hundred minutes, and it lasted barely two years before clockmakers and habit defeated it. The calendar itself survived until Napoleon abolished it at the end of 1805, restoring the Gregorian year from 1 January 1806, by which point most of France had already gone back to counting Sundays.

Galileo is said to have first noticed a swinging lamp in Pisa cathedral and timed it against his own pulse, finding that it took the same time to complete a swing whether the arc was wide or narrow. Around 1602 he set out this principle of isochronism in a letter, describing pendulums of the same length as keeping the same beat regardless of how far they swung.

The claim is only approximately true and fails for wide swings, something later physics would correct, but the practical insight held well enough to matter. It gave clockmakers a way to regulate timekeeping far more precisely than existing mechanisms, and decades later Christiaan Huygens built the first working pendulum clock directly on the principle Galileo had described.

Evariste Galois died in a duel in 1832, aged twenty, having spent the night before writing frantic annotations on his mathematical papers in case he did not survive. He had already had one paper rejected as incomprehensible and another lost by the referee who took it home. For fourteen years his work on when polynomial equations can be solved by a formula sat unpublished and largely unread.

In 1846 Joseph Liouville, convinced of its value, edited and printed Galois' papers in the Journal de Mathematiques. They showed that the symmetries of an equation's roots form a structure, later called a group, and that the general equation of the fifth degree has no such formula because its group is too tangled. Group theory built on that idea now underlies much of modern algebra and physics.

George Gamow left Stalin's Soviet Union in 1933 by defecting during a physics conference abroad, and by 1946 he was applying nuclear physics he had studied to the universe's first moments. He argued that an expanding cosmos must once have been compressed hot enough for nuclear reactions to fuse hydrogen into helium in the first minutes after the beginning.

With his student Ralph Alpher, and a joke credit given to Hans Bethe, Gamow's calculations predicted a faint afterglow of radiation that should still be detectable, cooled by billions of years of expansion. That prediction sat mostly ignored until 1965, when two Bell Labs engineers stumbled on exactly that radiation while trying to track down noise in a radio antenna.

Indira Gandhi, daughter of India's first prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru but no relation to Mohandas Gandhi, took office in January 1966 after Lal Bahadur Shastri's sudden death. Congress Party leaders reportedly saw her as a figure they could control, an assessment that did not hold for long.

She went on to dominate Indian politics for most of the next two decades, including the 1975 to 1977 Emergency, during which she suspended civil liberties and jailed opponents. She was assassinated by her own bodyguards in 1984, in retaliation for a military operation she had ordered against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple.

Pedro de Mendoza had founded a settlement at the mouth of the Rio de la Plata in 1536, but Indigenous resistance and starvation forced the Spanish to abandon it within years, and the site sat empty for decades. Juan de Garay marched settlers south from Asuncion in 1580 to try the same river mouth again.

Garay's second attempt survived where Mendoza's had not, partly because he brought cattle and settlers experienced in the region rather than an expedition equipped for conquest alone. Those first cattle, left to breed on the open pampas, later underpinned the beef trade that made Buenos Aires one of the wealthiest cities in the Americas.

Two men in police uniforms buzzed the night entrance of Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in March 1990, told the guards they were responding to a disturbance, and handcuffed both of them in the basement. Over the next eighty-one minutes they cut thirteen works, including a Vermeer and three Rembrandts, from their frames.

Empty frames still hang on the museum's walls where the paintings once were, honouring a condition of Gardner's will that the collection never be rearranged. The FBI has said it believes it knows which criminal organisation was responsible, but no art has surfaced and no one has ever been charged over a theft valued at roughly half a billion dollars.

Andre-Jacques Garnerin had been a prisoner of war for three years in Hungary, reportedly spending part of that time designing an escape by parachute he never got to use. On 22 October 1797 he tested the idea over Paris, ascending in a hydrogen balloon and cutting himself loose at around 900 metres.

His basket swung violently under the unvented silk canopy on the way down, but he landed without serious injury in a field outside the city. It is generally treated as the first descent by parachute from that height, and Garnerin went on to make further jumps across Europe, including one over London a few years later.

A force of Senone Gauls under a chieftain named Brennus defeated a Roman army at the Allia river around 390 BCE and marched on the poorly defended city itself, one of the few times before the empire's fall that an enemy army occupied Rome.

Most Romans fled or held out on the Capitoline Hill, and later legend claimed sacred geese woke the defenders during a night attack. Roman accounts say the Gauls eventually agreed to withdraw for a payment of gold, weighed out on scales the Romans complained had been rigged against them.

Gauss was twenty-four when Disquisitiones Arithmeticae appeared in 1801, written in Latin and dense enough that few contemporaries could follow it in full. It gathered scattered results from Fermat, Euler and Lagrange into one structure and gave the field a notation, writing a is congruent to b modulo n, that every later number theorist simply adopted rather than replaced.

The book proved the law of quadratic reciprocity, which Gauss called the golden theorem and had already spent a year finding a rigorous proof for, and it worked out which regular polygons could be constructed with compass and straightedge, settling a question open since antiquity. Number theory as a distinct discipline is usually dated from this one volume.

James Weatherby, the official record-keeper for English racing, compiled a registry tracing the pedigree of every listed thoroughbred back through recorded sires and dams, aiming to fix which horses counted as authentic racing stock. Publication turned an informal, often disputed set of claims about bloodlines into a single agreed record.

Nearly every thoroughbred alive today traces its male line back to just three imported stallions named in the book's early volumes, a concentration the registry itself made visible and, in effect, permanent. The General Stud Book is still maintained and remains the model for pedigree registries in other breeds and species.

France's defeat at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954 forced it to negotiate an end to eight years of colonial war in Indochina. The Geneva Accords, signed that July, split Vietnam at the seventeenth parallel into a communist north under Ho Chi Minh and a non communist south, meant as a temporary military line rather than a permanent border.

Nationwide elections to reunify the country, promised for 1956, never took place: the southern government and the United States refused to sign the accords' final declaration. The temporary line hardened into the border of a war that would draw in American forces within a decade.

In 1616 the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence accepted Artemisia Gentileschi into its membership, a body that had never before enrolled a woman in her own right rather than as an artist's wife or daughter. Membership let her sign contracts and buy materials without a male guardian's approval, a practical freedom most women painters of the period lacked.

She had moved to Florence the year before, following a Rome trial in which she testified against the painter Agostino Tassi over an assault, testimony given under judicial torture to test her honesty. Her Florentine years produced some of her best-known work, including versions of Judith beheading Holofernes painted for the Medici court.

Queen Anne died in August 1714 without a surviving child, and under the Act of Settlement of 1701 the crown could not pass to any Catholic, which ruled out more than fifty people with a closer blood claim than the man who actually inherited it. George, Elector of Hanover and a great-grandson of James I through a Protestant line, became George I of Great Britain and Ireland instead.

He arrived from Germany speaking little English and kept his attention largely on Hanoverian affairs, leaving day-to-day government to his ministers. Robert Walpole rose under him and by 1721 was governing in the king's name, generally reckoned Britain's first prime minister. The House of Hanover he founded held the British throne for nearly two centuries.

George III came to the throne on 25 October 1760 at twenty two, on his grandfather's sudden death, and was the first Hanoverian monarch born and raised in England rather than Germany. He spoke English as his first language and made a point of it in his opening address to Parliament, breaking with two reigns of noticeably German kings.

His sixty year reign, the longest of any English king to that point, spanned the loss of the American colonies, war against Napoleon, and his own recurring bouts of mental illness, now generally attributed to a hereditary blood disorder rather than the madness his contemporaries assumed. His son ruled as regent for the last decade of his life.

King George V travelled to India in 1911 for the Delhi Durbar, a ceremony staged to display imperial pageantry to hundreds of thousands of spectators and Indian princes gathered on a specially built plain outside the old city. At its climax he announced that the capital of British India would move from Calcutta to Delhi.

Calcutta had grown unwieldy and its Bengali politics increasingly hostile to colonial rule, while Delhi carried older associations with Mughal imperial authority that the British hoped to inherit visually. Construction of New Delhi, designed largely by architect Edwin Lutyens, took two decades and was not formally inaugurated until 1931.

Germany did not choose gold out of monetary theory. France paid a five-billion-franc war indemnity after its 1871 defeat, largely in gold, and the new German Empire used the windfall to fund a currency reform it had already been planning, replacing a patchwork of regional silver talers and guilders with a single gold-backed mark from 1873.

The reform came with a side effect nobody had priced in: Germany's demonetised silver flooded onto world markets just as other countries were reconsidering silver too, helping drag its price down for a generation. Britain, already on gold, gained company. Within a decade most of Europe had followed Germany onto the same standard.

From 1942, Germany constructed thousands of bunkers, gun batteries and obstacles along the coastline of occupied Europe, from Norway to the Spanish border, intended to defeat any Allied invasion at the water's edge. Adolf Hitler ordered the project after commando raids showed the coast was vulnerable to attack from the sea.

The defences were strongest around the Pas-de-Calais, where German planners expected the main invasion to land, and comparatively thin around Normandy. When Allied forces landed there in June 1944, the wall slowed but did not stop them, and its uneven strength across hundreds of miles of coastline proved decisive.

Giselle premiered at the Paris Opera in June 1841, telling of a peasant girl who dies of a broken heart after learning her suitor is secretly a nobleman engaged to someone else, then returns as a spirit who protects him from vengeful ghosts of other jilted women.

Its choreography, built around the contrast between a lively village first act and an ethereal, otherworldly second act, became a structural model widely imitated afterward. Giselle has remained continuously in the ballet repertoire since its premiere, longer than almost any other work from the period.

Kurt Godel was twenty-five and working in Vienna when he published his incompleteness theorems in 1931, aimed squarely at a project David Hilbert had set for mathematics: prove that arithmetic could be built on a fixed set of axioms strong enough to settle every true statement, with no contradictions.

Godel showed this was impossible. Any consistent system rich enough to describe arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove from within its own axioms, and the system cannot prove its own consistency either. The result did not stop mathematicians working, but it closed off Hilbert's programme for good and reshaped what a proof could be asked to guarantee.

After his mother Helena travelled to Jerusalem, Constantine ordered a temple to Jupiter, or in some accounts to Venus, torn down on a site local Christians had long identified as Golgotha. Workers digging beneath it uncovered a rock-cut tomb that Bishop Eusebius, writing at the time, described as the burial place venerated as Christ's.

Constantine had the surrounding rock cut away to leave the tomb standing free, and built the Church of the Holy Sepulchre around it, completed around 335 CE. Almost nothing of that first Constantinian church survives after later destructions and rebuildings, but the site itself has been continuously venerated and fought over ever since.

Google Earth grew out of a program called EarthViewer 3D, built by a company called Keyhole that Google bought in 2004. The software stitched together satellite photographs and aerial imagery over a rotating three-dimensional globe, and Google released it free to the public in June 2005, letting anyone zoom from orbit down to street-level rooftops.

The tool had been built for intelligence and defence work, and its name nodded to the Keyhole spy satellite program, but the free release opened the same imagery to journalists tracking troop movements, archaeologists spotting buried structures from above, and ordinary users looking up their own house for the first time from space.

Gorm is the earliest Danish king named in a source contemporary with his own reign rather than written generations later, which is why historians treat him, ruling from around 936, as the first Danish monarch who can be placed with any confidence rather than a legendary figure.

He ruled from Jelling in Jutland, where he raised a burial mound and the older of the two Jelling runestones, carved by his son Harald Bluetooth in his memory. The present Danish monarchy still traces its line back to Gorm without a break, which makes it, by that reckoning, the oldest continuous monarchy in Europe.

The United States Air Force declared the Global Positioning System fully operational on 17 July 1995, once 24 satellites were in place across six orbital planes, enough for a receiver anywhere on the ground to see at least four at once at all times. Earlier satellites had already let the system work intermittently since the late 1980s, but full coverage removed the gaps.

The constellation had been built chiefly for military navigation and precision weapons targeting, and civilian receivers were deliberately fed a degraded signal under a policy called Selective Availability. That restriction was switched off in 2000 on presidential order, sharpening civilian accuracy from roughly 100 metres to about 10, and opening the door to the everyday car and phone navigation that followed.

Grace O'Malley, an Irish chieftain who had led her clan's ships in raiding and trade for decades, sailed to England in 1593 after English forces seized two of her sons and her half brother. Rather than send another petition, she travelled to Greenwich to argue her case to Elizabeth I directly, the two speaking through interpreters since neither shared the other's language.

She had already answered a formal set of written questions from Elizabeth's officials before the meeting took place, so the encounter was the conclusion of months of negotiation rather than a sudden appearance. Elizabeth granted most of what O'Malley asked, on condition she cease raiding against the crown, though no transcript of their conversation survives to confirm the details later writers supplied.

The Graf Zeppelin was built to carry paying passengers rather than to set records, but in August 1929 it set out from Lakehurst, New Jersey, to circle the globe with a crew and a handful of journalists aboard, funded largely by newspaper publisher William Randolph Hearst. It crossed Europe to Friedrichshafen, then flew nonstop across Siberia to Tokyo, a leg of over 6,000 miles with no landing possible along most of it.

From Japan it crossed the Pacific to Los Angeles and continued back across the United States to Lakehurst, completing the circuit in just over three weeks of actual flying time spread across about twenty-one days. Passengers dined at set tables and slept in cabins while the ground below scrolled past for days at a stretch, a way of crossing the world that no aircraft would offer again.

Frederick Graff worked as chief engineer of the Philadelphia Waterworks, a system built to supply the city's homes through underground pipes rather than open wells or cisterns. In 1801, as that network expanded, he devised a hydrant that stood upright above ground and connected directly to the water main below.

Earlier hydrant designs had left the valve mechanism buried or awkward to reach, slowing a brigade trying to connect hoses in an emergency. Graff's post design let firefighters attach hoses quickly at street level, and variations on its basic shape, a valve housed in an above-ground post over a buried main, remain the standard fire hydrant form in American cities today.

Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, working at the University of Manchester, used ordinary sticky tape to peel flakes off a block of graphite, the material in a pencil, then pressed the tape together and pulled it apart repeatedly to thin the flakes further. Some ended up only one atom thick, a sheet of carbon arranged in a honeycomb lattice that nobody had isolated and tested before.

Graphene turned out to conduct electricity better than copper, hold more strength for its weight than steel, and remain flexible, properties that had mostly been predicted on paper. The two shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics, and the tape-and-graphite method, dubbed exfoliation, is still taught as an entry point into two-dimensional materials research.

A run of unusually cold, wet summers between 1695 and 1697 ruined successive grain harvests across Sweden, Finland and the Baltic provinces of Estonia and Livonia, a region already close to the limits of what its short growing season could reliably support. Grain reserves that might have cushioned one bad year could not absorb three in a row.

Roughly a fifth of the population across the affected Baltic lands is estimated to have died, with Finland hit especially hard as both crops and livestock failed together. The famine weakened Sweden's Baltic empire at the very moment rival powers were preparing to challenge it, feeding directly into the instability that helped trigger the Great Northern War only a few years later.

Antoine Rossignol and his son Bonaventure built their cipher for Louis XIV's most sensitive correspondence around 1650, using numbers to stand for whole French syllables rather than single letters, with some numbers assigned to cancel the syllable before them. That trick alone defeated the usual frequency-counting attacks that broke ordinary substitution ciphers of the age.

When the Rossignols died, nobody who knew the system remained, and encoded despatches sat unread in French archives for two centuries. Army cryptographer Etienne Bazeries spent three years on it and cracked the syllable structure around 1893, finally reading letters that included the identity of a long-rumoured masked prisoner, the Man in the Iron Mask.

The clock above the new Palace of Westminster, rebuilt after the 1834 fire that destroyed most of the old Houses of Parliament, was designed to unusually strict standards: lawyer and clockmaker Edmund Beckett Denison insisted it strike the first stroke of each hour accurate to within a second. Astronomer Royal George Airy backed the demand, and it took engineer Edward Dent years to build a mechanism that could meet it.

The clock began keeping time in 1859, and its bell, cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry and officially named the Great Bell, quickly picked up the nickname Big Ben, later applied loosely to the whole tower. The tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower only in 2012, for the queen's diamond jubilee.

The Sabaean kingdom of southern Arabia, in what is now Yemen, built a great earthen dam across the Wadi Adhanah near Marib around 750 BCE, using it to divert seasonal floodwaters into a network of irrigation channels rather than to hold a permanent reservoir.

The dam sustained a large oasis for many centuries, supporting agriculture that helped Marib grow into a major trading city on incense routes. Its final collapse around the sixth century, after repeated repairs, is remembered in Arabian tradition as a disaster significant enough to be cited in the Quran as a warning against ingratitude.

By the mid 1540s Henry VIII had spent through the wealth seized from the monasteries and was still fighting wars in France and Scotland. The mints began replacing silver in the coinage with copper, dropping the fineness of the shilling from around 92 per cent silver toward a fraction of that, while keeping the coin's face value and stamped weight unchanged.

Silver-plated copper wore through fastest at the king's own nose on the coin's profile, earning Henry the nickname Old Coppernose. Prices rose sharply as merchants adjusted for the debased metal, and the mess took until 1560, under Elizabeth I, to unwind through a formal recoinage that withdrew the bad silver from circulation.

The monsoon failed across southern and western India in 1876, and the drought that followed coincided with a strong El Nino event now understood to have disrupted rainfall across much of the tropics that year. Colonial administrators kept grain exports moving from Madras and Bombay even as local prices climbed beyond what labourers could pay.

Relief was organised around a policy of minimal intervention, on the theory that free markets and limited public works would correct the shortage without distorting prices. Estimates of the dead run from several hundred thousand to well over five million across the famine's spread into 1878, and the scale of it prompted the inquiry that produced India's first formal famine code.

The Nile's annual flood failed in consecutive years around 1200, a rare event for a civilisation entirely dependent on the river's seasonal rise to irrigate its fields. Grain prices in Cairo rose to levels ordinary households could not meet, and the physician Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi recorded the famine in detailed, harrowing accounts written from the city itself.

Al-Baghdadi's writings describe corpses left unburied in the streets and instances of cannibalism driven by starvation, testimony historians treat as broadly credible given his standing as a trained physician present in the city. The Ayyubid state, then ruling Egypt after Saladin, struggled to organise relief, and the death toll is estimated to have reached hundreds of thousands across the country.

Two consecutive poor harvests in 1693 and 1694, worsened by an unusually cold, wet growing season, sent French grain prices to levels far beyond what ordinary households could afford. The crisis struck near the end of Louis XIV's long and costly reign, when years of war spending had already strained the crown's ability to organise relief or import grain from abroad.

Roughly two million people are estimated to have died across France, a toll comparable in scale to the plague outbreaks of earlier centuries, though caused entirely by weather and administrative failure rather than disease. The famine weakened the kingdom's finances and manpower on the eve of further wars, contributing to a broader sense of crisis that shadowed the final decades of Louis XIV's rule.

A fire that broke out in October 1728 burned through Copenhagen for roughly three days, spreading through narrow streets of timber-framed houses faster than the city's limited firefighting resources could contain. It consumed a large share of the medieval city centre, including much of the university district.

The University of Copenhagen's library, one of the largest in northern Europe at the time, was destroyed along with its collection of manuscripts and books. The rebuilding that followed widened several streets and introduced stricter rules on building materials, part of a broader shift toward brick construction in the Danish capital.

A fire broke out in a cigar warehouse in Hamburg in May 1842 and burned for roughly four days, spreading through the old city's tightly packed streets before firefighters, hampered by a shortage of water and inadequate equipment, managed to contain it. It destroyed a large part of the historic centre, including several churches.

Around 20,000 people were left homeless by the fire, and the city used the disaster as an opportunity to rebuild with wider streets, a modern sewer system and improved water supply. The rebuilt Hamburg that emerged over the following years looked markedly different from the medieval town that had burned.

The fire that swept Edo over three days in March 1657 is popularly traced to a Buddhist priest burning a cursed kimono that had allegedly killed three teenage owners in succession, though the story is likely legend layered onto a more mundane blaze that spread fast through a city built almost entirely of wood and paper.

Strong winds carried the flames across most of Edo, destroying Edo Castle's main keep along with hundreds of temples and shrines. Estimates of the dead range widely, with many modern accounts putting the toll above 100,000 in a city of roughly 300,000, making it one of the deadliest urban fires on record. The disaster prompted the shogunate to widen streets and create firebreaks in the rebuilt city.

On the night of 15 May 1855, gold bullion and coin worth about twelve thousand pounds vanished from locked safes aboard a South Eastern Railway mail train running from London Bridge to Folkestone for shipment to Paris. When the safes were opened at their destination, they contained lead shot instead of gold.

The plot was organised by Edward Agar and William Pierce, aided by two railway employees who took wax impressions of the safe keys and had copies cut. The gang swapped the gold for shot during the journey itself, and the theft went undetected for months until a falling-out among the conspirators exposed the scheme, by which point most of the gold had already been sold off.

The engineer Cornelius Vermuyden, a Dutchman brought in for his experience reclaiming land at home, cut the New Bedford River alongside the Old Bedford River he had already built decades earlier, giving the Great Ouse a straighter, faster route to the sea. The works were declared complete in 1652, opening roughly 40,000 acres of former marsh to farming.

Local fen dwellers, who had fished and grazed the wetland for generations, resisted the drainage and sabotaged the new banks more than once during construction. Even after 1652 the reclaimed land kept subsiding as the drained peat dried and shrank, so the fens needed further pumping and repair for generations afterward.

France adopted the Great Paris Cipher at the end of 1811, a table of roughly 1,400 numbers standing for letters, syllables and whole words, meant to defeat exactly the kind of interception Wellington relied on. Major George Scovell built up a stack of captured despatches through 1812, using the fragments of plain French that crept into supposedly coded letters to work back toward the substitutions.

The breakthrough came in December 1812, when Scovell decrypted a letter from Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother and the nominal king of Spain, that laid out French troop movements in enough detail to shape Wellington's own planning. Scovell kept working the cipher through the war's final campaigns, and his notebooks survive in the National Archives.

The fire that destroyed Seattle's business district in June 1889 began in a basement cabinet shop, where a worker named John Back had been heating a pot of glue on a stove fed by turpentine-soaked wood shavings. When the glue caught fire, he threw water on it, scattering burning glue and igniting the wood-frame building around him.

Dry weather and a stiff wind carried the fire through some 64 acres of downtown Seattle before it burned out, destroying the wharves and most of the business core. No one died in the fire, and the city used the disaster to rebuild in brick and stone, raising street levels above the old tideflat in the process.

Displaced from Rhodes decades earlier, the Knights Hospitaller had rebuilt their order on Malta, and in May 1565 an Ottoman fleet estimated at close to 200 ships landed a large invasion force intending to take the island and its fortified harbour.

Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette led a garrison heavily outnumbered but well fortified, holding key positions through months of bombardment and assault before a relief force from Sicily arrived in September. The Ottoman withdrawal, with heavy losses, was seen across Christian Europe as a rare check on Ottoman expansion, and Valette founded the city of Valletta soon after.

A gang of around fifteen men ambushed the Glasgow to London mail train at Bridego Bridge in Buckinghamshire in August 1963, having rigged a signal to show red and stop the train in open countryside. Armed with coshes, they overpowered the crew and unloaded 120 mailbags packed with used banknotes.

The haul came to around two and a half million pounds, worth tens of millions today, most of it never recovered. The gang's hideout at a nearby farm yielded fingerprints that led to swift arrests, and long prison sentences followed, though escapes by Ronnie Biggs and Charlie Wilson kept the case in headlines for years afterward.

William Lambton began the survey in 1802 under the East India Company, dragging a half-ton theodolite across southern India to chain a continuous line of triangles from Cape Comorin northward. He called the project the Great Indian Arc of the Meridian, aiming simply to fix the exact curvature of the Earth along one long north-south line.

The survey outlived Lambton, who died in the field in 1823, and ran under his successor George Everest for decades more before reaching the Himalayan foothills around 1841. It was there that surveyors, working from triangulated distances rather than direct measurement, calculated the height of a peak later named Everest after him, though he himself never saw it.

At a Greek symposium, wine was never drunk neat. It was mixed with water in a large krater, typically at ratios weighted toward water, and ladled out to guests reclining on couches, since drinking wine unmixed was considered a habit of barbarians rather than civilised men.

A symposiarch set the mixing ratio and paced the evening's toasts, while poetry, riddles and music filled the gaps between rounds of drinking. The practice, attested from around 600 BCE onward in Greek pottery and poetry, treated drunkenness as something to be managed by convention rather than avoided outright.

A trireme carried around 170 rowers arranged in three tiers, each pulling a single oar, which needed exact timing to avoid tangling the blades of the man above or below. Crews trained for months before a ship could row in formation, and the coordination itself became a form of naval power that few states could afford to maintain.

The design's whole purpose was the bronze ram fixed at the waterline: a trireme aimed to punch a hole below an enemy hull rather than board it. Athens built the largest fleet of them in the fifth century BCE, funding it from silver mines, and used it to hold an empire together across the Aegean.

The Julian calendar overcounted the year by about 11 minutes, which by 1582 had pushed the spring equinox ten days out of line with the calendar date used to fix Easter. Pope Gregory XIII's bull Inter Gravissimas ordered ten days struck from October that year, so 4 October was followed directly by 15 October in the countries that adopted it immediately.

The reform also changed which century years count as leap years, dropping three leap days every four centuries so the calendar and the solar year would stay aligned far longer. Catholic states adopted it at once, but Protestant and Orthodox states held out for generations. Britain and its colonies did not switch until 1752, and Russia waited until 1918.

William Grey Walter was a neurologist at the Burden Neurological Institute in Bristol, studying brainwaves with EEG machines, when he built two small three-wheeled robots between 1948 and 1949 to test how few components could produce lifelike behaviour. He named them Elmer and Elsie, acronyms built loosely around electro-mechanical robot and light sensitivity.

Each had a single photocell and a touch sensor wired to two motors, giving it just two working nerve cells, yet the tortoises wandered rooms, steered toward dim light while avoiding glare, and nosed their way back to a hutch to recharge when their batteries ran low. Walter used them to argue that complex behaviour did not require a complex nervous system, an early and influential claim of the new field of cybernetics.

British merchants began importing bird droppings from islands off the Peruvian coast in 1840, after chemists identified the nitrogen and phosphate rich deposits, built up over centuries by seabird colonies in an almost rainless climate, as a powerful fertiliser for depleted European farmland. What had been dismissed as waste became one of the century's most valuable exports almost overnight.

Peru's government made guano a state monopoly and used the revenue to fund railways and public debt, while labourers, many of them indentured Chinese workers, mined the deposits under brutal conditions on the islands. The trade transformed European crop yields for several decades before the richest deposits were exhausted and cheaper synthetic fertilisers replaced it entirely.

Arthur Guinness took over the disused St James's Gate brewery in Dublin on 31 December 1759 on a lease running nine thousand years at an annual rent of 45 pounds, terms generous enough that the brewery still occupies the site under a version of that same agreement today, long after the figure became a marketing story in its own right.

Guinness brewed ale at first and only later switched the site over to the dark porter that made the name famous, a style he had already brewed elsewhere in Dublin. The nine thousand years have outlasted the Georgian city around the gate, several changes of Irish government and the brewery's own growth into a multinational company.

Divers off Bahrain and the wider Persian Gulf worked oyster beds on a single held breath, weighted by a stone tied to one foot and guided down by a rope, surfacing after roughly a minute with a net of shells. Assyrian and Indian traders bought the pearls, a trade attested by the eighth century BCE and likely older still.

The diving season ran through the hot summer months, and divers worked in teams from small boats, splitting the season's haul with the boat's owner under customary shares that persisted into the twentieth century. Cultured pearls from Japan collapsed this economy in the 1930s, ending a livelihood the Gulf had kept for centuries.

Gustav Vasa had spent the previous years leading a rebellion against Danish rule that began among the miners and farmers of Dalarna, after Christian II of Denmark executed dozens of Swedish nobles and clergy in the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520. By the time he was elected king at Strangnas on 6 June 1523, Stockholm itself was about to fall to his forces.

His election ended the Kalmar Union, which had bound Sweden, Denmark and Norway under one crown since 1397, and Denmark formally recognised Swedish independence within weeks. Gustav went on to break the church's landholdings and pass the crown to his own descendants, turning a wartime election into the founding reign of an independent Swedish state.

King Gustav Vasa of Sweden wanted a trading town that could compete directly with the Hanseatic city of Reval, now Tallinn, across the Gulf of Finland. In 1550 he ordered merchants from several existing Finnish towns to relocate to a new site at the mouth of the Vantaa river, founding what he intended as a rival port.

The location proved poorly chosen: the harbour silted and shipping never rivalled Reval's, and the town stayed a minor backwater for two centuries. Helsinki only grew into a major city after Russia annexed Finland in 1809 and later moved the capital there from Turku, long after Vasa's original commercial ambitions for it had failed.

At the 1996 International AIDS Conference in Vancouver, researchers including David Ho presented results showing that combining a protease inhibitor with two older antiretroviral drugs could drive HIV to undetectable levels in the blood. Any one of the drugs alone let the virus mutate around it within weeks; three together closed off that escape route.

Death rates from AIDS in the United States fell sharply within a couple of years of the therapy reaching clinics, and obituary pages that had listed young men by the column shrank. The drugs were expensive and demanding, dozens of pills on a strict schedule, and for years reached wealthy countries long before they reached the parts of Africa where the epidemic was worst.

Hair transferred to Broadway in April 1968 after runs off-Broadway and in Los Angeles, its story of countercultural young people resisting the Vietnam War draft set to a rock score, a genre Broadway had largely kept off its stages in favour of traditional show tunes.

The production included nudity, drug references and a cast that mixed races and genders in ways then unusual for a mainstream Broadway house, drawing both controversy and enormous ticket sales. Its success opened Broadway to rock and pop scores that later shows would build on.

John Scott Haldane approached diving sickness as a plumbing problem rather than a mysterious ailment. Divers surfacing quickly from depth were falling ill and sometimes dying because nitrogen, dissolved in their blood under pressure, formed bubbles as that pressure dropped, and his 1908 study set out to work out how slowly a diver had to rise to let the gas leave the body without bubbling.

Haldane's tables, produced with the Royal Navy, prescribed a series of stops at set depths on the way up rather than a single steady ascent, giving tissues time to release nitrogen gradually. Staged decompression, refined many times since, remains the basic method divers use to avoid decompression sickness, still generally known by its old nickname, the bends.

Edmond Halley is remembered for the comet, but in 1690 he was also building diving equipment, an open-bottomed bell weighted with lead and supplied by a second, smaller weighted barrel lowered from the surface. Water pressure forced fresh air from the barrel up into the bell as it was drawn level with the opening, letting a diver breathe without ever surfacing.

In a demonstration in the Thames, Halley and several companions sat inside the bell at a depth of about 60 feet for over an hour and a half, and he later extended dives to more than four hours with refinements. The bell proved too heavy and cumbersome for real salvage work, but it showed that a supplied air pocket, rather than held breath, was the way to keep divers down.

Operation Gomorrah, a series of British and American bombing raids on Hamburg in late July 1943, produced a firestorm on its second night after successive waves of incendiaries ignited fires across a densely built residential district. The heat generated winds strong enough to uproot trees and pull people into the flames.

Estimates of the dead vary by source, with figures commonly cited between roughly 34,000 and over 40,000, most killed by asphyxiation or extreme heat rather than the bombs themselves. The scale shocked planners on both sides, and Hamburg's firestorm became a reference point for later debates over the ethics and effectiveness of area bombing.

Hamilton opened on Broadway in August 2015 after an acclaimed off-Broadway run earlier that year, retelling the life of American founding father Alexander Hamilton through a hip hop and R&B score written and originally performed in the title role by Lin-Manuel Miranda.

The show cast actors of colour as the Founding Fathers and framed Hamilton's rise from an orphaned immigrant to treasury secretary and his fatal duel with Aaron Burr as an immigrant's story. It won eleven Tony Awards and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and tickets remained among the hardest to obtain on Broadway for years.

William Rowan Hamilton had spent years trying to extend complex numbers into three dimensions, to describe rotations in space with a single algebra, and kept failing because a three-term system would not multiply consistently. Walking with his wife along the Royal Canal in Dublin on 16 October 1843, he suddenly saw that four terms, not three, would work if he let multiplication stop being commutative.

Unable to find paper, he carved the founding formula, i squared equals j squared equals k squared equals ijk equals minus one, into the stone of Broom Bridge. A plaque there still marks the spot. Quaternions never replaced ordinary vectors for most physics, but they survive today inside the software that rotates objects in video games and spacecraft without the errors ordinary rotation matrices accumulate.

The rule usually retold as a ban on watering down beer is something narrower. Law 108 of Hammurabi's code, cut into diorite around 1750 BCE, targeted tavern keepers who took payment in silver rather than grain and shortchanged the customer on the price. Beer was rationed and traded in fixed grain measures, so a mismatch was easy to prove, and the law punished it by drowning.

Other clauses in the same code fixed how much beer a labourer, a temple worker or a child was owed as a ration, because beer was a barley staple rather than a luxury. The keepers named in these laws were usually women, running the alehouses that were Babylon's ordinary drinking houses, open to the same scrutiny as any bread or grain seller.

The law code of the Babylonian king Hammurabi, inscribed on a stone stele around 1754 BCE, sets out fees a surgeon could charge for operating on a patient with a bronze lancet, scaled by the patient's social rank. A successful operation on a free man's eye earned a fixed payment in silver.

The penalties were as precise as the fees: if the patient was a noble and died, or lost the use of an eye, the surgeon's hand was to be cut off. The code did not distinguish negligence from a poor outcome, tying a surgeon's own body directly to the risk taken on by every patient he treated.

Earlier North Sea cargo boats were open or shallow craft rowed and steered with a side oar. The cog changed both: a single square sail on a tall mast for power, a flat bottom that could sit upright on a tidal beach to load and unload, and a rudder hinged on the sternpost for tighter steering than a side oar allowed.

Hanseatic merchant cities adopted the design through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries to move bulk cargo, timber, grain, wax and cloth, between Baltic and North Sea ports. Its high, straight sides also made it easy to fortify with fighting platforms, so the same hull could double as a warship when a Hanseatic city needed one.

Kamala Harris was a United States senator from California and a former state attorney general when Joe Biden chose her as his running mate in 2020, and their ticket won that November's election. She was inaugurated vice president on 20 January 2021.

The role made her the first woman, and the first Black and South Asian American, to hold the office. She presided over the Senate as its constitutional tie-breaking vote more often than most modern vice presidents, reflecting how narrowly divided the chamber was during her term.

The Massachusetts Bay Colony's General Court voted in 1636 to found a college, only sixteen years after the Mayflower landed, chiefly to train ministers for a Puritan settlement anxious not to leave learning behind in England.

It was renamed two years later for John Harvard, a young minister who left it his library of some four hundred books and half his estate when he died of tuberculosis at twenty-nine. No older institution of higher learning existed anywhere in the American colonies.

Hatshepsut began as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, a conventional enough role for a royal widow. Within a few years of his accession, around 1473 BCE, she took the unusual step of assuming full pharaonic titles herself, having her monuments show her with the ceremonial false beard and regalia of a king rather than a queen consort.

She justified the move partly through claims of divine birth, carved at her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, and ruled for roughly two decades overseeing major building projects and trade expeditions to Punt. Decades after her death, many of her images were defaced or removed, though the reasons and timing remain debated among Egyptologists.

Hatshepsut began as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III but within a few years was carved into temple reliefs with the full titulary of a reigning pharaoh, including the false beard worn in royal statuary. Her rule lasted roughly two decades and was marked by extensive building, including the terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari.

Later in the dynasty, many of her monuments were defaced or her name chiselled out, a campaign long read as an act of revenge by Thutmose III but now more often explained as an attempt to smooth the succession's legitimacy rather than personal spite. Egyptologists only reconstructed the full sequence of her reign from surviving inscriptions in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

Over the Easter bank holiday weekend of April 2015, a crew of burglars in their sixties and seventies, using a heavy drill to bore through a concrete wall, broke into the underground vault of Hatton Garden Safe Deposit in London's jewellery quarter and forced open dozens of boxes.

The gang, led by veteran thief Brian Reader, got away with jewellery and valuables estimated at up to 200 million pounds before a faulty alarm delayed any police response. Several members were later caught after being recorded discussing the job, and most of the loot was traced and seized, though some was never found.

In a 1974 paper in Nature, Stephen Hawking argued that black holes should not be perfect traps at all. Applying quantum theory to the region just outside the event horizon, he found that pairs of particles constantly flicker into existence there, and occasionally one escapes while its partner falls in, carrying mass away from the hole as it goes.

The consequence unsettled physicists more than the mechanism did: a black hole radiating energy must slowly lose mass and, given enough time, evaporate completely. No instrument has yet detected the effect directly, since the radiation from any real astrophysical black hole would be far fainter than the cosmic background around it, but the prediction reshaped how physicists think about gravity and information.

John Gibbon had spent two decades building a machine to take over the work of a patient's heart and lungs during surgery, after watching a patient die from a blocked pulmonary artery in 1930. On 6 May 1953 in Philadelphia, he used his machine on eighteen-year-old Cecelia Bavolek, keeping her circulation running mechanically for twenty-six minutes.

In that time Gibbon closed a hole between the chambers of her heart, a defect that could not have been repaired on a beating, blood-filled organ. Bavolek lived for decades afterward, and the operation is generally counted as the first successful open-heart surgery performed with a heart-lung bypass machine.

Helike was a leading city of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, prosperous enough to have founded colonies in Italy, when an earthquake and a wave from the sea struck it in the winter of 373 BC. Ancient writers say the destruction was total and that every inhabitant died, with only fragments of buildings left showing above the waterline.

For centuries the site was known only from those accounts, visible as ruins under shallow water that later silted over and vanished. A Greek-American survey team located the buried city on the coastal plain in 2001, using sonar and drilling rather than diving, and continuing excavation has since raised a competing theory that the flooding came from landward drainage rather than a tsunami alone.

Peter Henlein was a Nuremberg locksmith, not a member of any watchmakers' guild, since no such guild yet existed for the trade he was effectively inventing. Around 1510 he was building small spring driven clocks, wound rather than weight driven, compact enough to be carried on the body rather than mounted on a wall or tower, work that later writers credited as the origin of the pocket watch.

Henlein's fame as the sole inventor rests heavily on a nineteenth century German novel that turned him into a folk hero long after his death in 1542, and other German clockmakers of the same period were producing similarly small spring driven timepieces. No verified example signed by Henlein survives, so his exact contribution is harder to pin down than the legend built around his name.

Henry was hunting in the New Forest when word reached him that his brother William II had died there, shot by an arrow whose origin was never satisfactorily explained. Henry rode straight for Westminster and was crowned within days, before his elder brother Robert, away on crusade, could contest the throne.

To buy the barons' support for a rushed and shaky claim, Henry issued a coronation charter promising to end the abuses of William's reign: arbitrary seizure of church property, forced marriages of heiresses, extortionate fines. Copies were sent to cathedrals across England, and one surfaced again over a century later as a template the barons handed to King John at Runnymede.

Nineteen years of civil war between Stephen and the Empress Matilda, later called the Anarchy, had left England's crown lands plundered and its baronage used to fighting each other. The 1153 Treaty of Wallingford let Stephen keep the throne for his lifetime on condition that Matilda's son Henry succeed him, and Stephen died the following October.

Henry was crowned in December 1154 already ruling Normandy, Anjou and, through his wife Eleanor of Aquitaine, territory stretching to the Pyrenees, an assemblage historians later called the Angevin Empire. He spent much of his 34 year reign rebuilding royal authority the Anarchy had let slip, reforming the courts and reasserting control over barons grown used to acting on their own.

Henry IV had ended decades of civil war between Catholics and Huguenots with the Edict of Nantes in 1598, granting Protestants legal toleration, though he himself had converted to Catholicism to secure the throne. On 14 May 1610, his carriage was stopped in a narrow Paris street by traffic, and Francois Ravaillac climbed onto a wheel and stabbed him.

Ravaillac, a fervent Catholic who believed the king was about to make war on the Pope, was captured on the spot and executed within days by public torture and dismemberment. Henry's death left the throne to his nine year old son, Louis XIII, under his mother Marie de Medici's regency, and reopened the political instability his reign had spent years closing down.

Henry VI was not yet ten years old when Notre-Dame Cathedral hosted his coronation as French king, on 16 December 1431, nine years after infancy had already made him King of England. English forces had held Paris since 1420 under the Treaty of Troyes, which disinherited the French dauphin, and the Paris ceremony was staged to make that claim visible to a population never fully persuaded by it.

By then Joan of Arc had already forced Charles VII's rival coronation at Reims two years earlier, and English fortunes in France were already turning. Henry remains the only English monarch ever crowned king of France, a title the English crown kept claiming on paper for centuries after the country itself was lost.

A well-digger near modern Resina, working in 1709 for a French prince building a villa above, struck marble far underground rather than the water he was after. The marble turned out to be seating from a Roman theatre buried under roughly twenty metres of hardened volcanic material, laid down when Vesuvius destroyed Herculaneum alongside Pompeii in 79 CE.

Early recovery was closer to looting than excavation: statues and inscribed marble were hauled up through shafts and tunnels dug straight into the rock, with little record kept of where anything had actually stood. Organised digging did not begin for decades, but the well is generally treated as the moment Herculaneum's existence, buried and largely forgotten, became known again.

Drawn on a single calfskin around 1300 and still hanging in Hereford Cathedral, this map is the largest medieval world map to survive intact. It puts Jerusalem at the centre of a circular world with east, not north, at the top, because the map orders the world through Christian history rather than through direction a traveller could use.

Around its edges are Biblical scenes, mythical peoples, and creatures like the manticore and the phoenix jostling with real cities and rivers, none drawn to a scale that would help anyone find their way. It functioned less as a navigational tool than as a visual encyclopaedia of everything believed about the world, compressed onto roughly five feet of stretched hide.

Herod the Great, the Roman-backed king of Judea, built a fortified palace complex atop the isolated plateau of Masada above the Dead Sea, finished around 35 BCE. The site included storehouses, cisterns cut into the rock, a Roman-style bathhouse and a palace built on three terraces cantilevered down the cliff face.

Herod built it as a refuge against both external enemies and his own restive subjects, stocking it with enough grain and water to outlast a long siege. It later became famous for an episode from over a century after his death, when Jewish rebels held the fortress against a Roman siege, but Herod's engineering made that later resistance possible at all.

Caroline Herschel spent her nights sweeping the sky with a telescope her brother William had built, cataloguing nebulae and star clusters as part of his astronomical survey work in England. On 1 August 1786 she found a comet on her own, independently of any assistance from William, who was away at the time.

It was the first of eight comets she is credited with discovering over the following years, work that later earned her a salary from King George III, the first paid scientific position given to a woman in Britain. She went on to receive a gold medal from the Royal Astronomical Society, an honour no other woman would receive from it for more than a century.

William Herschel, who had discovered Uranus four years earlier, spent the mid-1780s pointing his own hand-built telescopes at hundreds of patches of sky and simply counting the stars visible in each, on the assumption that stars thinned out evenly toward the galaxy's edge and that their density told him its shape.

From those counts he published a diagram in 1785 showing the Milky Way as a flattened, irregular disc with the sun somewhere near its middle, the first attempt to chart the galaxy's structure from direct observation rather than speculation. The method's assumptions were flawed, since interstellar dust hid distant stars and skewed the counts, but the basic disc shape held up.

Judean workers cut the roughly 530-metre Siloam Tunnel through solid limestone beneath Jerusalem around 700 BCE, working from the Gihon Spring at one end and the Pool of Siloam at the other. An inscription found inside, now in Istanbul, describes the moment the two crews heard each other's picks and broke through.

The tunnel's winding, S-shaped course has puzzled engineers, since a straight line would have been shorter; one theory is that the diggers followed a natural crack in the rock rather than a surveyed line. It gave Jerusalem a hidden water supply during Sennacherib's siege, when the Assyrian king cut off the spring outside the walls.

Excavations at Hierakonpolis, one of the earliest major settlements of pre-dynastic Egypt, uncovered an elite cemetery containing the remains of elephants, hippopotamuses, baboons, wildcats and other animals buried alongside their human owners. Many showed healed injuries from captivity, evidence they were kept alive rather than simply hunted and eaten.

Archaeologists read the collection as an early royal menagerie, a display of a ruler's power to command exotic and dangerous creatures from distant regions. The practice anticipates the animal collections later Egyptian pharaohs and, much further on, Mesopotamian and Roman rulers would keep for the same purpose.

Muslim administrators around 638 needed to date letters and contracts, and the caliph Umar had to pick a starting point. He rejected Muhammad's birth and settled on the migration, the hijra, from Mecca to Medina in 622, fixing that year as year one of a lunar calendar of twelve months with no leap month to keep it aligned to the sun.

Because the lunar year runs about eleven days shorter than the solar year, Islamic dates drift steadily against the seasons rather than repeating on fixed solar dates, which is why Ramadan falls in a different season each decade. The Hijri calendar remains the official calendar of Saudi Arabia and is used alongside civil calendars across the Muslim world.

David Hilbert had prepared far more than he delivered. His lecture to the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris in 1900 covered only about ten of the problems he had drafted; the full list of twenty-three was printed afterwards, and it is the printed list, not the speech, that mathematicians have chased ever since.

The problems ranged from Cantor's continuum hypothesis to the consistency of arithmetic itself, and Hilbert framed them less as a checklist than as a bet on where the field's effort would pay off. Some were settled within years, some took most of a century, and one, the Riemann hypothesis, is still open, still treated as one of mathematics' hardest unsolved questions.

Hipparchus worked from Rhodes with a catalogue of star positions and a set of Babylonian eclipse records already centuries old by his time. Checking his own measurements against them, he found that the equinox point had shifted against the fixed stars, a drift too small to see in one lifetime but unmistakable across generations of records.

He put the shift at roughly one degree per century, close to the modern figure of about one degree every seventy two years. The effect, precession of the equinoxes, comes from the Earth's axis slowly tracing a circle rather than pointing at one fixed spot in the sky, something no observer in the second century BCE could have known the cause of.

Physicians working in the tradition attributed to Hippocrates circulated treatises describing fractures, dislocations and head wounds in systematic detail, including specific methods for reducing a dislocated shoulder or setting a broken limb that were built on direct clinical observation.

The texts describe technique with a precision unusual for the period, distinguishing this medical tradition from purely religious or magical approaches to injury common elsewhere in the ancient world. Some of the reduction methods they describe remained in medical use, largely unchanged, well into the modern era.

Histiaeus, tyrant of Miletus, was held as a guest-prisoner at the Persian court in Susa when he decided to incite revolt back home. According to Herodotus, he had a trusted slave's head shaved, tattooed a message onto the scalp, and waited for the hair to regrow before sending the man to Miletus around 499 BCE.

The recipient, Aristagoras, was told only to shave the messenger's head and read what was written there: an instruction to revolt against Persian rule. Whether or not the story is literally true, the revolt it triggered spread across Ionia and drew Athens into the fight, a chain of events that helped provoke the Persian invasions of Greece.

Battleships before 1906 mixed a few large guns with many smaller ones of varying range, which made it hard to judge fall of shot at long distance. HMS Dreadnought abandoned the mix entirely for a uniform battery of ten large guns, all capable of engaging at the same extended range, and steam turbines rather than older reciprocating engines.

Built in Portsmouth and launched within a year, remarkably fast for a warship of her size, she made every existing battleship instantly outclassed, a shift so sharp that all capital ships built afterward, on any side, were simply called dreadnoughts. The naval race the name set off helped shape the alliances that went to war in 1914.

By the 1890s cheap torpedo boats threatened even the largest battleships, so the Royal Navy commissioned a new class of ship built purely to hunt them down. HMS Havock, commissioned in 1893, was faster than any torpedo boat and armed to sink one before it closed within range.

Officially termed a torpedo boat destroyer, the name shortened over the following years to simply destroyer, the class name still used for warships today. Havock and her sister ship Hornet, tested together, both proved capable of speeds beyond twenty-six knots, setting the pattern for a type that would outlast the torpedo boats it was designed to kill.

King Charles I ordered the ship built without asking Parliament for the funds, financing it instead through a deeply unpopular tax called Ship Money that helped push England toward civil war. Launched in 1637, she carried over a hundred guns across three full decks, more firepower than any warship afloat.

Elaborately gilded and carved, she was as much a political statement as a weapon, and contemporaries mocked her cost. Later rebuilt and reduced in armament, she still fought through decades of Anglo-Dutch wars, and her three-decker, hundred-gun layout became the template later English first-rate ships of the line followed.

Britain's reply to the French ironclad Gloire went a step further. Launched in 1860, HMS Warrior was built with an iron hull from the outset rather than iron plate bolted onto timber, giving her greater strength and, combined with steam power, a speed no wooden warship could match.

She never fired a shot in anger; her presence alone was the point, deterring any rival navy from testing her. Preserved today at Portsmouth, Warrior marked the moment iron hulls replaced wood as the basis of naval construction, opening a rapid design race that made her own class obsolete within a decade.

The Hohokam dug their canals by hand from the Salt and Gila rivers, without draft animals or metal tools, moving the earth on foot with wooden and stone implements. By around 700 the network had grown into hundreds of kilometres of interconnected channels irrigating the Sonoran Desert floor where modern Phoenix now stands.

Some canals ran more than twenty kilometres from their river intake, engineered with a gentle enough gradient to move water by gravity alone across flat, arid terrain. Phoenix's own canal system, dug centuries later by settlers, largely followed the routes the Hohokam had already proven worked.

A hominin with a notably larger brain than its predecessors appears in the African fossil record around this time, later spreading into Europe and parts of Asia. Genetic comparisons between Neanderthal and modern human DNA point to a shared ancestor in roughly this period, with the population that stayed in Africa eventually giving rise to Homo sapiens.

Those that migrated into Europe are considered ancestral to the Neanderthals, while a further eastward group is linked to the Denisovans, making this single, loosely defined population the likely root of three separate human lineages. No single skeleton defines the species cleanly; it is reconstructed from scattered skulls and jaws found across three continents.

Grace Hopper's A-0 System, completed in 1952 while she worked at Remington Rand, took mathematical code written by a programmer and translated it into machine instructions a computer could run directly. Programmers had previously written those instructions by hand for each machine.

Hopper called the resulting program a compiler, coining the term still used for the software that does this today, and her work fed directly into the design of COBOL later in the decade. She kept working in computing into her eighties, retiring from the Navy as a rear admiral, one of the oldest officers still on active service at the time.

The United Nations declared famine in parts of Somalia in July 2011, after two consecutive failed rainy seasons combined with high grain prices and an ongoing conflict that blocked aid agencies from much of the worst-affected territory. The militant group al-Shabaab controlled areas where relief could not safely operate.

A later mortality study put the death toll at roughly a quarter of a million people, about half of them children under five, across Somalia between 2010 and 2012. The famine was formally declared over in February 2012, but the study's authors argued the world had been slow to respond even after the warning signs the Famine Early Warning Systems Network had already flagged.

George V had ruled since 1910 as a member of the House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, a name that had suited nobody's mood by 1917, with Britain three years into a war against Germany and Zeppelins bombing London. On 17 July he issued a proclamation dropping every German title held by his family and adopting Windsor, after the castle, instead.

Cousins and in-laws followed suit: the Battenbergs became Mountbattens and other relatives took plain English surnames. The change was cosmetic in the sense that the bloodline did not alter, but it answered a real political problem, a monarchy whose family tree read as enemy aristocracy to a public burying its dead.

Baghdad's House of Wisdom, founded under the Abbasid caliph al-Mamun in the early ninth century, had gathered scholars translating and expanding on Greek, Persian and Indian learning for generations when a Mongol army under Hulagu Khan besieged the city in 1258.

After the city fell, Mongol forces destroyed the library along with much of Baghdad, and later chroniclers wrote that so many books were thrown into the Tigris that its water ran black with ink for days. The siege also killed the last Abbasid caliph, ending a dynasty that had ruled for five centuries.

The H. L. Hunley was a cramped iron tube barely wide enough for its crew, propelled by eight men turning a hand crank connected to the propeller shaft, and it had already killed two previous crews, including its own inventor, in accidental sinkings during testing in Charleston harbour. On the night of 17 February 1864 it went out anyway, commanded by a fresh volunteer crew, to attack the Union blockade.

It rammed a spar tipped with a black powder charge into the hull of the USS Housatonic, sinking the sloop in minutes and killing five of her crew, the first warship ever destroyed by a submarine in combat. The Hunley itself vanished that same night with all eight men aboard, and its wreck was not located until 1995, still lying near the site of the attack.

Alexander the Great faced King Porus across the swollen Hydaspes River in what is now Punjab, and Porus deployed a corps of war elephants meant to break the Macedonian line and terrify horses unused to the animals. Alexander's cavalry and light infantry instead learned to target the elephants' handlers and hamstring the animals from the flanks.

The battle was among the hardest fought of Alexander's campaigns, with heavy losses on both sides, and it was reportedly costly enough that Alexander's own troops, exhausted after years of campaigning, refused to march further east afterward. He allowed Porus to keep his kingdom as a subject ruler rather than deposing him.

A team aboard the research vessel Knorr set out in February 1977 to study the Galapagos Rift, roughly 400 miles west of Ecuador, expecting only to measure heat escaping through the seafloor. Within days of arriving, scientists riding in the submersible Alvin spotted a shimmering plume of hot water rising from cracks in the rock, and around it something nobody had predicted: dense clusters of life.

Foot-long white clams and thickets of tube worms crowded the vents in total darkness, thousands of metres below any sunlight. The find overturned an assumption that all life ultimately depends on photosynthesis, since these communities instead feed on bacteria that convert chemicals from the vent water into food. More than 500 vent fields have since been catalogued around the world's ocean ridges.

In March 415 a mob of Christian monks and their allies dragged Hypatia from her carriage in Alexandria, stripped her, and killed her inside a church. The killing followed a bitter feud between the city's prefect, Orestes, whom Hypatia advised, and Cyril, the bishop of Alexandria, over who held real authority in the city.

She had taught mathematics and Neoplatonist philosophy in Alexandria for decades, drawing pupils regardless of their faith. Almost none of her own writing survives; what is known of her work comes mostly through letters from her student Synesius and later Christian and pagan historians, whose accounts of her death do not fully agree on the details.

Ibn al-Haytham's Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, written around 1028, did not offer a replacement cosmos. It laid out, point by point, where Ptolemy's own geometry contradicted itself: the equant point that let planets move at uneven speed around no physical centre, a device Ptolemy needed to match observation but could not explain mechanically.

Ibn al-Haytham insisted that a true model of the heavens had to correspond to real physical bodies moving uniformly, not just save appearances on paper. That demand shaped astronomers across the Islamic world for two centuries afterward, and historians now trace a line from his objections through later reworkings of planetary theory toward the eventual break with an Earth centred sky.

Ibn al-Shatir worked in Damascus as the muwaqqit, the mosque official responsible for timing the call to prayer by astronomical calculation, a job that demanded models accurate enough for practical use rather than philosophical elegance. Around 1350 he produced a full planetary theory that discarded Ptolemy's equant, using instead combinations of uniformly rotating circles in the tradition developed at the Maragha observatory.

His lunar model in particular corrected a long standing flaw in Ptolemy's, which made the Moon's apparent size vary far more than observation showed. The geometry Ibn al-Shatir used to fix it reappears, essentially unchanged, in Copernicus's own lunar theory two centuries later, though no direct transmission route between the two has ever been proven.

Ibn Sahl worked at the Abbasid court in Baghdad on a treatise called On Burning Mirrors and Lenses, finished around 984. To design lenses that focus light without distortion, he needed to know exactly how a ray bends when it passes from air into glass, and he worked out the constant ratio that governs it.

That ratio is what later became known in Europe as Snell's law, after the Dutch astronomer who reached it independently more than six centuries afterward. Ibn Sahl's manuscript, rediscovered in a Damascus library only in the twentieth century, shows the same geometry drawn out with a straightedge and compass, six hundred years earlier.

Denmark could not object. Nazi Germany had occupied it since 1940, and Iceland, garrisoned instead by British and American troops, held a referendum in May 1944 in which nearly every voter backed severing the centuries-old link to the Danish crown. The break was less a rupture than a formality nobody in Copenhagen was in a position to contest.

On 17 June 1944, the birthday of the independence campaigner Jon Sigurdsson, delegates gathered in the rain at Thingvellir, the site of Iceland's medieval assembly, to proclaim the republic and swear in Sveinn Bjornsson as its first president. The date has been Iceland's national day ever since, tying the new republic to a parliament nearly a thousand years older than it.

Australia's environment minister, Malcolm Turnbull, announced in February 2007 that the country would stop selling incandescent filament bulbs by 2010, framing it as an easy way to cut household electricity use and greenhouse emissions since the bulbs waste most of their power as heat rather than light.

The idea spread fast: the European Union adopted a similar phase-out later that year, and the United States followed with efficiency standards in its 2007 energy bill that effectively ended the century-old bulb by the mid-2010s. Compact fluorescents and then LED bulbs took its place, using a fraction of the electricity for the same brightness.

The 1880 code followed directly from the criticism of how the 1876 to 1878 famine had been handled, when relief arrived late and grain exports continued through the worst of the shortage. It set out early warning signs, such as crop and price data, that district officers were required to act on before deaths began mounting rather than after.

Relief took the form of public works: labourers were paid in cash or grain for building roads and canals, on the theory that work-tested aid would not encourage dependency. The code was revised repeatedly over the following decades, but its basic structure, treating famine as a predictable administrative failure rather than an act of nature, shaped Indian relief policy well into the twentieth century.

The Irish Crown Jewels, a diamond star and badge of the Order of St Patrick along with several ceremonial collars, were kept in a strongroom in Dublin Castle's Bedford Tower under the care of Sir Arthur Vicars, the Ulster King of Arms. In July 1907, days before King Edward VII was due to visit for an investiture, Vicars discovered the safe empty.

No sign of forced entry was ever found, and suspicion fell on figures within Vicars's own circle, though no one was ever charged. The king was furious enough to have Vicars dismissed from his post, and the jewels have never been recovered, leaving the case one of the most enduring unsolved thefts in Irish history.

The Iroquois Theatre in Chicago had opened only a few weeks earlier and was billed as fireproof when a stage light ignited a curtain during a matinee performance of Mr. Bluebeard on 30 December 1903. The safety curtain meant to seal the stage off from the audience jammed partway down.

Exit doors that opened inward, some bolted shut, and unmarked exits behind curtains trapped much of the crowd, and 602 people died, making it the deadliest single-building fire in American history. The disaster led cities across the country to require outward-opening exit doors, illuminated exit signs and panic bars, reforms still standard in public buildings today.

No text from the discovery survives, and even the name attached to it is uncertain. Later Greek writers credit a Pythagorean, sometimes named as Hippasus, with the proof around the mid fifth century BC, though the school itself is said to have treated the finding as unwelcome rather than triumphant.

The proof works by contradiction: assume the diagonal of a unit square can be written as a fraction in lowest terms, and the arithmetic forces both its numerator and denominator to be even, which lowest terms forbids.
