The pope agreed, and on 6 July 1253 papal legates anointed Mindaugas and his wife Morta at a ceremony whose exact site is still argued over, somewhere near Vilnius or Novogrudok.

The gambit was political as much as religious: a crown made Lithuania a recognised Christian kingdom, not a pagan target for the Teutonic Knights' crusading claims. It did not last. Mindaugas was assassinated by rival nobles in 1263, Lithuania reverted to paganism, and no ruler after him used the royal title again until the modern republic revived the date as a national holiday.

Tin had been found in the Malay interior, and in 1857 a group of Chinese prospectors, backed by a local Malay chief, pushed upriver by boat to reach it, landing at a muddy confluence where two rivers met. They named the spot Kuala Lumpur, meaning muddy river mouth, and built a trading post to move tin ore out to the coast.

Malaria and clan warfare between rival mining factions killed a large share of the early settlers within its first decades, and the town nearly collapsed more than once. It survived because the tin kept coming, and British colonial administrators later chose it as the capital of the Federated Malay States, a status it kept into independent Malaysia.

The Zhengtong Emperor personally led a Ming army north to confront Mongol raiders under Esen Taishi, against the advice of his own ministers, and marched it into a poorly supplied position near the Tumu fortress. Mongol cavalry surrounded the exhausted column, routed it, and took the emperor himself prisoner, an outcome unthinkable to the court that had sent him.

Beijing refused to ransom him and crowned his brother instead, leaving Esen holding an emperor with no leverage left to sell. He was eventually released and returned to reclaim the throne years later, but the crisis exposed how fragile Ming military prestige had become and forced a lasting retreat from active campaigning on the northern frontier.

Around 2450 BCE, the Indus Valley city of Mohenjo-daro had brick-lined drains built beneath its streets, covered with fitted brick slabs, carrying wastewater away from individual houses rather than letting it collect in the open. Many homes also had their own wells and bathing platforms connected to the system.

The scale of the planning was unusual for its time: uniform street grids, standardised brick sizes and municipal-level sanitation appear across the city rather than in a few wealthy households only. No comparably systematic urban drainage appears elsewhere in the ancient world for well over a thousand years afterward.

Vincenzo Peruggia had once worked at the Louvre building protective glass cases for paintings, including the one that held the Mona Lisa. On a Monday in August 1911, when the museum was closed to the public, he slipped into a service stairwell, took the painting off the wall, removed it from its frame and case, and walked out with it hidden under his smock.

The theft went unnoticed for a full day, and the painting stayed hidden in Peruggia's Paris apartment for two years while investigators, including a young Pablo Picasso briefly questioned as a suspect, chased other leads. Peruggia was caught in 1913 after trying to sell the painting to a Florence art dealer, and its disappearance had already made it far more famous than it had been before.

Henry Morgan, a Welsh buccaneer operating with English backing from Jamaica, led close to two thousand men across the Panamanian isthmus in early 1671, aiming at one of Spain's wealthiest cities in the Americas. Spanish defenders met his force outside the city but were routed, opening the way in.

Panama City burned during or shortly after the attack, with responsibility for the fire disputed between the retreating Spanish and the buccaneers themselves, and much of the treasure the raiders hoped for had already been shipped out beforehand. The raid came after a peace treaty with Spain had technically already been signed, and the resulting diplomatic complaint saw Morgan briefly arrested and shipped back to England to answer for it.

Toni Morrison had already won a Pulitzer Prize for Beloved when the Swedish Academy awarded her the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature, citing novels marked by visionary force and poetic import that gave life to an essential aspect of American reality. She had worked for years as an editor at Random House before her own fiction found a wide readership.

She was the first Black woman to receive the prize and only the second American woman after Pearl Buck decades earlier. Her Nobel lecture used the parable of a blind woman asked whether a bird held by visitors is alive or dead, turning the question into an argument about the responsibility carried by language itself.

Moscow existed before 1147, but that year is when it first appears in writing: the Hypatian Chronicle records that Prince Yuri Dolgoruky invited an ally, Prince Svyatoslav, to a banquet at a place called Moscow, then a minor fortified outpost on the edge of his territory rather than any kind of capital.

The chronicle gives no description of the settlement beyond the invitation itself, so historians date the city's founding to this mention for lack of anything earlier, not because the banquet created the place. Moscow stayed a minor principality for another century before Mongol devastation elsewhere in Russia let it rise, eventually, into the centre it later became.

Bubonic plague had been killing over a thousand Muscovites a day by September 1771 when crowds gathered around an icon of the Virgin at the Barbarian Gate, believing it could cure them. Archbishop Ambrosius, trying to stop a crowd that spread the disease faster than it prayed it away, had the icon moved and its donation box sealed.

On 15 September the crowd stormed the Kremlin, wrecked the archbishop's residence and killed him the next day. Catherine the Great sent troops under Grigory Orlov to put the riot down; the wider epidemic, one of the last major outbreaks of plague in Europe, is thought to have killed roughly a third of Moscow's population before it ended.

Islamic State fighters occupying Mosul from 2014 burned libraries across the city as part of a campaign against material they judged un-Islamic, including centuries-old manuscripts and printed collections built up over generations.

The University of Mosul's central library, holding hundreds of thousands of books and rare documents, was set on fire in 2015. The destruction drew comparisons to the Mongol sack of Baghdad's House of Wisdom nearly eight centuries earlier, a comparison Iraqi academics themselves made at the time.

Saint-Pierre's authorities kept residents in the city as Mount Pelee rumbled through April 1902, partly to avoid disrupting an election and partly because nobody nearby had seen a pyroclastic flow before and did not know to fear one specifically. On the morning of 8 May a superheated cloud of gas and ash raced down the mountain's slope and reached the port town within about a minute.

Nearly all of Saint-Pierre's roughly 28,000 residents died, most from the heat itself rather than from ash or falling debris; ships anchored in the harbour caught fire and sank. A handful of survivors were found, including a prisoner in a partly underground cell. The disaster gave volcanology the term pyroclastic flow and a clear demonstration of how fast such a flow moves.

Madrid began as a garrison outpost rather than a capital. Around 865, Emir Muhammad I of Cordoba, needing to guard the northern approach to Toledo against Christian raids from the mountains beyond, had a fortress raised on a bluff above the Manzanares river. Contemporary sources call the site Mayrit, a name later Castilianised into Madrid.

The fortress held a garrison and little else for centuries, one link in a chain of similar strongholds built across the frontier. It became the seat of a small Christian county after conquest in 1085, and its rise to national capital did not come until 1561, when Philip II moved the Spanish court there for its central position rather than any grandeur it had accumulated by then.

Just after two in the morning on 10 February 1567, an explosion tore apart the Kirk o' Field house in Edinburgh where Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, was staying. Two barrels of gunpowder had been packed into a room beneath his lodging. His body and that of a servant were found in the garden outside, apparently strangled rather than killed by the blast, suggesting he had escaped the building before it collapsed.

Suspicion fell immediately on the Earl of Bothwell, and by extension on Mary, Queen of Scots, whose marriage to Darnley had already broken down. Bothwell stood trial and was acquitted, then married Mary within three months, a decision Scottish nobles used to force her abdication the following year. No account of who planned the killing has ever been settled beyond dispute.

Decimus Brutus was besieged inside Mutina, in northern Italy, by forces loyal to Mark Antony, cut off from the consular armies that might relieve him. According to the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, Brutus attached messages to pigeons and released them to carry word out to his allies beyond the siege lines.

The pigeons reportedly flew to a perch near the consuls' camp that Brutus had trained them to recognise, letting coordinated relief efforts break the blockade. Pliny's account is the earliest detailed description of pigeons used as wartime messengers, a role they would keep for the next two thousand years.

Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, dug into the ruined ziggurat of Ur around 550 BCE while restoring it, searching for the temple's original foundation deposits. He found inscribed cylinders naming earlier builders, including Ur-Nammu, and had his own account of the discovery buried inside the walls he rebuilt.

He did the same at the Ebabbar temple in Sippar, uncovering an inscription of the much older king Naram-Sin and estimating, wrongly but seriously, how many centuries had passed since it was buried. Historians count these digs among the earliest deliberate excavations aimed at recovering the past rather than reusing building material.

Nalanda in northeastern India had operated as a Buddhist centre of learning for roughly seven centuries, since its founding around 427 CE, drawing students from as far as China and Tibet to study philosophy, medicine and logic under thousands of resident monks.

Around 1193, forces under the Turkic general Bakhtiyar Khalji, expanding Muslim rule into Bihar, attacked and burned the monastery complex. Later accounts, written well after the event, describe its library burning for days, though contemporary detail is thin. Nalanda's role as a major seat of learning did not resume.

Fridtjof Nansen chose to ski from Greenland's sparsely inhabited east coast toward the populated west, deliberately cutting off any easy retreat once the party landed. That decision forced his team across the unmapped interior ice sheet rather than risk turning back partway, a calculated gamble on committing fully to the crossing.

The six-man expedition hauled sledges of supplies across roughly 500 kilometres of featureless ice in 1888, facing temperatures that dropped well below minus forty degrees. Their success proved a small, self-sufficient party could cross the world's second-largest ice sheet without support, a method Nansen would later apply to his Arctic drift toward the North Pole.

John Napier was a Scottish laird who spent twenty years on the side project that made his name, working it out by hand with no algebra beyond what he invented for the purpose. His Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio, published in 1614, gave astronomers and navigators a table that turned lengthy multiplication and division into simple addition and subtraction.

Henry Briggs, a London mathematician, read the book, travelled to Edinburgh to meet Napier, and spent the rest of his career refining the tables into the base-10 logarithms still taught today. Napier never saw that version finished. He also invented Napier's bones, a set of numbered rods for mechanical multiplication, which spread further and faster than the logarithms themselves.

After German forces crushed the Warsaw Uprising in early October 1944, Heinrich Himmler ordered the city destroyed as a reprisal and a warning, rather than simply reoccupied. Specialist demolition units moved through Warsaw block by block over the following months, torching and dynamiting buildings largely emptied of their surviving residents.

By the time Soviet and Polish forces entered the city in January 1945, an estimated 85 percent of Warsaw's buildings had been destroyed, including the historic Old Town almost entirely. The destruction was documented in detail by the Germans themselves, footage later used as evidence of a deliberate campaign rather than incidental war damage.

Pharaoh Necho II marched his army north through the Levant in 609 BCE to reinforce the remnants of Assyria against a rising Babylonian threat, judging a weakened Assyria a safer neighbour than an ascendant one. King Josiah of Judah, for reasons the biblical account leaves only partly explained, moved to block the Egyptian army's path at Megiddo.

Josiah was killed in the ensuing battle, ending a reign remembered in Judah for major religious reforms. Necho continued north but arrived too late to save Assyria's last stronghold, and within a few years Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II had turned its attention toward Egypt's own new sphere of influence.

Nectanebo I seized the Egyptian throne around 380 BCE, founding what proved to be the country's final native dynasty, its Thirtieth. Persia, which had briefly lost control of Egypt decades earlier, tried repeatedly to retake it, and around 373 BCE sent a large invasion force up the Nile.

Nectanebo's defenders held key delta crossings, and seasonal Nile flooding disrupted the Persian advance before it could reach the capital, forcing a withdrawal. He used the reprieve to fund an unusually active building programme across Egypt's temples, work that continued under his son and grandson before Persia finally returned.

Lake Nemi, a flooded volcanic crater south of Rome, was known to hold two enormous barges built as floating palaces for the emperor Caligula, roughly seventy metres long and lost since antiquity. In July 1535 the engineer Francesco de Marchi hired Guglielmo de Lorena to go down and find them, using a bell of Guglielmo's own design that rested on the diver's shoulders and trapped air around his head.

The bell was small enough to hold only a few minutes of breathable air, but it had a mechanism for venting used air while keeping the water out, letting Guglielmo work submerged far longer than a single breath allowed. He never explained how it worked. De Marchi had sworn an oath of secrecy, and the two brought up marble and bronze fragments from the barges without disclosing the device that got them there.

Coca-Cola introduced a reformulated, sweeter recipe on 23 April 1985 after blind taste tests suggested drinkers preferred it, and quietly retired the 99-year-old original in the same move. The company had been losing ground to Pepsi's sweeter cola and treated the switch as a straightforward fix to a market research problem.

The reaction was fury rather than gratitude. Tens of thousands of complaint calls and letters poured in, some from drinkers who said the old formula tasted like home rather than a beverage. Coca-Cola brought the original recipe back on 10 July 1985, marketed as Coca-Cola Classic, just 79 days after New Coke launched, in what became a textbook case of underestimating brand loyalty.

Fire insurance underwriters in the late nineteenth century faced a patchwork of incompatible local standards for sprinkler pipe sizes and fittings, which made installations unreliable across different cities. In 1896, a group of insurers and engineers meeting in New York agreed to form a new body, the National Fire Protection Association, to settle on a single set of sprinkler specifications.

The organisation's remit widened well beyond sprinklers over the following decades into building codes, electrical wiring standards and the National Electrical Code still used across the United States. Its founding meeting drew representatives from a handful of insurance companies, a small start for a body whose codes now shape how buildings are constructed nationwide.

The Niagara Falls Power Company's 1895 station settled a fight that had run for years between Thomas Edison's direct current and George Westinghouse's alternating current. Westinghouse won the contract, using Nikola Tesla's patented AC induction motor design, partly because AC could be transformed to high voltage for the journey and stepped back down at the far end without the huge losses DC suffered over distance.

The station's generators sent power some twenty miles to Buffalo, lighting streets and running factories far from the turbines that made the electricity. It was the demonstration the AC side needed: cheap, distant power was possible, and within a few years AC transmission became the standard that electrical grids were built on.

On the night of 10 to 11 December 969, John Tzimiskes and three fellow conspirators crossed the storm tossed Bosphorus and reached the Boukoleon Palace, where the emperor's own wife Theophano lowered a basket on a rope to bring them inside. She had persuaded Nikephoros not to lock his bedchamber door.

A eunuch pointed out where the emperor lay asleep on the floor, having given up his bed for austerity's sake. The attackers struck him awake with a sword, and Tzimiskes kicked him before finishing him. Nikephoros's guards, rushing in on the noise, are said to have stopped short at the sight of his severed head. Tzimiskes took the throne within days.

The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art survives as a collection of practical problems: dividing land, taxing grain, sizing canals, split into nine chapters by subject. It was compiled from older material by unnamed authors, then expanded with a commentary by Liu Hui in the third century CE that explained why the methods worked rather than just stating them.

Among its methods is fangcheng, a rule for solving several equations with several unknowns at once by arranging their coefficients in a grid and cancelling terms, the same idea western mathematics would later call Gaussian elimination. Red and black counting rods let the text represent negative numbers directly, well before European mathematics accepted them.

Nine Men's Morris boards from around 1400 BCE are cut, not drawn: grids of three concentric squares scratched into the roofing slabs at the temple of Kurna in Egypt, where workers waiting out slow hours scored a game into stone rather than papyrus. Players moved counters along the lines, trying to land three in a row.

The Kurna boards are only the earliest surviving examples, not proof the game began there. Similar grids turn up cut into temple steps and floors across the ancient Mediterranean, Rome included, wherever masons or guards had stone underfoot and time on their hands. The rules travelled without needing a single point of origin.

Austen Henry Layard was a broke young traveller with no formal training when he began digging at the mound of Kuyunjik, opposite Mosul, in the 1840s, funded on a shoestring by the British ambassador in Constantinople. Local workers had already found stone fragments there, but Layard's trenches in 1847 struck the palace of the Assyrian king Sennacherib, buried and forgotten for over two thousand years.

He shipped enormous winged bull statues and slabs of battle relief down the Tigris on rafts and across the desert by cart to reach the sea, a feat nearly as remarkable as the finds themselves. The reliefs, now largely in the British Museum, gave Europe its first direct look at Assyrian court life and warfare, and the site later also yielded the clay tablets that let cuneiform be checked and confirmed.

Nizam al-Mulk had run the Seljuk empire's administration for three decades, founding the Nizamiyyah colleges that trained its bureaucrats and shaping policy under two sultans. In October 1092 he was stabbed to death near Nihavand by a man disguised as a Sufi petitioner, on the orders of the Nizari Ismaili leader Hassan i Sabbah from the mountain fortress of Alamut.

The Nizaris used targeted, individual killings rather than open rebellion against a far larger Seljuk state, and their agents became known to Crusader chroniclers as hashishin, a name that passed into European languages as assassin. Nizam al-Mulk is usually counted as the sect's first prominent victim, killed within weeks of the sultan he served.

Nikolai Lobachevsky published his geometry in 1829 in a Kazan University journal few outside Russia read, working out what followed if Euclid's parallel postulate, that exactly one line through a point never meets a given line, was simply false. He built a consistent system, later called hyperbolic geometry, where infinitely many such parallels exist.

Janos Bolyai reached similar conclusions independently around the same years in Hungary, and Gauss had worked out much of it privately without publishing, fearing the reaction it would provoke. Only decades later, once Bernhard Riemann and others showed the new geometries were as sound as Euclid's, did mathematicians accept that space need not obey the axioms taught since antiquity.

In December 2004, armed men held the families of two Northern Bank employees hostage overnight in separate houses in Belfast, then forced the staff to let them into the bank's cash centre the following evening and load a van with money over several hours.

The gang made off with roughly 26.5 million pounds, still the largest bank robbery in British or Irish history. Police blamed the Provisional IRA, which denied involvement, and the bank issued new coloured banknotes to devalue the stolen bills, though most of the cash was never recovered.

Keeping Arctic shipping lanes open through the Soviet Union's northern coast needed an icebreaker with far more endurance than any coal or diesel ship could carry, since refuelling stations along that route barely existed.

Built at the Admiralty Shipyard and commissioned in December 1959, NS Lenin ran on a nuclear reactor that let her operate for long stretches without returning to port, becoming the world's first nuclear-powered surface vessel of any kind. She served the Northern Sea Route for three decades before her worn hull forced retirement in 1989, and survives today as a museum ship in Murmansk.

Sandra Day O'Connor graduated near the top of her Stanford law class in 1952 but could not find a law firm willing to hire a woman as an attorney rather than a secretary. President Ronald Reagan nominated her to the Supreme Court in 1981, fulfilling a campaign promise to appoint the first woman to the bench.

The Senate confirmed her unanimously, and she was sworn in that September as the court's 102nd justice. She often held the decisive vote in closely divided cases during her twenty-four years on the bench, on issues including abortion rights and the disputed 2000 presidential election, before retiring in 2006.

Offa ruled Mercia for nearly forty years and dominated the other Anglo-Saxon kingdoms so completely that he struck his own gold coinage and had his daughters married into rival royal houses. Around 785 he had a bank and ditch raised along much of the border with the Welsh kingdoms, running roughly 130 kilometres from the Dee estuary toward the Severn.

The dyke was never a continuous wall and did not need to be; long stretches used rivers and existing ridges to fill the gaps, with the earthwork itself concentrated where the ground gave no natural barrier. Much of it still stands, and a long-distance footpath now follows its line, making it one of the largest surviving works of Anglo-Saxon England.

Oklahoma opened on Broadway in March 1943, the first collaboration between composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist Oscar Hammerstein II, setting its story of frontier settlers and rival suitors with songs and dance numbers that advanced the plot rather than pausing it.

Its opening scene, a lone woman churning butter onstage while a cowboy sings offstage with no chorus line in sight, broke sharply from the era's usual splashy openings. The show ran for over five years on Broadway and became the template later writers called the integrated book musical.

Heinrich Olbers set out the puzzle formally in 1823, though he was refining an argument earlier astronomers, including Johannes Kepler, had already raised: if the universe is infinite, static and evenly filled with stars, every line of sight should eventually end on a stellar surface, making the whole sky as bright as the Sun.

Olbers guessed the answer was dust absorbing distant starlight, which turned out to be wrong, since absorbed light would simply heat the dust until it glowed as brightly. The real resolution came only with an expanding universe of finite age: light from the most distant stars has not had time to reach us, and the universe's youth, not its dust, is what keeps the night dark.

Old Hemp was a working sheepdog bred in Northumberland by a farmer named Adam Telfer, notable even as a puppy for herding sheep by quiet stalking and eye contact rather than the barking and nipping common among sheepdogs of the time.

His calm, controlling style proved so effective at trials that he was used extensively at stud, and pedigree records trace the vast majority of modern Border Collies back to him through his many working offspring. The breed's defining herding style is essentially his, standardised through generations of descendants.

At a coal mine near Schoningen in Germany, workers uncovered wooden spears preserved for hundreds of thousands of years in waterlogged clay, alongside the butchered bones of more than fifty wild horses. The wood, ordinarily the first material to rot away, survived only because the site's mud sealed out the oxygen that would have let it decay.

The spears are shaped and weighted like modern javelins, balanced for throwing rather than thrusting, which argues for hominins capable of planning an ambush hunt rather than merely scavenging. Their exact age has been revised more than once as dating methods improved, but they remain the oldest known hunting weapons made by any human relative.

Britain's Board of Ordnance began a national survey in 1791, prompted partly by fears of French invasion and a need for maps good enough to move troops on, and partly by an earlier boundary dispute with France that had shown how poor existing charts were. Work started from a baseline measured across Hounslow Heath, chosen because it was flat and open enough to lay a chain accurately.

Surveyors triangulated outward from that baseline across the whole country, publishing the first one-inch-to-the-mile sheets over the following decades. The organisation that grew from that survey, still called the Ordnance Survey, remains Britain's national mapping agency more than two centuries later, long after the invasion threat that started it had passed.

Aeschylus's Oresteia won first prize at the City Dionysia festival in Athens in 458 BCE, tracing the killing of Agamemnon by his wife, her killing by their son Orestes, and his eventual trial and acquittal by a court the goddess Athena establishes.

It is the only complete trilogy of Greek tragedies to survive from antiquity, giving scholars a rare view of how a single story could be built across three full plays rather than a lone episode. Its final movement, replacing a cycle of family vengeance with a formal jury, was read even by ancient audiences as a myth about the birth of civic justice.

Built to broadcast television and radio across Moscow, the Ostankino Tower is a freestanding concrete structure reaching about 540 metres, a form distinct from the guyed masts that had briefly held taller records elsewhere. On completion it became the tallest freestanding structure ever built, a title guyed masts could not claim since they rely on cables rather than standing unsupported.

Its design, using pre-stressed concrete cables inside a tapering shaft, influenced later towers built on the same principle, including Toronto's CN Tower. Ostankino held its freestanding record for well over a decade before the CN Tower surpassed it.

Ota Dokan was a samurai retainer and poet serving the Uesugi clan when he was ordered to fortify a strategically placed but otherwise unremarkable fishing village on Edo Bay. In 1457 he built a castle there, choosing the site for its access to the bay and the rivers feeding it rather than for any prestige the village already held.

Dokan's castle was modest by the standards of the fortresses that came after it, and he was assassinated by his own lord's family within decades of building it. The site he chose mattered more than the structure: when Tokugawa Ieyasu made Edo his headquarters in 1590, he expanded Dokan's castle into the core of a city that later became Tokyo.

The Knights Hospitaller had held Rhodes as a fortified base for over two centuries, using it to raid Ottoman shipping in the eastern Mediterranean, when Suleiman the Magnificent landed an army reportedly many times the size of the island's garrison in 1522.

The siege ran for nearly six months, with the knights' engineers countermining Ottoman tunnels dug beneath the walls, before dwindling supplies and casualties forced surrender in December. Suleiman allowed the surviving knights to leave under safe conduct, and they eventually resettled on Malta, where they would face an even larger Ottoman siege decades later.

Borge Ousland skied across Antarctica alone in 1996 and 1997, hauling all his food and fuel on a heavy sledge and using a kite sail to gain speed across the flatter stretches of ice. The roughly 2,845 kilometre crossing took sixty-four days, completed without resupply drops or support from any other party along the route.

No one had previously crossed the continent solo and unsupported, a combination that had defeated or gone unattempted by earlier expeditions relying on dog teams, motor vehicles or air support. Ousland's crossing extended the unsupported-travel standard that he and Erling Kagge had already set at the North Pole seven years earlier to the opposite end of the planet.

Pancho Villa had accepted a government pardon in 1920 and settled on a ranch at Canutillo, running it as a colony for his former soldiers. On 20 July 1923 he was driving into the town of Parral in his Dodge touring car when gunmen firing from a house on the route killed him and several companions.

The assassination was never conclusively tied to a single sponsor, though suspicion fell on local and national political figures wary of Villa re-entering public life ahead of the 1924 presidential succession. One of the ambush party, Jesus Salas Barraza, was tried, convicted, and served under a year before receiving a commission in the army.

On 20 February 1943 a Purepecha farmer named Dionisio Pulido was burning brush in his cornfield near Uruapan when the ground swelled, cracked open, and hissed sulphur smoke. Within a day the fissure had thrown up a cinder cone roughly 50 metres high. Pulido tried to protect his plot with a shovel before giving up and fleeing with his family.

The cone kept growing for nine years, reaching about 424 metres, while lava and ash buried the villages of Paricutin and San Juan Parangaricutiro. No one died in the eruption itself, though the displacement scattered thousands of residents permanently. Because it was watched from its first hour, geologists got a rare full record of a volcano's entire birth and adolescence.

Etienne Boileau, provost of Paris under Louis IX, faced a problem that had nothing to do with wax: trade rules in the city existed only as oral custom, passed master to apprentice, and disputes had no written text to settle them. Around 1268 he asked each Parisian craft to write down its own statutes and compiled the results into the Livre des metiers, the Book of Trades.

Among roughly a hundred crafts recorded were the tallow chandlers, who rendered animal fat into cheap everyday candles, and the wax chandlers who supplied the costlier light burned in churches and wealthy houses. Their entries fixed apprenticeship terms, quality checks and who could sell what, giving Paris its earliest surviving written regulation of the trades that lit it.

In May 2010, a lone thief named Vjeran Tomic climbed to a locked gate and forced a window at the Musee d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris overnight, bypassing a broken alarm system the museum had not repaired for months, and removed five paintings from their frames.

The works, by Picasso, Matisse, Braque, Modigliani and Leger, were valued afterward at well over a hundred million euros combined. Tomic was arrested two years later, but the paintings were never recovered; a middleman he had passed them to claimed to have thrown them in the rubbish after learning police were closing in.

Long before Rome reached Gaul, a Celtic people called the Parisii had settled along the Seine, drawn to a spot where an island and a ford made the river easy to cross and to defend. Archaeologists still argue over whether their main settlement sat on what is now the Ile de la Cite or elsewhere along the river, since the earliest layers are thin and scattered.

The Parisii minted their own gold coins and traded along the river network long before any Roman arrived, evidence that the site was already a working crossing point rather than empty ground waiting to be claimed. When Rome eventually took the area, it kept the tribe's name for the town that grew there, Lutetia Parisiorum, which outlasted the empire that renamed it and became Paris.

Louis XIV appointed Gabriel Nicolas de la Reynie as Paris's first lieutenant general of police in March 1667, giving him a mandate to make the streets safer that went well beyond simply hiring more officers. Among his measures was ordering metal-and-glass lanterns hung on poles above the main streets and asking residents to keep windows lit with candles or oil lamps after dark.

By 1668 nearly three thousand of these lanterns were burning across the city, a scale no other European capital had attempted, meant to strip criminals of the darkness they relied on rather than to simply light the way for pedestrians. The measure is the origin most often given for Paris's later nickname, the City of Light, though the phrase would come to mean something closer to intellectual brilliance than street lamps.

Henry S. Parmelee ran a piano factory in New Haven, Connecticut, and worried about fire risk from the varnishes and sawdust involved in the trade. In 1874 he patented a sprinkler head that released water automatically once heat melted a solder link holding its valve shut, rather than waiting for a person to notice the fire and act.

Parmelee installed the system in his own factory first, and insurers took note of how quickly it could contain a blaze before it spread. His design was refined by later engineers into the fusible-link sprinkler still recognisable in ceilings today, and automatic sprinklers gradually became a standard feature of industrial insurance requirements.

Bartolomeu de Gusmao, a Brazilian-born Jesuit priest working in Lisbon, demonstrated a small hot air balloon before King John V and the Portuguese court on 8 August 1709. Accounts describe a paper globe rising several metres into the air on heated air before the flame went out and it settled back down.

The device became known as the Passarola after a separate, more elaborate bird-shaped flying machine Gusmao had earlier proposed, though it was the small working model that actually flew. The king reportedly rewarded him with a canonry and a patent granting him exclusive rights over any future flying craft, decades before European balloon flight became widely known.

On Easter Sunday, 26 April 1478, during High Mass in Florence's cathedral, conspirators from the rival Pazzi banking family and allies of Pope Sixtus IV attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici at the ringing of the sanctus bell. Giuliano was stabbed repeatedly and died where he fell; Lorenzo, wounded in the neck, drew his sword, vaulted a low barrier and escaped through the sacristy with the help of friends.

Florence's response was immediate and brutal. Conspirators were hunted down and hanged from the windows of the Palazzo della Signoria within days, including the archbishop of Pisa, who had helped plan the attack. The failed plot left Lorenzo more securely in control of Florence than before, while Sixtus IV, implicated in the plot, placed the city under a papal interdict and pushed it into a two year war.

Ancient sources credit an Athenian statesman named Callias with negotiating a peace with the Persian Empire around 449 BCE, supposedly ending decades of intermittent warfare that had begun with the Persian invasions of Greece earlier in the century and continued through the Delian League's campaigns.

No contemporary fifth century text mentions the treaty directly, and the earliest surviving references date from over a century later, which has led many historians to doubt whether a formal agreement was ever signed rather than an informal lull in fighting. The debate over its existence remains unresolved.

The Peace of Constance was sealed in 1183 between Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and the Lombard League, an alliance of northern Italian city-states that had defeated his forces at the Battle of Legnano seven years earlier, ending a long revolt against imperial control.

Under its terms Barbarossa recognised the cities' rights to elect their own officials, raise militias and manage local justice, while they in turn acknowledged his nominal overlordship. The settlement let cities such as Milan continue functioning as effectively self-governing communes under a loose imperial umbrella.

Milan had spent decades warring with Venice over Lombard territory, and the fighting had drained every treasury involved without settling the border. In 1454 Francesco Sforza's Milan and the Venetian Republic finally agreed terms at Lodi, on the Adda river, fixing a frontier neither could push further.

Naples, Florence and the Papal States joined soon after in the Italic League, a mutual defence pact meant to freeze the peninsula's five main powers in place. It largely worked for four decades, until the French invasion of 1494 exposed how brittle a peace built on exhausted rivals rather than settled grievances had been.

Athens and Sparta signed the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE, named for the Athenian general who negotiated it, agreeing to a fifty year truce meant to end the first ten years of fighting in the Peloponnesian War and restore territory each side had seized.

The peace never held in practice: both sides kept fighting through allied cities almost immediately, and outright war resumed within a few years. Ancient historian Thucydides treated the uneasy interval as part of a single continuous conflict rather than a genuine pause, and modern accounts of the war generally follow him.

Prussia crushed Austria in seven weeks in 1866, a war so short some German states barely mobilised before it ended. Bismarck deliberately kept the peace terms mild, refusing Prussian generals who wanted to march into Vienna and annex Austrian land outright.

The Peace of Prague dissolved the old German Confederation and let Prussia absorb Hanover, Hesse and several smaller states into a new North German Confederation, while Austria kept its territory intact. That restraint left Austria resentful but not vengeful, clearing the way for the Franco-Prussian War four years later without a two front problem.

Pei Xiu was a minister under the Jin dynasty after the fall of Wei, and used his access to court archives to revise a large regional map of the empire that he judged inaccurate. His preface to that revised atlas, rather than the map itself, is what survives, and it is the earliest Chinese text to state cartographic principles explicitly.

He listed six rules a mapmaker had to hold together: consistent scale, a grid for measuring distance, correct orientation of features to each other, accounting for the actual shape of terrain, the true length of roads, and adjustment for the curve of hills and rivers. The map he drew from them is lost, but the six principles were cited by Chinese cartographers for centuries afterward.

Petrus Peregrinus was a French soldier and scholar who, in 1269, wrote the earliest surviving treatise devoted entirely to magnetism, the Epistola de magnete. He carved a lodestone into a sphere, laid a needle flat on its surface at different points and marked the direction it swung until the marks traced circles converging on two opposite points.

He called those points poles by analogy with the Earth's own axis, the first clear statement that a magnet has two poles that behave differently towards each other. The letter also describes a pivoted compass needle housed for use at sea, a genuine improvement on floating needles, three centuries before William Gilbert's more famous study of magnetism built on the same groundwork.

Isabel Peron was Argentina's vice president when her husband, President Juan Peron, died in office in July 1974, and the constitution moved her into the presidency without an election. She became the first woman anywhere to hold the office of president of a nation.

Her government struggled against inflation, left and right wing violence, and a weak hold on the military, and she governed for less than two years before a coup removed her in March 1976. She was placed under house arrest and later left Argentina, and the military junta that replaced her launched the so called Dirty War against suspected dissidents.

Athens had already evacuated its population to Salamis and the Peloponnese by the time Xerxes's army entered the city in 480 BCE, so the burning destroyed buildings rather than people. A small garrison that had barricaded itself on the Acropolis was overrun and killed, and the temples there were torched along with the rest.

The Athenians later left some of the burned temple wreckage where it lay, incorporating fragments into new walls, a choice some archaeologists read as a deliberate memorial. The Persian fleet was destroyed at Salamis within weeks of the burning, and Athens rebuilt the Acropolis decades later under Pericles.

Peter III had ruled Russia for six months when his wife Catherine, backed by the Imperial Guard regiments he had alienated by favouring Prussia and cutting their privileges, had him arrested at his summer palace in June 1762 and forced his abdication within days.

He was moved under guard to the estate of Ropsha, where he died on 17 July, officially of haemorrhoidal colic. Catherine's own circle, including the guards officer left in charge of him, gave differing and contradictory accounts of a fight, leaving the exact cause disputed while the outcome was not: Catherine took the throne as Catherine the Great.

Petra sits in a desert that gets barely fifteen centimetres of rain a year, most of it in violent, brief storms. The Nabataeans met that with plaster-lined channels cut into the sandstone gorge walls, feeding cisterns hidden along the approach to the city so a flash flood became months of stored water rather than a hazard to be survived.

The system also protected the site itself: dams and a diversion tunnel at the mouth of the Siq kept floodwater out of the processional canyon, since a single storm could otherwise fill it in minutes. Without that engineering a caravan city with no river of its own could not have supported the population Petra reached by the first century BCE.

Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, a Swiss traveller working for the African Association under the name Sheikh Ibrahim, learned Arabic and Islamic law well enough to pass as a pilgrim among the Bedouin who controlled the Wadi Musa gorge. In August 1812 he persuaded a local guide to lead him through the narrow Siq, telling him he wished to sacrifice a goat at what he had heard was a tomb inside.

What he found was the rock-cut facade of the Khazneh, the centre of a Nabataean city carved into sandstone cliffs and abandoned to Bedouin use for centuries after trade routes shifted away from it. Burckhardt wrote up the discovery in a journal published after his death, and Petra became a fixed destination for European travellers within a generation.

Petrarch spent years hunting monastic libraries for manuscripts abandoned since antiquity, convinced that classical Rome held wisdom the medieval schools had buried under commentary. In 1345, searching the chapter library of Verona cathedral, he came across a manuscript of Cicero's letters to his friend Atticus, personal correspondence rather than the polished oratory Cicero was already known for.

Reading a great Roman statesman's private doubts and grievances gave Petrarch a model for a self scrutinising, individual voice that his own letters and sonnets then imitated. Historians of the Renaissance treat this find, one of several Petrarch made, as the moment humanist scholarship turned from admiring antiquity at a distance to reading it as one person addressing another.

The map that survives is a medieval copy, made around 1200 from a Roman original, of the empire's road network stretched into an impossibly long, thin strip nearly seven metres long and only about thirty four centimetres tall. Rivers, mountains and seas are squeezed to fit the shape, which is why the geography looks so distorted next to any modern map.

What it actually records are way stations along the roads and the distances between them, information a traveller or courier using the imperial post could use directly. It survived in a library at Worms until a scholar named Konrad Peutinger acquired it in the early sixteenth century, and it is now the only substantial map of the Roman road system to survive at all.

Phil Zimmermann released Pretty Good Privacy in 1991 as free software, built partly from RSA's public-key method, so that ordinary people, not just governments and corporations, could encrypt email strongly enough that even well-resourced attackers could not readily break it. He wrote it, by his own account, out of concern for activists and dissidents whose communications could otherwise be read.

Because PGP used strong cryptography and spread online beyond American borders, the United States government opened a criminal investigation into Zimmermann under export control laws that treated powerful encryption like a weapon. The case dragged on for three years before being dropped in 1996 without charges, by which point PGP had already become a fixture of digital privacy tools.

The Phantom of the Opera opened at Her Majesty's Theatre in London's West End in October 1986, adapting Gaston Leroux's novel about a disfigured composer who haunts the Paris Opera House and grooms a young singer he becomes obsessed with, staged with a falling chandelier as its signature effect.

Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote the title role for Sarah Brightman, his wife at the time, and cast Michael Crawford as the Phantom opposite her. The production transferred to Broadway the following year and became one of the longest-running and highest-grossing stage shows in history.

Philip II was killed in 336 BC at Aegae during festivities for his daughter's wedding, stabbed by Pausanias, one of his own royal bodyguards, as he walked into the theatre. Pausanias was cut down by other guards while fleeing, before he could be questioned, which left his motive a matter of ancient speculation rather than confirmed record.

Ancient historians offered rival explanations, from a personal grievance over an unpunished assault to a wider court conspiracy possibly involving Persia or rivals close to the throne, and no version is provable from what survives. The immediate effect is not in doubt: Philip's twenty-year-old son Alexander was proclaimed king within days, inheriting an army and a kingdom Philip had spent his reign building.

Rowing a warship faster meant either a longer hull, which made it fragile, or more rowers on the same length, which meant stacking them. Phoenician builders solved it by raising a second bank of oarsmen above the first on a stepped hull, roughly doubling the number of oars without doubling the ship's length.

Assyrian palace reliefs from the 700s BCE show these two tiered galleys serving Phoenician cities under Assyrian control, rowers packed close with a ram at the bow. Greek shipwrights later added a third bank to produce the trireme, but the bireme's stacked layout was the design that made a longer warship possible in the first place.

Bertrand Piccard came from a family of record-setting explorers, his grandfather having been the first person to reach the stratosphere by balloon and his father the deepest point of the ocean. Piccard and British co-pilot Brian Jones lifted off from Chateau d'Oex in Switzerland on 1 March 1999 in the Breitling Orbiter 3, a helium and hot-air hybrid balloon.

They rode the jet stream eastward across Africa, the Middle East and Asia, sleeping in shifts in a pressurised capsule for nearly three weeks, and landed in the Egyptian desert on 21 March after almost twenty days aloft. It was the first nonstop circumnavigation of the world by balloon, a feat that had eluded dozens of earlier attempts, several of them fatal.

Dutch admiral Piet Heyn, sailing for the Dutch West India Company, trapped an entire Spanish silver fleet in the Bay of Matanzas off Cuba in September 1628, catching its ships before they could unload or scatter. The Spanish crews, facing an unwinnable fight, mostly abandoned their vessels rather than engage.

The captured cargo, mainly silver bullion along with gold, pearls and dyes, was worth roughly twelve million guilders, funding a dividend the Dutch West India Company paid out to its shareholders that same year. The loss briefly pushed Spain toward financial crisis and made Heyn a celebrated figure in the Dutch Republic, later commemorated in a children's song still sung today.

Plzen's brewers had a public reason to want a new beer: in 1838, townsfolk publicly dumped dozens of barrels of the local ale, judging it undrinkable. The city built a new civic brewery and hired a Bavarian brewer, Josef Groll, who brought bottom-fermenting lager yeast and a technique for pale malting that had just spread from Britain.

Groll's first batch, tapped in October 1842, came out a clear golden colour nobody in Bohemia had produced before, in a country used to darker, cloudier beers. Improved glassware let drinkers actually see that clarity, and the style, sold as Pilsner, was copied so widely across Europe and beyond that the city name became shorthand for an entire category of beer.

By the eighth century BCE, Egypt had fragmented into competing local rulers, several of them controlling only a single city in the Nile Delta. Piye, king of Kush ruling from Napata in Nubia, marched north around 728 BCE, defeating a coalition of these Delta princes in a campaign he recorded in unusual detail on a granite stele.

That stele describes him imposing ritual purity on defeated rivals before allowing them into his presence, a display of moral as much as military superiority. Having secured the crown, Piye returned south to Nubia rather than ruling from Egypt directly, leaving the throne to his successors of what became Egypt's Twenty Fifth Dynasty.

Francisco Pizarro had already captured and executed the Inca emperor Atahualpa when he chose a site for a new colonial capital rather than ruling from the Andean city of Cusco. In January 1535 he founded a city on the banks of the Rimac river near the Pacific coast, naming it Ciudad de los Reyes, City of Kings.

The coastal location gave Spain easy shipping access for the silver being extracted from Andean mines, which mattered more to Pizarro than Cusco's highland prestige. The name Lima, likely a Spanish corruption of Rimac, eventually replaced the formal one in common use, and the city became the seat of Spanish colonial government for most of South America.

Ralph Plaisted was a Minnesota insurance salesman and amateur explorer, not a career adventurer, when he led a snowmobile expedition across the frozen Arctic Ocean to the North Pole in April 1968. His team's arrival, confirmed by satellite navigation, made them the first confirmed surface party verified to have reached the pole, since Robert Peary's 1909 claim had never been independently substantiated.

The expedition relied on air-dropped fuel and supplies along its route rather than travelling fully unsupported, a distinction later expeditions would treat as a separate category of achievement. Plaisted's success nonetheless settled a question that had lingered for nearly sixty years: whether anyone had actually stood at the pole itself, on the surface, and could prove it.

Charles Wheatstone, already known for early telegraph work, devised his letter pair cipher around 1854, but it carries a different man's name because his friend Lord Playfair was the one who pushed it in front of the government. Wheatstone reportedly demonstrated it to officials at the Foreign Office, only to be told it was too complicated for their clerks to learn.

Playfair's advocacy eventually won the cipher a place in British military use, and it saw real service in the Boer War and the First World War, encrypting messages by substituting pairs of letters according to their position on a five by five grid built from a keyword. It was not unbreakable, but it was far sturdier against casual attack than the simple letter for letter substitutions officers had relied on before.

Playing cards had circulated in the Islamic world for generations before Europe took any documented notice of them. The change came abruptly: city councils across the continent began banning or taxing card games within a few years of each other, suggesting the cards themselves, likely carried through Mamluk Egypt and Mediterranean trade, spread with unusual speed once they arrived.

In 1377 a Dominican friar named John of Rheinfelden wrote a treatise in Basel describing a fifty-two card deck of ten numbered cards and three court figures, the earliest detailed European account of how the game was played. Florence's city records mention card playing that same year, and by 1380 cards are attested in Basel, Regensburg, Brabant, Paris and Barcelona alike.

Poggio Bracciolini was a papal secretary who spent his idle stretches at the Council of Constance combing German monastery libraries for classical texts the Church had let rot. In 1417, at a monastery usually identified as Fulda, he found a manuscript of Lucretius's On the Nature of Things, a poem arguing that the world is made of atoms moving through empty space, with no gods intervening and no soul that survives the body.

Poggio had it copied and sent to Italy; that copy is lost, but it was copied again, and one of those descendants survives today in Florence. The poem's account of a universe without divine oversight unsettled and fascinated readers across the Renaissance, feeding arguments that would later trouble Galileo's contemporaries and, further off still, Enlightenment materialists.

Henri Poincare posed the question in 1904, and for the rest of the twentieth century it resisted every attempt to settle it, becoming one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems with a million dollar reward. In 2002 and 2003, Grigori Perelman posted three papers to an online preprint server rather than a journal, sketching a proof built on Richard Hamilton's earlier work on Ricci flow.

It took other mathematicians several years to verify the argument in full, since Perelman had left gaps for others to fill rather than writing every step out. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2006 and the million dollar Clay Prize in 2010, and turned both down, saying he had already decided what mattered to him and it was not recognition.

Polybius was a Greek hostage turned historian, taken to Rome after Macedon's defeat and later attached to the Roman general Scipio. His histories cover the rise of Rome, but the grid he is remembered for was originally a signalling method, meant to be read at a distance rather than kept secret.

Two banks of torches, raised in groups, could spell out a row and column number for each letter, so a message could cross a valley without a runner. Centuries later cryptographers reused the same five by five grid to turn letters into number pairs, which is why a device built for line of sight ended up naming an early cipher.

Piracy had grown so severe by the late 60s BCE that it was strangling Rome's grain shipments and driving up food prices in the capital itself. The Lex Gabinia of 67 BCE granted Pompey extraordinary powers over the entire Mediterranean and its coasts, an unprecedented concentration of command that many senators distrusted.

Pompey divided the sea into zones under subordinate commanders and swept through them methodically rather than chasing individual raiders, clearing organised piracy from the Mediterranean within a matter of months. The speed of the campaign, achieved in roughly a single season, made his name and set the template for the extraordinary commands he would seek again.

Paris bridges before this one were crowded with houses and shops built along their length, so a crossing gave no view of the river at all and often blocked it from passersby entirely. Work on a new bridge near the tip of the Ile de la Cite began under Henry III in 1578 and dragged through the wars of religion, finishing under Henry IV, who opened it in 1607.

Built with twelve stone arches and, deliberately, no buildings on its deck, the Pont Neuf gave Parisians their first open sightline down the Seine from a bridge. Its raised pavements, separating pedestrians from cart traffic, were also new to the city. Despite its name, meaning new bridge, it is now the oldest standing bridge across the Seine in Paris.

Telford's aqueduct opened on 26 November 1805 after ten years of building, carrying the Llangollen Canal some 38 metres above the River Dee on eighteen stone piers. The trough itself is cast iron, bolted and flanged rather than riveted, and sealed with a mortar of Welsh flannel soaked in sugar and lead, a detail from the site records rather than folklore.

William Jessop was the engineer of record and Telford the resident engineer who oversaw construction, a division of credit that later biographies often collapse into Telford alone. Boats still cross it today on a towpath cantilevered off one side, with nothing but the iron trough wall between the water and a considerable drop, and it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.

Florence had already rebuilt its crossing of the Arno at this narrow point several times since Roman days, each version lost to flood. A catastrophic flood in November 1333 destroyed the previous medieval bridge entirely, and the city commissioned a sturdier replacement, completed by 1345 and credited in tradition to the architect Taddeo Gaddi.

Shops were built directly onto the bridge from the start, originally butchers and tanners whose waste could be tipped straight into the river below, later replaced by goldsmiths after a sixteenth century decree cleaned up the trade. The bridge survived the 1966 Arno flood and, alone among Florence's bridges, was spared deliberate demolition by retreating German forces in 1944.

Charles Ponzi promised Boston investors returns of fifty percent in weeks by claiming to profit from international postal reply coupons, a genuine but tiny financial instrument that could not possibly generate the volume of profit he described. Money from new investors simply paid off earlier ones, a structure that could only ever collapse once new money slowed.

A newspaper investigation in 1920 found that Ponzi's operation had never bought coupons anywhere near the scale needed to cover his promises, and a run on his company followed. Investors lost an estimated fifteen million dollars, and Ponzi's name became the generic term for the scheme, even though the underlying fraud had been used by others long before him.

Afonso Henriques had already been calling himself king for years, since routing his own mother Teresa at the battle of Sao Mamede in 1128 and later claiming a victory over the Moors at Ourique in 1139. What changed in 1143 was recognition: at Zamora, his cousin Alfonso VII of Leon accepted him as king rather than as a rebellious count owing homage.

The Treaty of Zamora did not settle everything, since the papacy withheld formal recognition of Portugal's independence until 1179, decades later. But 1143 is the point at which the county of Portugal, carved out of Leon and Castile during the reconquest, stopped being a contested vassal territory and became a kingdom other rulers had to deal with as one.

The Orloj was installed on the south wall of Prague's Old Town Hall in 1410, built by the clockmaker Mikulas of Kadan with astronomical advice from Jan Sindel, an astronomer at Charles University. Its dial tracks the sun and moon against the zodiac using a geocentric model, so it still shows Earth fixed at the centre with everything else turning around it, exactly as its first audience understood the sky.

A calendar wheel of the months was added later, and a set of moving figures, including a skeletal figure of death that tolls the hour, dates from the nineteenth century rather than 1410. The mechanism itself has been rebuilt and repaired repeatedly after fires and wartime damage, so almost none of the metal turning today is original to the fifteenth century, only the design.

Evangelical Presbyterians shaped by the religious revival known as the Great Awakening chartered the College of New Jersey in 1746, seeking to train ministers sympathetic to their movement rather than the more traditional clergy other colonial colleges produced.

It moved twice, first from Elizabeth to Newark, before settling in the town of Princeton in 1756, and over the following century grew from a small seminary-adjacent school into a broader university, eventually adopting the town's name as its own.

The Kingdom of Hungary had installed a march, a border province, east of the Carpathians to guard against Tatar raids, ruling it through vassal voivodes answerable to the Hungarian crown. Bogdan of Cuhea, a Romanian voivode from neighbouring Maramures who had fallen out with the Hungarian king, crossed the mountains around 1359 and drove out the Hungarian appointed ruler.

Bogdan's revolt turned the Hungarian march into an independent principality, Moldavia, with its own line of rulers and, eventually, its own church hierarchy. Hungary tried repeatedly and failed to reassert control over the following decades. Modern Moldova and much of eastern Romania trace their historical identity to the state Bogdan founded by that act of defection.

In 1477, a Bologna press issued the first printed edition of Ptolemy's Geographia with its maps rendered as engravings rather than hand copied by scribes. Ptolemy had compiled coordinate tables in Alexandria around 150 AD, and for a thousand years each copy of his atlas had drifted slightly from the last through manual reproduction, so no two readers were quite looking at the same world.

Engraving fixed the image once and let a press strike hundreds of identical copies, meaning a scholar in Nuremberg and one in Florence could now argue over exactly the same lines. Later fifteenth century editions began correcting and adding to Ptolemy's outdated Old World geography, but this Bologna printing came first, and it made a shared, checkable map available at a scale no scribe could match.

In 1156 the emperor Frederick Barbarossa issued the Privilegium Minus to settle a dispute over Bavaria, raising the Babenberg march of Austria, previously a lesser border territory, into a duchy in its own right. The charter granted Duke Henry II Jasomirgott special rights, including a rule that let Austria pass to a daughter if no son survived, unusual for the time.

The document survives only as a later, contested copy, which is why historians distinguish it from a hypothetical original, the Privilegium Maius forged two centuries afterward to inflate Habsburg claims further. Genuine or not in every clause, the 1156 charter is the point historians mark as the birth of Austria as a distinct political entity rather than a frontier march.

Utah's ratification on 5 December 1933 gave the Twenty-first Amendment the three-quarters of states it needed, ending the nationwide ban on alcohol that the Eighteenth Amendment had imposed fourteen years earlier. It remains the only constitutional amendment ratified specifically to undo an earlier one.

The new amendment did not simply switch alcohol back on. It handed control to the states, several of which kept their own prohibition laws running for years afterward, Mississippi longest of all, into 1966. It also barred alcohol from being shipped into any state in violation of that state's own laws, a clause still cited in disputes over interstate liquor sales today.

After crushing the French field armies within weeks of the war's opening in 1870, Prussian and allied German forces surrounded Paris rather than storming it, calculating that hunger would do the work artillery could not against the city's extensive fortifications.

The siege lasted through the winter of 1870 into 1871; residents ate horses, rats and eventually animals from the zoo as supplies collapsed, while balloons carried mail out over the encirclement. Paris surrendered in January 1871, and the humiliation, followed by the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, left a resentment that shaped French policy for decades.

Przewalski's horse had vanished from the wild by the 1960s, surviving only in zoos descended from a small number of animals captured decades earlier. Coordinated breeding programmes across several countries slowly rebuilt a genetically viable population in captivity over the following decades.

In 1992, captive-bred horses were released into the Mongolian steppe, into reserves established specifically for their return, restoring a wild population of the only horse species that had never been domesticated. Later reintroductions expanded the wild range further, and the species' conservation status has since improved from extinct in the wild.

Egypt in the mid seventh century BCE was governed as a set of Assyrian backed local rulers, a legacy of Assyria's own conquest of the country. Psamtik I, one of these vassal princes based at Sais, gradually built power and alliances, reportedly using Greek and Carian mercenaries paid for with royal favour.

Around 664 BCE he moved against his rival delta rulers and expelled the remaining Assyrian influence, reuniting Egypt under native rule for the first time in decades. His Twenty Sixth Dynasty went on to rule for over a century, a period later remembered as a deliberate revival of much older Egyptian art and religious forms.

Ptolemy worked in Alexandria, where the old Library still gave a scholar access to centuries of travellers' and surveyors' reports gathered from across the empire and beyond it. His Geographia turned that material into a gazetteer of roughly eight thousand places, each given a latitude and longitude rather than a description in prose.

He also set out mathematical methods for projecting a curved surface onto a flat page, including a conic projection that tried to preserve relative distances. His coordinates were often wrong, sometimes by a wide margin, but the idea of a place fixed by a grid of numbers rather than a story about how to reach it shaped every map that followed.

Before these coins, exchange across northern India ran on weighed metal and barter rather than a struck currency. Around the fifth century BC, the Mahajanapada kingdoms, a cluster of rival states along the Ganges including Magadha and Kosala, began cutting silver into standard weights and stamping each piece with a punch, sometimes several from different issuing authorities on one coin.

The symbols, suns, hills, trees, elephants, are not a script and carry no ruler's name or date, so dating and attributing individual issues still relies on hoards found alongside better-dated material. They mark the start of a monetary economy in South Asia, one that Mauryan and later kingdoms built directly on.

The Greek city of Tarentum in southern Italy, threatened by Rome's expansion, appealed to King Pyrrhus of Epirus for help around 280 BCE. Pyrrhus crossed with an army that included war elephants, animals Roman soldiers had never faced in battle.

He won two costly victories against Roman legions but lost so many veteran officers doing it that he is said to have remarked another such win would ruin him, the origin of the phrase 'pyrrhic victory'. He eventually withdrew from Italy without securing lasting control of it.

Ming general Qi Jiguang, appointed to Zhejiang province after years of ineffective wokou suppression, rejected the poorly trained militias that had failed before him and instead recruited and drilled a new force from local farmers and miners. His so called Mandarin Duck formation grouped soldiers with spears, shields and bamboo pikes to counter the long Japanese style swords wokou raiders favoured.

From 1559 his retrained troops won a string of victories against wokou bands along the Zhejiang coast, breaking the raiders' grip on the region within a few years. Qi later wrote influential military manuals based on the campaign, and his methods were applied again when he was posted north to defend against Mongol incursions.

Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard published their scheme, later called BB84 for the year, in 1984, proposing to send a secret key encoded not in numbers on a wire but in the polarisation of individual photons of light. Quantum mechanics guarantees that measuring a photon's polarisation in the wrong way disturbs it, so the two ends of the link could compare a subset of their results afterward to check whether anyone had been listening in.

If an eavesdropper intercepts and measures the photons to read the key, that same disturbance shows up as detectable errors, letting the sender and receiver discard the compromised key and try again. Unlike RSA, whose security rests on a problem believed to be hard, BB84's security rests on a law of physics, and small networks using it have since been built.

Anne became queen in March 1702 on the death of her brother-in-law William III, having already outlived every one of her own seventeen pregnancies, none of which produced a child who survived her. She was the last Stuart to rule and the last British monarch to exercise a personal veto over an act of Parliament, which she used in 1708 to block a Scottish militia bill.

The defining act of her reign was the Union of 1707, which merged the separate Parliaments of England and Scotland into a single Kingdom of Great Britain with one flag and one sovereign. Because she left no heir, the crown passed on her death in 1714 not to a closer Catholic relative but to her German cousin George, Elector of Hanover, under the terms of the earlier Act of Settlement.

Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada led an expedition inland from the Caribbean coast in search of gold and El Dorado, losing most of his men to disease and hunger along the way before reaching the high plateau of the Muisca people. In 1538 he founded a settlement there among huts he called Santa Fe, after his birthplace in Spain, on the site of a former Muisca town.

The Muisca had already built a dense network of settlements across the plateau, drawn by fertile soil and salt deposits Quesada's expedition prized as much as any gold. Santa Fe grew into the colonial capital of New Granada and was later renamed Bogota, a name derived from the Muisca settlement it replaced rather than anything Spanish.

Harriet Quimby had been flying for barely a year when she decided to cross the Channel that had made Bleriot famous. She had earned her pilot's licence in August 1911, the first American woman to do so, after training in secret so newspapers would not mock her if she failed.

On 16 April 1912 she flew a borrowed Bleriot monoplane from Dover to a French beach in under an hour, navigating by compass through fog thick enough that she lost sight of land almost immediately. The achievement barely registered in the press: the Titanic had sunk the day before, and Quimby's crossing was pushed off nearly every front page in America and Britain.

The Quran's ban on intoxicants did not arrive as a single flat rule. Earlier verses had only warned that wine carried both benefit and sin, or barred prayer while drunk; a later revelation, traditionally placed around 625, called wine and gambling handiwork of Satan to be avoided outright, and it is this verse that later jurists read as a full prohibition.

The change reordered what was grown and traded across a region where vineyards had supplied Roman and Persian tables for centuries. Grape production shifted toward raisins and syrups, and later Islamic law extended the ban to any fermented drink capable of intoxicating, not wine alone, a scope debated by scholars ever since.

Yigal Amir fired three shots at close range as Yitzhak Rabin walked to his car after a Tel Aviv peace rally on 4 November 1995. Amir was a law student and religious nationalist who had tried at least twice before to get near Rabin, and he later told investigators he acted alone to stop the Oslo Accords from ceding land he believed belonged to Israel by right.

Rabin had signed the accords with Yasser Arafat two years earlier and shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize for it. His killing came amid a campaign of rabbinic rulings and rally placards branding him a traitor and a Nazi, and it hardened rather than paused the argument over the accords, which stalled in the years that followed.

Rachel Wall worked the New England coast with her husband George in the early 1780s, stealing a boat and drifting it into shipping lanes after storms to look wrecked. When she called out for help from the deck, rescuers who came aboard were robbed, and sometimes killed.

George drowned in a storm around 1782, and Wall returned to Boston as a servant. She was hanged there in October 1789, formally for a robbery on land rather than piracy at sea, and reportedly asked to be remembered as a pirate instead. She was the last woman executed in Massachusetts.

Engineers building the Uganda Railway needed a depot roughly halfway between Mombasa and Lake Victoria, and in 1899 they chose a swampy plain around a Maasai watering hole they called Ewaso Nyirobi, cold water, for lack of any better feature to build around.

The site was picked for its flat ground and central position on the rail line, not for its climate or drainage, and early accounts describe a camp plagued by mud, plague and malaria. It grew anyway, first into the railway's headquarters and then into the colonial capital of British East Africa, becoming Nairobi, the capital of independent Kenya.

Before 1840, a traveller crossing England could reset their watch several times over, because each town kept its own solar noon: Bristol ran about ten minutes behind London, Exeter further still. That patchwork was tolerable on foot or by coach but dangerous on a railway running to a printed timetable, where two trains could occupy the same track at what each crew thought was a different time.

In November 1840 the Great Western Railway ordered every station along its line to keep London time, set by the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, rather than local time. Other companies followed through the 1840s, long before Parliament made Greenwich Mean Time the legal standard for the whole country in 1880. The railway, not the state, was what actually synchronised Britain's clocks.

The Siamese capital of Thonburi sat on the western bank of the Chao Phraya river, a site King Taksin had chosen after Ayutthaya fell to Burmese invasion. When Rama I took the throne in 1782, he judged Thonburi's ground too soft and its layout too exposed, and moved the capital across the river.

He built a new city on the eastern bank around a site called Bang Makok, laying out a royal palace, temples and canals modelled on the destroyed splendour of Ayutthaya. The new capital took the ceremonial name Krung Thep, but foreigners kept using Bangkok, the old fishing village's name, which stuck internationally even as Thais call their capital something else entirely.

A secondary wife of Ramesses III, Tiye, organised a conspiracy to have her own son placed on the throne instead of the designated heir, drawing in harem officials, a military commander and even a magician who supplied wax figures for a ritual curse. Court records of the trial, the Judicial Papyrus of Turin, survive describing the plotters' punishments.

For a long time it was unclear whether the plot actually succeeded in killing the king around 1155 BCE. A 2012 forensic study, including a CT scan of his mummy, found his throat had been cut deeply enough to be immediately fatal, confirming that the conspiracy reached its target before it was uncovered.

A coalition of seaborne groups collectively called the Sea Peoples had already toppled several Bronze Age kingdoms across the eastern Mediterranean by the time they turned toward Egypt around 1175 BCE. Ramesses III met them with a defence planned in advance, positioning archers along the Nile Delta's mouths rather than waiting to be overrun inland.

Reliefs at his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu show a naval battle in which Egyptian ships pinned the invaders' vessels against the shore while land forces closed in. The victory did not restore Egypt's earlier reach abroad, but it kept the invasion from reaching the Nile Valley itself, unlike several neighbouring powers that did not survive the same wave.

Jeannette Rankin won her Montana House seat in November 1916, four years before the nineteenth amendment gave women the vote nationwide, because Montana had already extended suffrage to women in 1914. She took office the following March.

Rankin voted against United States entry into both world wars, the only member of Congress to vote against both, a stance that cost her re-election after the first vote and ended her second term after the vote in 1941. She never framed her pacifism as separate from her feminism, arguing throughout her career that women in office should change how power was used, not just who held it.

On 3 April 1845 the Royal Navy lashed the propeller-driven HMS Rattler to the paddle steamer HMS Alecto stern to stern, both ships fitted with engines of similar power, and set them running against each other in a straight tug of war to settle which propulsion suited a warship better.

Rattler eased ahead within minutes and towed Alecto backward at roughly two and a half knots. The result persuaded the Admiralty that the screw propeller, tucked below the waterline and safe from gunfire, beat exposed paddle wheels, and new British warships were built with screws from that point on.
