Piracy and armed robbery against ships had surged in Southeast Asian waters through the 1990s, particularly around the Malacca Strait, without any shared system for nations to exchange warnings or evidence. In November 2004, sixteen governments concluded the ReCAAP agreement in Tokyo.

It was the first treaty of its kind negotiated directly between states rather than through shipping industry bodies. An information sharing centre, eventually based in Singapore, began circulating incident reports so that a hijacking spotted by one navy could be flagged to every signatory at once.

Sneferu's engineers had already tried and failed to build a true smooth-sided pyramid once, at the same Dahshur site, when the Bent Pyramid's angle had to be lowered partway up to stop it cracking. The Red Pyramid, built at the shallower angle from its base, is the first pyramid to reach the sky in one clean, unbroken line.

It takes its modern name from the reddish limestone exposed once the outer white casing was stripped away centuries later for other buildings. At roughly 105 metres it held the record for the tallest structure on Earth only briefly, since Sneferu's son Khufu soon built the Great Pyramid at Giza and eclipsed it.

Followers of a millenarian Buddhist movement rose against Mongol rule across central China, wrapping red cloth around their heads as a battlefield marker and drawing recruits from famine relief workers conscripted to repair the flooding Yellow River. What began as scattered local unrest spread quickly into an organised uprising against a Yuan government already weakened by plague and grain shortages.

The rebellion splintered into rival warlord factions almost as soon as it began, but one of its commanders, a former monk named Zhu Yuanzhang, outlasted the others and eventually drove the Mongols from China entirely. He founded the Ming dynasty in 1368, making the Red Turban uprising the opening chapter of a war that ended nearly a century of Mongol rule.

Wilhelm Justus, a young gardener, was stabbed near his heart and found unconscious in a Frankfurt park in September 1896. Surgeon Ludwig Rehn opened his chest, located a wound in the right ventricle, and did what surgical convention still held to be lethal by definition: he stitched a beating heart.

By the third suture the bleeding had stopped and the heart kept beating. Justus survived, and Rehn later collected over a hundred similar cases from other surgeons to show the operation could work reliably. Before this, a wound to the heart itself was assumed to be a death sentence no surgeon should try to interrupt.

On 23 April 1516, Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria issued a decree at Ingolstadt fixing what beer sold in his territory could legally contain: barley, hops and water, with yeast's role not yet understood and so left unmentioned. The rule also fixed prices by season, and it was partly a food security measure, since it kept wheat and rye reserved for baking bread rather than competing with brewers for the same grain.

Bavaria's version was not the first such law in German lands, but it outlasted the rest and was extended across a unified Germany in 1906, still cited today as the Reinheitsgebot, the purity law. Brewers elsewhere in Europe used a much wider range of flavourings and preservatives well into the nineteenth century, which is part of why Bavarian beer developed a distinct reputation.

Marian Rejewski was a young mathematician at Poland's Cipher Bureau in 1932, working from intercepted traffic and a commercial Enigma manual, but not from a captured military machine. Germany had wired its army version differently, and nobody outside the factory knew the internal connections of its rotors.

Rejewski used group theory, treating the daily key settings as a mathematical permutation, to deduce that wiring by pure deduction from the patterns in the traffic. French intelligence supplied stolen operating documents that confirmed his reconstruction. The break gave Poland, and later Britain, a working understanding of Enigma years before the war that made codebreaking at Bletchley Park possible.

The Colossus had stood for barely half a century when an earthquake struck Rhodes around 226 BC. Ancient writers say the bronze statue snapped at its weakest point, the knees, and toppled onto land rather than into the harbour it is often shown straddling in later drawings, which have no ancient basis.

Rhodes chose not to rebuild it. An oracle was said to have warned against re-erecting the statue, and the broken bronze pieces lay where they fell for centuries, still impressive enough that Pliny the Elder wrote most people could not span even a single finger with both arms. The remains were eventually sold as scrap metal after the Arab conquest of Rhodes in the seventh century AD.

Matteo Ricci had spent two decades in China learning the language and adapting his Jesuit mission to Ming court conventions before the emperor Wanli asked for a copy of a world map Ricci had shown local officials. Working with the scholars Li Zhizao and Zhong Wentao, Ricci produced Kunyu Wanguo Quantu in 1602, printed as six large woodblock panels meant to be mounted like a folding screen.

The map placed China centrally on the sheet rather than at either edge, a deliberate accommodation of Chinese expectations, and it was the first map in Chinese to include the Americas at all. Only a handful of original copies survive today. It let European geography reach an educated Chinese audience while letting Ricci frame his own presence as one more curiosity worth a place on the map.

Historians had long placed the grave of Richard III somewhere under Leicester, in the ruins of Greyfriars church torn down in the sixteenth century, but the exact spot was gone from memory. In August 2012 a University of Leicester team dug trial trenches in a council car park and, on the first day, found a skeleton with a curved spine and battle wounds to the skull.

DNA taken from two of his living matrilineal descendants matched the remains, confirming in February 2013 that the last Plantagenet king, killed at Bosworth in 1485, had spent over five centuries under a parking bay marked with a painted letter R that nobody had connected to him. He was reburied at Leicester Cathedral in 2015.

Richard was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 3 September 1189, a ceremony marred by a riot against London's Jewish community that broke out after rumours spread that Jews had tried to attend uninvited. Richard had already taken the cross before his father's death and treated the English crown chiefly as a source of money to fund the crusade he intended to lead.

He sold offices, castles and even royal rights to raise funds, reportedly joking that he would have sold London itself if a buyer could be found. Of his ten year reign he spent perhaps six months in England, the rest on crusade, in captivity after being seized on his return journey, or fighting to hold his French territories.

Sally Ride had a doctorate in physics and no astronaut ambitions when she answered a newspaper advertisement seeking scientists for NASA's astronaut programme in 1977, one of the first classes to accept women. She was selected from thousands of applicants and spent years training before her first flight was announced.

She launched aboard Challenger on 18 June 1983 as a mission specialist, becoming the first American woman in space, two decades after the Soviet Union sent Valentina Tereshkova. Ride later served on the boards investigating both the Challenger and Columbia shuttle disasters, and after her death in 2012 it became publicly known that she had spent 27 years in a relationship with a woman.

The Venetian state rented a wing of the Palazzo Dandolo near San Moise in 1638 and turned it into a public gaming house, partly to draw players away from the unlicensed rooms already thriving across the city and partly to tax them properly. It ran chiefly during Carnival, when Venice already tolerated a level of disguise unthinkable the rest of the year.

Patrons wore the bauta mask and tricorn hat required at the tables, which let nobles and commoners gamble side by side without anyone officially knowing who was losing what. Games included biribi and basetta, played for stakes high enough that the less wealthy were effectively priced out despite the open door. Mounting complaints about ruin and addiction led the Senate to close it in 1774.

In May 1578, workmen digging along the Via Salaria outside Rome broke through into a network of underground galleries lined with early Christian burials, sealed and largely forgotten since late antiquity. The find drew the antiquarian Antonio Bosio, later called the Columbus of the catacombs, who spent decades crawling through miles of the tunnels by lamplight, mapping passages that had swallowed earlier explorers who lost their way in the dark.

Bosio's survey, published after his death as Roma Sotterranea in 1632, became the foundation of Christian archaeology, cataloguing inscriptions, frescoes and burial niches that offered direct physical evidence of Rome's early church. The rediscovery reframed the catacombs from a rumour into a subject scholars could actually study underground.

By the first century CE, workshops in central Italy were casting oil lamps in two-piece moulds rather than shaping each one by hand, which let a single master pattern be copied thousands of times. The moulds themselves were taken from an existing lamp, so decoration spread from workshop to workshop faster than any individual potter could have carved it.

Many lamps carry a maker's stamp on the base, names like Fortis appearing on finds from Britain to the Black Sea, evidence of production and export on an industrial scale rather than local craft. Those stamps are largely how archaeologists trace trade routes and date the layers they turn up in, since the lamps themselves rarely carry any other record.

Rome's river port at Ostia handled grain, oil and wine unloaded from ships too large to reach the city itself, and cargo regularly went overboard in accidents or storms. The urinatores, whose Latin name simply means divers, worked as an organised trade rather than casual salvagers, diving without any breathing apparatus to recover what had sunk.

Inscriptions record their pay as a fixed share of whatever they brought up, scaled to depth: a diver working in deeper water kept a larger fraction of the goods than one working shallow. That sliding scale, preserved on stone rather than in any literary account, is most of what is known about how the guild actually operated.

Romania's independence was won on a battlefield it did not choose alone. Its army fought alongside Russia against the Ottomans in the war of 1877 to 1878, most visibly at the siege of Plevna in Bulgaria, and that shared campaign was the price of admission when the great powers met afterwards to settle the peace.

The Congress of Berlin in 1878 confirmed Romanian independence but also redrew its map, handing southern Bessarabia back to Russia and giving Romania the Danube delta region of Dobruja in exchange. Full recognition still came with conditions attached: the powers pressed Romania to grant citizenship rights to its Jewish population before treating the new state as fully sovereign.

Roman London began not as a fort or a palace but as a bridgehead: engineers found a stretch of the Thames narrow and firm-banked enough to cross, and built a timber bridge there a few years after the invasion of Britain in 43 CE. A trading settlement, Londinium, grew up on the north bank around it almost immediately.

It had no natural advantages that older British towns lacked; it existed because Roman surveyors chose that exact bend for a bridge. Boudica's revolt burned it to the ground within two decades of its founding, but it was rebuilt and grew into the largest town in Roman Britain, the direct ancestor of the City of London that still marks roughly the same ground today.

Rome had no permanent fire service for most of its early history, relying instead on private brigades, including one the wealthy Marcus Licinius Crassus reportedly used to buy burning buildings cheap before agreeing to put the fire out. Augustus replaced that arrangement in the year 6 with the Vigiles, a state corps organised into cohorts stationed across the city's districts.

The Vigiles carried buckets, hooks, ladders and a vinegar-soaked cloth called a centones, and they patrolled at night watching for both fire and burglary. Membership was open to freedmen, and after six years' service a vigile could earn Roman citizenship, making the corps as much a route into civic status as a fire brigade.

Birds kept on the Capitoline Hill as sacred to the goddess Juno were said to have honked and flapped when Gallic attackers tried to scale the hill at night, waking the sleeping garrison in time to repel the climbers. Rome's guard dogs, by contrast, reportedly slept through the whole thing.

The story comes down through later Roman historians writing centuries after the event, so its exact details cannot be verified, but it left a lasting mark on Roman religious practice: geese continued to be honoured on the Capitoline afterward, while a dog was reportedly punished each year in mock reenactment of the guards' failure.

Illyrian raiders operating under Queen Teuta's authority had been preying on merchant shipping in the Adriatic for years, and Roman envoys sent to protest were reportedly killed or mistreated rather than heard. Rome responded in 229 BCE by sending a large fleet and army across the Adriatic, its first major military intervention east of the Italian peninsula.

Teuta's forces could not hold against the Roman campaign, and she surrendered within a year, agreeing to withdraw her ships from most of the Adriatic and pay tribute. The war gave Rome its first direct foothold on the Balkan coast, a toehold that would grow into deeper involvement in Greek affairs within a generation.

James Clark Ross pinpointed the spot where compass needles pointed straight down, on the Boothia Peninsula's western coast, in June 1831, using a dip circle, an instrument that measures how steeply a suspended needle points downward as it nears the pole. When the needle registered nearly ninety degrees, almost straight down, Ross knew he was standing on the spot itself.

He planted the British flag there, though the pole itself is not fixed: it drifts continually as Earth's magnetic field shifts, and has since moved hundreds of kilometres from where Ross stood. His expedition was the first to pin it down at all, converting a theoretical point on a compass chart into a place a person could physically reach.

Rouen Cathedral's existing spire had burned down in the mid-nineteenth century, and its replacement was built not in stone or timber but cast iron, an unusual choice that let it reach an ambitious height quickly. Completed at roughly 151 metres, it briefly made Rouen the tallest building in the world.

The record did not last long. Within a few years the Washington Monument in the United States, then Cologne Cathedral in Germany, both surpassed it, and Rouen's iron spire settled into being simply the cathedral's most distinctive feature rather than a world record holder.

Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman worked through much of 1977 at MIT trying to build a workable version of the key-exchange idea Diffie and Hellman had published the year before. Shamir and Adleman have said the breakthrough came to Rivest one night after a Passover Seder, and the trio published their scheme, taking their initials as its name, in 1978.

RSA lets anyone encrypt a message using a freely published public key, while only the holder of a matching private key can decrypt it. Breaking it means factoring an enormous number into its two prime components, a problem with no known fast solution. Decades later the algorithm still secures much of the internet, from banking to browser certificates.

Russborough House, a Palladian mansion in County Wicklow, held a major private art collection assembled by Sir Alfred Beit when armed raiders broke in during April 1974, tied up Beit and his wife, and cut nineteen paintings from their frames, including works by Vermeer, Goya and Gainsborough.

The raid was organised by Rose Dugdale, an English heiress turned republican militant, as part of a plan to trade the paintings for the release of imprisoned IRA members. Police recovered the works within weeks after a tip led them to a rented cottage, and Dugdale was convicted and imprisoned, though Russborough's collection would be targeted in further burglaries over the following decades.

Magdeburg had sided with the Protestant cause during the Thirty Years' War, and in May 1631 Catholic League troops under Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, broke through its defences after a lengthy siege. What followed was one of the war's worst massacres, with soldiers killing residents in the streets and setting fire to buildings across the city.

Estimates of the dead vary widely between contemporary and later accounts, but a large majority of the roughly 25,000 people thought to have been in the city did not survive, and the fire left only a small fraction of Magdeburg's buildings standing. The destruction became a byword across Protestant Europe, invoked for the rest of the war as proof of what Catholic forces would do.

Anwar Sadat was killed in Cairo on 6 October 1981, during a military parade marking the anniversary of Egypt's crossing of the Suez Canal in the 1973 war. As a truck towing artillery passed the reviewing stand, Lieutenant Khalid Islambouli forced the driver to stop, then led an armed squad toward Sadat firing rifles and throwing grenades. Sadat reportedly stood to salute them, apparently mistaking the attack for part of the display.

The assault lasted under two minutes and killed Sadat along with several others in the stand. The attackers belonged to Egyptian Islamic Jihad, who regarded Sadat's 1979 peace treaty with Israel as a betrayal deserving death. Islambouli and three co-conspirators were tried and executed the following year; Hosni Mubarak, seated nearby and wounded slightly, succeeded him as president.

The Salisbury clock has no dial and never had one. It exists to ring bells on the hour, striking through a wrought iron frame of weights, gears and a verge escapement built around 1386, work that predates the pendulum by nearly three centuries. It sat first in a bell tower beside the cathedral and was moved inside once that tower was demolished in the eighteenth century.

Restored to running order in 1956 after decades stopped, it is presented as one of the oldest working mechanical clocks anywhere, though a near contemporary at Rouen Cathedral makes the same claim and the two are hard to rank precisely. Both descend from the same monastic need: knowing exactly when to ring the bells that told a town when to pray.

Arthur Samuel wrote his checkers program at IBM in 1959 on a machine, the 701, with barely enough memory to hold the board state, let alone search deep into future moves. His solution was to have the program play thousands of games against itself and against human opponents, adjusting the weights it used to score a position after each game based on whether it had won or lost.

The phrase machine learning appears in the title of Samuel's paper describing the work, one of its earliest uses. By the mid-1960s his program could beat strong amateur players, and IBM used a televised match against Samuel himself, whom it eventually surpassed, to demonstrate that a computer could improve at a task without being reprogrammed by hand.

Teatro San Cassiano opened in Venice in 1637 as the first theatre built specifically for opera performed for a paying public, rather than for aristocratic patrons at court. Anyone able to afford a ticket, not only invited nobility, could attend a fully staged opera for the first time.

The venue's tiered box seating, sold or rented to wealthy families, funded the productions and became the template for opera houses across Europe. It turned opera from a courtly entertainment into a commercial business with a paying audience, a shift that shaped how the art form was funded for centuries afterward.

Tradition holds that Marinus, a stonemason from the Adriatic island of Rab, worked on the rebuilding of Rimini before fleeing Diocletian's persecution of Christians. He climbed nearby Monte Titano and settled there as a hermit rather than as any kind of founder of a state, building a small chapel that drew a community around it.

That settlement is dated to 301 CE and is the basis of San Marino's claim to be the oldest surviving republic in the world, celebrated every year on the third of September as its national day. The tiny state has kept some form of self-government through the fall of Rome, the medieval city-states and Italian unification, never fully absorbed into any of the larger powers around it.

A ship's clock could not survive the pitching of a hull, so European sailors turned to the sandglass, whose falling sand kept time regardless of motion. By the mid-1300s crews were using half-hour glasses to mark the changing of watches, with a ship's boy tasked with turning the glass and striking a bell at each run, work precise enough that a missed turn could throw the whole day's reckoning off.

The same glass, paired with a line knotted at even intervals and trailed behind a moving ship, let sailors count how many knots ran out in a fixed number of turns and so estimate speed. That combination, refined over the following centuries, gave the vocabulary still used for a ship's speed today.

Alberto Santos-Dumont had already made his name in Paris flying dirigibles between the Eiffel Tower and his apartment. The 14-bis he unveiled in 1906 looked ungainly beside them, a boxy biplane hung nose-down from cellular wings, but on 23 October it lifted off before an official crowd at Bagatelle and covered a short measured distance.

European aviation had, until then, relied on the Wright brothers' own reports of flights made in private in Ohio and North Carolina. Santos-Dumont's hop was brief and low, but it happened in front of judges from the Aero Club de France, which is why French sources for decades called it the first flight anyone in Europe could actually verify.

Bosnian Serb forces besieging Sarajevo shelled the National and University Library in August 1992, setting it ablaze during the night. Firefighters trying to reach it came under sniper fire, and the building burned for days.

The library held over a million items, including rare Ottoman-era manuscripts and irreplaceable regional archives, and most of the collection was destroyed. Librarians and residents had formed human chains earlier in the siege trying to save what books they could carry out.

Johann Jacob Schweppe was a Geneva jeweller with a sideline in gasfitting when he refined a process, building on work by Joseph Priestley and others, for saturating water with carbon dioxide under pressure and bottling it so the fizz survived. He began selling it commercially in 1783 and moved the business to London within a decade to reach a bigger market.

Bottled mineral water was sold at first as a health tonic rather than a refreshment, marketed to physicians and sold through chemists. Schweppe's firm went on to supply carbonated water to the royal household and outlasted its founder by more than two centuries, eventually adding the flavoured mixers that carry the name today.

Herodotus was sceptical of his own story. He wrote that Scyllis, a diver from Scione who had recovered wreckage for the Persians after a storm off Mount Pelion, defected to the Greeks before the battle of Artemisium, swimming the whole way underwater, and added that he marvelled if the tale commonly told were true.

What Herodotus does trust is what Scyllis brought with him: a full account of storm damage to the Persian fleet and word that ships were being sent around Euboea to trap the Greeks. Acting on that intelligence, the Greek captains sailed out after midnight and destroyed the detached squadron before it could close the trap.

The first Treaty of Paris in 1814 had been lenient, letting France keep its 1792 borders after Napoleon's abdication. His return during the Hundred Days changed the calculation entirely, and after Waterloo the allies signed a second treaty in November 1815 that pushed France back to its 1790 boundaries and imposed an indemnity.

An army of occupation, funded by France itself, was stationed in the north for up to five years to guarantee the terms were kept. It left early, in 1818, once the payments were settled, and the settlement held for the rest of the century without another general European war.

The Seeing Eye was founded in Nashville before relocating to Morristown, New Jersey, becoming the first school in the United States to train dogs specifically to guide blind handlers safely through everyday obstacles like traffic and steps. The idea was adapted from a German programme that had trained guide dogs for blinded veterans of the First World War.

Its founder, Dorothy Harrison Eustis, had written about the German programme after visiting it, prompting a blind American reader to ask her to train him a dog of his own. That request led directly to the school's founding, and its training methods became the model most guide dog organisations still follow.

Sennacherib, the Assyrian king whose army besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE, was murdered in Nineveh in 681 BCE. Babylonian chronicles and biblical accounts agree only that sons of his killed him, disagreeing on which son and on whether it happened while he was at prayer inside a temple.

The killing set off a succession war won by his son Esarhaddon, who hunted down his rival brothers and later had his own account of the murder carved into official inscriptions, blaming them for it. Assyria's throne passed to Esarhaddon within months, though the killers themselves are never securely named in the surviving record.

The Assyrian king Sennacherib completed a stone aqueduct at Jerwan around 690 BCE, part of a larger canal system he built to bring water from the mountains to his capital at Nineveh, in what is now northern Iraq. An inscription on the structure credited the king directly with its construction.

The aqueduct carried water across a valley on a raised stone channel supported by arches, a technique that predates the aqueducts Rome later became famous for by several centuries. Sennacherib used the water partly to irrigate royal gardens at Nineveh, which some scholars have argued may be the true origin behind later legends of Babylon's hanging gardens.

Stefan Nemanjic, son of the Serbian state's founder Stefan Nemanja, had ruled as grand prince for years before seeking a crown that would put him on equal footing with neighbouring kings rather than as a lesser regional ruler. In 1217 he obtained one from Pope Honorius III, earning him the byname Stefan the First Crowned.

The choice of a papal, rather than Byzantine, crown was pragmatic: Constantinople was under Latin occupation after the Fourth Crusade and in no position to grant one. His brother Sava, already a monk of standing, secured Serbia's own autocephalous Orthodox church a few years later, so the kingdom's crown and its church came from different, deliberately balanced directions.

Roman tradition dated the city's first defensive wall to King Servius Tullius in the sixth century BCE, but the stone wall archaeologists have actually found, enclosing all seven of Rome's hills, was built around 378 BCE. It followed the Gallic sack of the city decades earlier, an event that exposed how undefended Rome had been.

Built from volcanic tuff blocks quarried locally, the wall ran for roughly seven miles and stood for centuries as the city's main defence, even after Rome's territory expanded far beyond any wall could enclose. Sections still visible today, including one near Termini railway station, are routinely mistaken by visitors for a much later structure.

Egypt's grip on the Levant had weakened during the religious upheaval of Akhenaten's reign, when royal attention turned inward to a new capital and a new cult. Seti I, taking the throne around 1290 BCE, moved quickly to campaign back into Canaan and Syria, restoring garrisons and vassal loyalties that had drifted away.

His war reliefs at the Karnak temple record the campaigns in detail, including a clash with Hittite forces over contested territory. The gains proved unstable: his son Ramesses II would fight the Hittites again at Kadesh a generation later over the same disputed ground.

The New Zealand Company sold land in London to settlers before it had secured any agreement with the Maori people who actually held it, then sent ships to find a site matching the promises made. In January 1840 the first colonists landed at Port Nicholson on the southern tip of the North Island and began building a settlement.

The harbour offered good anchorage but little flat ground, forcing early streets onto steep hillsides that still shape the city today. Named Wellington after the Duke of Wellington, it became the colonial capital in 1865, chosen chiefly for its central position between the North and South Islands rather than for the cramped site itself.

Shakey, built at the Stanford Research Institute between 1966 and 1972, got its name from the way its television camera and rangefinder rig visibly wobbled on top of its wheeled base as it moved through a set of rooms built specifically to test it, furnished with wedge- and block-shaped obstacles it had to navigate around.

What made Shakey notable was not the hardware but the software: it could take a general instruction, break it into a sequence of smaller actions, and replan if a planned move turned out to be blocked, rather than simply executing a fixed script. The STRIPS planning system written for it influenced automated planning in artificial intelligence for decades afterward.

Claude Shannon had already founded information theory when, in a 1949 Bell Labs paper on communication theory of secrecy systems, he asked what a cipher would need to be mathematically unbreakable rather than merely hard to break in practice. He defined perfect secrecy as a cipher whose output reveals nothing about the message, even to an attacker with unlimited computing power.

He then proved that only one cipher meets that standard: the one-time pad, a key as long as the message, used once and never reused, with each key never repeated across messages. Every other cipher, however elaborate, leaks some statistical trace of the plaintext. The proof gave cryptographers a fixed benchmark for exactly what security a system could and could not claim.

The game arrived in Persia from India as chaturanga, four battlefield divisions represented by pieces on a board, and Persian players renamed it shatranj and reworked its rules within a few generations. They kept the elephant, chariot, horse and foot soldier but sharpened the endgame, and Persian scribes began writing down finished problems rather than leaving the game to be played and forgotten.

Those written studies, some surviving in Arabic translation, are the earliest chess literature known. When Arab armies took Persia in the seventh century they took shatranj with them, and its vocabulary followed: the shah, or king, is why a losing king is checkmated, from shah mat, the king is helpless.

Show Boat opened on Broadway in December 1927, adapting Edna Ferber's novel about performers on a Mississippi riverboat into a musical that wove its songs, including Ol' Man River, directly into a plot dealing with interracial marriage and the hardships of Black characters, rather than treating the story as mere scaffolding for numbers.

Earlier Broadway musicals had largely been revues or light comedies strung together with unrelated songs. Show Boat's integration of serious drama with a fully composed score, by Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II, is widely credited with reshaping what an American stage musical could attempt.

Until 1967 the second was defined as a fixed fraction of a mean solar day, a unit tied to how fast the Earth happens to spin. That spin turns out to wobble very slightly as tides, earthquakes and the shifting mass of ice sheets nudge it, which made the second an unreliable ruler for physics that needed better precision than the planet could offer.

The 13th General Conference on Weights and Measures redefined the second in 1967 as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation absorbed by a caesium-133 atom transitioning between two energy states, a number chosen to match the old astronomical second as closely as possible. Caesium clocks built to that definition can run for millions of years without gaining or losing a second, and every atomic clock since has used the same standard.

Augustus Siebe, a German instrument maker working in London, sealed his helmet directly to a full waterproofed canvas suit in 1837, closing the open neck the Deane brothers' helmet had left exposed. A valve inside kept the suit from flooding no matter which way the diver turned or bent, unlike the open design it replaced.

Air still came down a hose from a surface pump, but the sealed suit meant a diver could work upside-down or lying flat without water pouring in. Siebe's closed dress became the standard diving suit worldwide, essentially unchanged in principle, and stayed in commercial use for salvage and engineering work into the mid twentieth century.

German forces launched a surprise offensive through the Ardennes forest in December 1944, and Bastogne's road junctions made the small Belgian town a target both sides needed. American paratroopers of the 101st Airborne, rushed in without winter gear, found themselves surrounded within days.

When a German commander demanded surrender on 22 December, acting commander Anthony McAuliffe's written reply was a single word: nuts, which the German officers receiving it had to have explained to them. Relief arrived days later as General Patton's forces broke through from the south, and the town's defence became a defining episode of the Battle of the Bulge.

France established a fortified base at Dien Bien Phu in a remote highland valley in late 1953, expecting to draw Viet Minh forces into a set-piece battle its artillery and air support could win. General Vo Nguyen Giap instead hauled heavy guns by hand through jungle terrain the French had judged impassable.

Viet Minh artillery, positioned on high ground overlooking the valley, began bombarding the French garrison in March 1954, and trench lines gradually closed in over the following weeks. The base fell on 7 May 1954, a defeat so total that it ended France's colonial hold on Indochina within months and led directly to the country's division at the Geneva Conference.

General Charles Gordon had been sent to evacuate Egyptian garrisons from Sudan but instead stayed to defend Khartoum against the forces of the Mahdi, a religious leader leading a rebellion against Egyptian and British rule, as Mahdist troops encircled the city through 1884.

A British relief expedition set out too late and too slowly. Mahdist forces stormed the city's weakened defences in January 1885 and killed Gordon, along with much of the garrison, just two days before the relief column's advance steamers came into sight of Khartoum, a delay that became a public scandal in Britain.

Boer forces surrounded the small British garrison town of Mafeking at the outbreak of the Second Boer War in October 1899, expecting a quick surrender from a force badly outnumbered and cut off from resupply on the open veld.

Colonel Robert Baden-Powell instead held the town through elaborate deceptions, fake minefields, dummy searchlights and decoy defences, that exaggerated its strength to the besiegers. The siege dragged on for 217 days before a relief column broke through in May 1900, and news of the relief triggered wild public celebrations across Britain.

English forces had besieged Orleans since October 1428, building a ring of fortified positions around a city whose fall would have opened the route deep into unconquered France, during a war that had already run for close to a century.

Joan of Arc arrived at the siege in the spring of 1429 claiming divine guidance, and her presence rallied a demoralised French garrison to attack the English fortifications directly. The siege broke within days, and the victory, her first, launched the campaign that led to the coronation of Charles VII and a decisive turn in the war.

Allied British, French and Ottoman forces landed in the Crimea in 1854 aiming to seize the Russian naval base at Sevastopol quickly, but its defenders, reinforced by engineer Eduard Totleben's earthworks, turned the assault into a siege lasting nearly a year.

Both sides dug extensive trench lines under artillery bombardment, a style of warfare that foreshadowed later conflicts far more than the cavalry charges the war is often remembered for. The city finally fell in September 1855 after the French captured the key Malakhov redoubt, and the war ended within months.

Vicksburg's position on a bluff above the Mississippi let Confederate guns control river traffic, making the city a Union objective almost from the war's start. General Ulysses S. Grant finally trapped its garrison inside the city's defences in May 1863 after a series of rapid manoeuvres south of it.

Civilians and soldiers alike dug caves into the hillsides to shelter from constant shelling as food ran short over the following weeks. The garrison surrendered on 4 July 1863, giving the Union control of the entire Mississippi and splitting the Confederacy in two, a strategic loss that coincided with the defeat at Gettysburg the day before.

King Kashyapa built a palace on top of a sheer granite outcrop rising nearly two hundred metres above the Sri Lankan jungle around 483, reportedly to secure a capital after seizing the throne from his father. Visitors climbed to the summit via a narrow stairway that passed between the paws of a giant brick lion.

The site combined defence with display: elaborate water gardens at the base, frescoes of women painted on a sheltered rock face partway up, and a mirror wall polished smooth enough to reflect a visitor's face. Kashyapa reigned there for roughly eighteen years before his death, after which Sigiriya reverted to a Buddhist monastery.

King Kashyapa built his fortress palace atop a 200 metre granite outcrop, and around its base his engineers laid out symmetrical water gardens fed entirely by gravity, no pumps involved. Underground ceramic pipes carried water to fountains that still spurt after rain today, sized and pitched precisely enough to work more than a thousand years later.

The gardens included pools, moats and a boulder garden threaded with water channels, all levelled with a precision archaeologists still find remarkable for the period. Kashyapa reigned only briefly before his half-brother reclaimed the throne, but the hydraulic layout beneath Sigiriya outlasted his short, contested rule by well over a millennium.

Ellen Johnson Sirleaf won Liberia's 2005 presidential election, held two years after the end of a civil war that had killed an estimated 250,000 people and left the country's institutions in ruins. She had trained as an economist and worked at the World Bank and Citibank before returning to Liberian politics.

Her inauguration in January 2006 was the first time any African nation had installed a woman as its elected leader. She shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize for work promoting women's participation in peacebuilding, and served two terms before stepping down in 2018 in Liberia's first peaceful transfer of power between elected presidents in decades.

Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia at midnight on 1 January 1993, an outcome negotiated entirely by parliament rather than settled by referendum or fighting. Polling at the time suggested most citizens on both sides actually opposed dividing the country, but the two dominant political leaders, Vaclav Klaus and Vladimir Meciar, pressed ahead regardless.

Journalists dubbed the split the Velvet Divorce, echoing the largely peaceful Velvet Revolution that had ended communist rule there in 1989. The two new states divided federal assets, including the army and diplomatic missions, through negotiation rather than conflict, and both went on to join the European Union together in 2004.

Diving bells before John Smeaton's version carried only the air trapped inside them when they were lowered, which fouled with carbon dioxide within minutes and forced divers back to the surface. Working on harbour repairs in the 1780s, Smeaton fitted a cast-iron bell with a hose connected to a force pump worked by assistants on a boat above.

The pump pushed a continuous supply of fresh air down into the bell, letting stale air escape and letting divers stay under far longer than any earlier design allowed. Smeaton used it on his own harbour works at Ramsgate, and the fed-air principle behind it carried through into the diving suits and caissons of the following century.

Sneferu's first attempt at a smooth sided pyramid, the Bent Pyramid, had to change its angle partway up when the structure began to show stress and crack. His engineers learned from the failure: the Red Pyramid at Dahshur, named for the reddish limestone left exposed where its white casing has fallen away, was built at a shallower, safer angle from the start.

Completed around 2600 BCE, it was the first true, smooth sided pyramid ever finished successfully and stands nearly as tall as its more famous successor at Giza. Sneferu's son Khufu inherited both the throne and the engineering lessons, and used them to build the Great Pyramid a generation later.

When cholera tore through Soho in the summer of 1854, killing roughly 600 people in the surrounding streets within about ten days, the accepted theory was that a poisonous miasma in the air caused it. John Snow, a local doctor already sceptical of that idea, instead walked the neighbourhood interviewing families of the dead and marking each death as a black bar on a street map.

The bars piled up thickest around a single public water pump on Broad Street. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle, and although the outbreak was already subsiding by then, his map and his interviews built a case for waterborne transmission that later investigation confirmed: a leaking cesspit near the pump had contaminated its well. The map is now treated as a founding document of epidemiology.

Solar Impulse 2 had a wingspan wider than a Boeing 747 yet weighed about as much as a family car, its wings covered in more than 17,000 solar cells feeding batteries that let it fly through the night on stored charge. Bertrand Piccard and Andre Borschberg took turns piloting it in stages, since no single leg could carry enough oxygen or endurance for one person to fly the whole route.

The circumnavigation, begun in Abu Dhabi in March 2015, stretched over sixteen months rather than a continuous flight, interrupted for months in Hawaii after the batteries overheated on the Pacific crossing. It finished back in Abu Dhabi in July 2016, the longest circumnavigation on record by elapsed time, powered the whole way by sunlight and stored charge alone.

At the peak of the crisis around 2011, Somali pirates were holding dozens of ships and hundreds of crew for ransom at once, forcing shippers to reroute or pay for armed guards. Naval patrols, private security teams and onshore counter-piracy efforts steadily cut into that success rate over the following years.

By 2017 a full calendar year had passed without pirates managing to seize a single large merchant vessel anywhere along the Somali coastline, the first such year since the surge began. Attempted attacks still occurred, but none succeeded in seizing a ship of that size.

The United Nations declared famine in parts of Unity state, South Sudan, in February 2017, its first such declaration anywhere since the Somali famine six years earlier. Roughly 100,000 people were said to face starvation, with a further million on the edge of famine, in a country then in its fourth year of civil war.

Aid agencies attributed the crisis to fighting that had displaced farmers from their land and disrupted markets rather than to drought, making it a famine caused primarily by conflict. Sustained relief efforts brought the formal famine classification to an end within months, though large parts of the country remained at severe risk of food insecurity for years afterward.

Balanguingui, a small island in the Sulu Sea, held four fortified strongholds used by Moro raiders to launch attacks on shipping and coastal settlements across the region. In February 1848 a Spanish force under Brigadier Jose Ruiz landed with nineteen ships to take it.

Against roughly a thousand defenders holding well over a hundred cannon, Spanish troops stormed three forts by assault and took the last after its defenders withdrew. More than five hundred captives held on the island were freed, and the base was destroyed.

A severe earthquake struck Sparta around 464 BC. Ancient sources, principally Plutarch and Diodorus, describe buildings collapsing across the city and heavy loss of life, though no reliable death count survives from a state that kept few written records of itself by design.

The disaster's real consequence was political. Sparta depended on enslaved Messenian helots to work its land, and the chaos of the quake gave them an opening: a revolt broke out that dragged on for roughly a decade, forcing Sparta to call on allied cities, including Athens, for help putting it down.

The scytale was a wooden rod, and a message written by winding a leather strip around it in a spiral came out as scattered letters once unwound flat. A commander in the field carried a rod of matching diameter; wind the strip around it the same way and the letters lined back up into readable text.

Plutarch describes Spartan generals receiving orders this way, including the recall of the admiral Lysander near the end of the Peloponnesian War around 404 BC. Modern cryptographers class it as a transposition cipher rather than genuine encryption, since the letters themselves are never changed, only their order, which a captured strip alone could not easily undo without the matching rod.

John Bellingham, a Liverpool merchant ruined by a failed business venture in Russia, blamed the government for refusing to compensate him and had petitioned Parliament repeatedly without result. On 11 May 1812 he waited in the lobby outside the House of Commons and shot Spencer Perceval once through the chest with a pistol he had commissioned specifically for the act.

Perceval died within minutes, the only British prime minister ever assassinated, and Bellingham made no attempt to escape, telling bystanders he had been denied justice. He was tried within a week, convicted, and hanged outside Newgate Prison on 18 May 1812, a trial widely criticised even at the time for its speed.

Spermaceti is the waxy oil found in a cavity in a sperm whale's head, and by the 1750s Rhode Island merchants had worked out how to press and refine it into a hard, pale candle that burned steadier and brighter than tallow and without tallow's smell or smoke. Newport and Providence families, the Rivera and Brown among them, built refineries around the trade.

The candles became a colonial luxury good and an export in their own right, sold from Newport to London at a fixed price the makers colluded to hold. The unit they burned in became a rough standard of brightness, later formalised as the candlepower still used to describe light output, well after gas and electric lighting had made whale oil obsolete.

Lawrence Sperry was twenty years old when he flew the first test of his father's gyroscope-driven stabiliser on a Curtiss flying boat at Hammondsport, New York, late in 1912. Two spinning gyroscopes sensed pitch and roll and moved the elevators and ailerons to correct them, keeping the aircraft level without a hand on the controls.

The idea proved itself two years later in Paris, where Sperry flew low over the Seine, stood up with both hands raised while his mechanic walked out onto the wing, and let the machine hold itself steady. The stunt won the Concours de la Securite prize of fifty thousand francs and made the case for automatic flight that the 1912 device had first demonstrated.

Prince Thutmose is said to have fallen asleep beside the half-buried Sphinx and dreamed that the monument, if freed of sand, would make him king. The pink granite Dream Stele he later placed between its paws records the promise. He did become king, as Thutmose IV, around 1400 BCE, and credited the clearing of the drifts to that dream.

The Sphinx was already thirteen centuries old at that point, carved from the Giza plateau's bedrock in the age of Khafre, and had already needed rescuing from the desert once before Thutmose's crews dug it out again. Wind-blown sand kept refilling the hollow around it for millennia, and later clearings, including a twentieth-century one, faced the same problem.

Loading cargo ship by ship, crate by crate, was slow and expensive, tying vessels up in port for days. Trucking executive Malcom McLean bought a war-surplus tanker, the Ideal X, and had it fitted with a deck rack that could carry loaded truck trailers straight onto the ship rather than unloading them piece by piece.

On its first voyage in 1956 the converted tanker carried 58 trailers from Newark to Houston, unloading in a fraction of the time a conventional cargo ship needed. The standardised steel shipping container that grew out of McLean's idea went on to remake global trade, cutting freight costs enough to make manufacturing thousands of miles from a market economically viable.

St. Nicholas Church in Hamburg was rebuilt in a neo-Gothic style after the original burned down in the great fire of 1842, and its new spire, designed by the English architect George Gilbert Scott, reached about 147.3 metres. That made it the tallest building in the world, overtaking Strasbourg Cathedral after more than two centuries.

The church itself would be gutted again, this time by Allied bombing in the Second World War, and was never rebuilt as a working church. Only the spire and part of the crypt survived, and they now stand as Hamburg's memorial to the raids.

Lightning struck St. Olaf's Church in Tallinn and set its timber spire ablaze, destroying the structure that had briefly made the church the tallest building in the world. Baltic churches of this height, built largely of wood above their stone bases, were especially vulnerable to exactly this kind of fire.

It was not the church's only such loss: St. Olaf's would burn again more than once in later centuries, each time rebuilt somewhat shorter. After 1625 the record for the world's tallest structure passed on to a cathedral spire in Strasbourg.

St. Olaf's Church, built for the Hanseatic merchant community in Tallinn, gained a spire tall enough to be used deliberately as a landmark for ships approaching the Baltic port. Once finished, no taller building or spire stood anywhere on the planet, a claim helped by the loss of Lincoln Cathedral's spire a year earlier.

Estimates put the original spire near 159 metres, though like most medieval height claims it rests on later measurement and reconstruction rather than a surviving contemporary record. The church would hold the title only into the next century before losing its spire to fire.

Leland Stanford, a railroad magnate and former California governor, and his wife Jane founded a university near Palo Alto in 1885 in memory of their only son, who had died of typhoid fever at fifteen during a family trip to Europe.

Leland reportedly said the children of California would be their children now. The university opened in 1891, admitting women alongside men from the start, and grew over the following century into one of the country's most prominent research institutions.

Konstantin Stanislavski staged Chekhov's The Seagull at the Moscow Art Theatre in December 1898, two years after its earlier St Petersburg premiere had been jeered off the stage by an audience expecting broad comedy rather than the play's quiet, unresolved melancholy.

Stanislavski's production, built on slower pacing, naturalistic pauses and actors inhabiting ordinary behaviour rather than declaiming, succeeded where the first staging had failed. The theatre later adopted a seagull as its emblem, and Stanislavski's rehearsal methods from the production became the basis of what he formalised as his acting system.

Suleiman the Magnificent ordered the bridge in 1557 to replace an older wooden suspension crossing over the Neretva that locals thought was unsafe. Its architect, Mimar Hayruddin, had trained under Sinan, the great architect of Ottoman Istanbul, and construction of the single stone arch took nine years, finishing in 1566.

The arch spans about 27 metres and rises 4 metres wide, high enough above the Neretva gorge that local divers jumping from it became a Mostar tradition of its own. The bridge stood for 427 years until Croat forces shelled it apart in November 1993 during the Bosnian war; it was rebuilt using much of the original stone recovered from the riverbed and reopened in 2004.

A 1957 paper by Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle, known ever since by the authors' initials as B2FH, ran to more than a hundred pages and worked through how stars fuse hydrogen and helium into carbon, oxygen, iron and almost every heavier element on the periodic table, using nuclear physics rather than assumption to fix the ratios.

The paper mattered because it broke with George Gamow's picture of the early universe forging all the elements in one hot burst; B2FH showed most of them are made continuously, inside stars, over billions of years. Elements heavier than iron require a dying star's supernova to force them into existence, meaning the calcium in bone and the iron in blood were both cooked in stars that exploded long before the Sun formed.

Stephen was born Vajk, a prince of the Magyar chieftain Geza, and took the Christian name Stephen at his baptism. On his coronation, traditionally dated to Christmas Day 1000 or 1 January 1001, he wore a crown said to have been sent by Pope Sylvester II, a gift that let him claim kingship rather than mere overlordship.

The crown became Hungary's central relic of legitimacy, though the surviving Holy Crown of Hungary is now dated by scholars to well after Stephen's lifetime. What is not in doubt is the change he forced through: the loose Magyar tribal confederation became a single Christian kingdom with dioceses, counties and a royal law code.

Klaus Stortebeker led the Victual Brothers, a Baltic raiding fleet that had begun as grain smugglers supplying a besieged Stockholm before turning to open piracy across northern waters. Hamburg, whose trade the raiders repeatedly disrupted, fitted out a fleet that finally caught and captured Stortebeker at sea.

He and roughly seventy of his crew were beheaded together at Hamburg's Grasbrook execution ground in 1401, their heads reportedly displayed on stakes as a warning to other raiders. A skull long claimed to be his, pierced by an iron spike, is still preserved in a Hamburg museum, though its authenticity has never been proven.

Once Tallinn's spire had burned down, the record for the world's tallest structure passed to Strasbourg Cathedral's single north tower, finished in the fifteenth century at around 142 metres. Strasbourg's builders had abandoned symmetry, leaving the south tower unbuilt, an asymmetry that gave the cathedral its unmistakable silhouette.

The title held for roughly two centuries, longer than any of the wooden church spires that preceded it, largely because Strasbourg's tower was built in stone rather than timber and so was far less likely to burn or blow down. It was eventually overtaken by St. Nicholas Church in Hamburg in the 1870s.

Strasbourg Cathedral installed an astronomical clock in the 1350s built to display far more than the hour: a calendar, the positions of the sun and moon, and moving figures that acted out the passage of time for a largely illiterate congregation. Its most talked about feature was a gilded copper cock mounted near the top.

At noon each day the mechanical bird spread its wings, parted its beak and let out a crow, driven by bellows and gears hidden inside the casing, likely the oldest automaton of its kind still known from medieval Europe. The clock as a whole was replaced twice in later centuries, but the surviving cock from this original machine is now kept and displayed separately as one of the few working parts of it left.

Su Song built his water driven clock tower at the Song capital, Kaifeng, work beginning around 1088 and the finished structure ready by 1092. Water filled buckets on a wheel at a steady rate, tripping an early escapement that let the wheel advance in fixed steps rather than spinning freely, the same basic problem later solved differently by mechanical clocks in Europe.

A chain drive Su Song called the celestial ladder linked the wheel to 133 wooden figures that emerged through doors to strike bells, beat drums and hold up placards marking the hour. His illustrated treatise on the mechanism survived, but the tower itself did not: Jurchen invaders dismantled it in 1126 and carried the parts north as war spoils.

The Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent ordered Jerusalem's old fortifications demolished and rebuilt starting in 1538, replacing walls that had fallen into disrepair since earlier medieval construction. The project took several years and defined the roughly four-kilometre circuit still standing today.

Suleiman's walls incorporated older gates and stonework from earlier periods alongside new Ottoman construction, and they enclosed the quarters and holy sites that still define the Old City's layout. They remain the boundary most visitors recognise as Jerusalem's historic core, built under a sultan who never set foot in the city himself.

The French frigate Confiance, under Robert Surcouf, carried roughly two hundred men and far fewer guns than the East India Company ship Kent, which had taken on survivors and troops until it held over four hundred people. Surcouf attacked anyway in the Bay of Bengal in October 1800.

His crew boarded in the confusion of a close broadside exchange, and after a fight of about two hours that killed the Kent's captain and more than twenty others, the larger ship surrendered. The capture, against those odds, made Surcouf one of France's most celebrated privateers.

Basil Brown was a self-taught archaeologist working for the landowner Edith Pretty when he opened the largest of the mounds at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk in 1939. The ship's timbers had rotted away entirely, but their impression survived in the sand as a ghost outline nearly ninety feet long, rivets still in place where the planks had been.

Inside a collapsed burial chamber at the ship's centre lay a hoard nobody had expected from Anglo-Saxon England: a helmet, gold buckles and shoulder clasps set with garnet, silver bowls, and coins that helped date the burial to around 620. No body was ever found, dissolved by the acidic soil, but the wealth argued for a king, most likely Raedwald of East Anglia.

Spanish colonial authorities in the Philippines restricted the export of sweet potato vines, fearing loss of a valuable crop, so the plant reached mainland China through smuggling rather than trade. A Fujianese merchant named Chen Zhenlong is credited with hiding cuttings and bringing them into Fujian province in 1593, introducing a crop that would reshape Chinese agriculture within a generation.

Sweet potatoes grew reliably on poor, sandy or hillside soil unsuitable for rice, letting farmers cultivate land previously left idle and providing a reserve harvest when the rice crop failed. Later Chinese officials credited the crop with easing regional famines, and its cultivation spread rapidly along the southeastern coast within decades of that first smuggled planting.

Kathrine Switzer registered for the 1967 Boston Marathon using her initials, K. V. Switzer, and was issued an official bib number because the race organisers did not check for gender. Women were not formally barred from entering, but none had run with a number before.

Race official Jock Semple tried to pull her bib off partway through the course, an attempt caught on camera and blocked by Switzer's boyfriend, who body-checked Semple off the road. She finished the race, and the photographs of the confrontation became a lasting image in the campaign that got women officially admitted to the Boston Marathon in 1972.

Thucydides describes the obstacle rather than naming the divers who beat it. Syracuse, besieged by an Athenian fleet during the Sicilian Expedition, drove rows of stakes into the harbour mouth, some visible and some cut off below the waterline where a ship's hull would strike them unseen.

Athenian sailors dived on the submerged stakes and sawed through them, though Thucydides notes some were bolted with iron and harder to shift than the wooden ones. Clearing them mattered less than the campaign around it: the siege of Syracuse ended in 413 BC in the destruction of the Athenian fleet and army, a defeat from which Athens never fully recovered.

Junko Tabei led an all-women Japanese expedition up Everest in 1975, financing much of the trip herself after companies declined to sponsor a climb led by women. An avalanche buried the team's camp days before the summit push, and Tabei was dug out unconscious by a Sherpa guide.

She resumed the climb and reached the summit on 16 May 1975, becoming the first woman confirmed to stand on top of the mountain. She went on to climb the highest peak on every continent and spent much of her later career on environmental campaigns to reduce the litter left behind by Everest expeditions.

King Taejo overthrew the Goryeo dynasty to found Joseon, and one of his first acts as king was to abandon its old capital for a site his advisers judged more auspicious under the principles of geomancy. In 1394 he moved the court to a walled city he named Hanseong, ringed by mountains on a bend of the Han river.

Construction followed a formal plan: a royal palace at the centre, a grid of ministries and markets around it, and gates set at the cardinal points to align with geomantic principle rather than convenience. That layout underlies modern Seoul, whose old city walls and gates, several rebuilt after war, still trace roughly the boundary Taejo's planners marked out.

Taharqa, a member of the Nubian royal house that had already ruled Egypt for decades, was crowned pharaoh around 690 BCE at the height of the Twenty Fifth Dynasty's power. His kingdom stretched from deep in Nubia north through Egypt and into the Levant, one of the largest realms the Nile had ever produced.

He is named in the Hebrew Bible as an ally who came to Jerusalem's aid against Assyrian siege during Sennacherib's campaign. Assyrian pressure eventually proved too strong: later in his reign Assyrian forces sacked Memphis and Thebes, driving Taharqa's dynasty back toward its Nubian homeland.

A Crimean Tatar army under Devlet I Giray reached Moscow's outskirts in May 1571 while much of the Russian defensive force was tied up fighting Sweden and the Livonian War elsewhere. The raiders set fire to the suburbs, and wind carried the flames into the wooden city itself.

Almost the entire city, built overwhelmingly from timber, burned within hours, and contemporary estimates of the dead run into the tens of thousands, though the exact figure is unrecoverable. Ivan the Terrible, who had fled before the raid, agreed to pay tribute afterward, though a second Tatar invasion the following year was defeated outright.

In 622 BCE, workmen repairing the Jerusalem Temple under King Josiah found a scroll of law that the high priest Hilkiah brought before the king. Hearing it read aloud, Josiah tore his clothes in grief at warnings his kingdom had apparently ignored, then ordered a purge of local shrines and a national Passover.

Many biblical scholars think the scroll was some version of Deuteronomy, either genuinely rediscovered or freshly written to justify reforms already under way, since its language and concerns match that book closely. Either way, the find gave Josiah's changes the weight of an old, forgotten law rather than a new royal decree.

Before the wheel-thrown terracotta lamp, households burned oil in open bowls or pinched-clay saucers, both wasteful and prone to spilling. From around 700 BCE, potters across the Mediterranean mass-produced a cheap, closed lamp with a spout to hold the wick, letting a household burn olive oil with far less waste and less fire risk.

These lamps are so common on excavation sites that archaeologists use their shape and decoration to date the layers around them almost like coins. Production stayed a household craft rather than an industry, made and sold in local workshops, until moulded lamps in Hellenistic and Roman times let makers copy one popular design by the thousand.

London built the barrier after a 1953 North Sea storm surge killed hundreds along the English coast and exposed how vulnerable the tidal Thames was to a similar event reaching the capital. Ten steel gates span the river at Woolwich, the four largest each 61.5 metres wide, normally resting on the riverbed and rotating upward to seal the channel when a surge threatens.

The barrier was tested with all gates together in 1982 and formally opened by the Queen in 1984, protecting around 125 square kilometres of London from tidal flooding. It has been raised many more times per year in recent decades than its designers originally expected, reflecting rising sea levels since the 1980s.

Marc Brunel's tunnel between Rotherhithe and Wapping had almost failed twice, flooded by the Thames in 1827 and again in 1828, an accident that nearly killed his young son and assistant engineer Isambard. The project then stalled for seven years for lack of money until a government loan let it resume. Marc's invention, a heavy iron shield that let miners dig a small face at a time while supported, was what made a river crossing survivable.

It opened to the public on 25 March 1843 as a pedestrian tunnel, not the road link originally planned, and became a tourist attraction and a market lined with stalls rather than the trade route investors had hoped for. It was later fitted with rails and is still in use, carrying London Underground trains through the same brick bore.

Marie Tharp was barred from the research ships that gathered sonar soundings of the Atlantic seabed in the 1950s because women were not allowed aboard, so she worked from the data her colleague Bruce Heezen brought back, plotting depth profiles by hand onto paper at Columbia's Lamont Geological Observatory through 1957.

When she drew the profiles side by side, a long valley kept appearing down the centre of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Heezen initially dismissed it as impossible, calling it girl talk, but the rift matched newly plotted earthquake locations exactly. It became key evidence for continental drift and seafloor spreading, ideas most geologists still rejected when Tharp first drew the line.

A stone theatre built into a hillside at the sanctuary of Epidaurus in the Peloponnese around the mid fourth century BCE was designed, ancient writers say, by Polykleitos the Younger, and could seat some 13,000 to 14,000 spectators for festivals honouring the healer god Asclepius.

Its limestone seating rows still carry sound with unusual clarity, a property later engineers attributed partly to the stone's ridged surface filtering out low background noise while preserving speech frequencies. Largely intact after more than two thousand years, it remains in active use for performances and is treated as a reference point for later theatre design.

Pompey the Great dedicated a vast theatre complex in Rome in 55 BCE, built of stone rather than the temporary wooden structures Roman law had previously required, and disguised its seating as steps leading up to a temple of Venus to satisfy conservative objections to permanent theatres.

It could reportedly hold tens of thousands of spectators and included gardens, meeting halls and a senate chamber attached to its portico, the very hall where Julius Caesar was stabbed to death in 44 BCE. Its scale made it a model that later Roman theatres across the empire followed.

On the opening morning of the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, burglars propped a ladder against Oslo's National Gallery, smashed a window and lifted Edvard Munch's The Scream from the wall in under a minute. A note left behind reportedly thanked the museum for its poor security.

The thieves later demanded a ransom, which the gallery refused to pay, and Norwegian police instead ran a sting with undercover British detectives posing as buyers. The painting was recovered undamaged three months later, and four men were eventually convicted, though the case took years to fully resolve.

Constantinople's land walls, finished in 413 under Theodosius II, were not a single barrier but three lines in sequence: a moat, then an outer wall, then a much taller inner wall studded with towers roughly every fifty metres. An earthquake damaged the newly built walls decades later, and they were repaired within two months as an invasion approached.

The system made a direct assault on the city's landward side nearly hopeless for close to a thousand years, and Constantinople repelled repeated sieges that any single wall would likely have failed to stop. It finally fell in 1453, and only after Ottoman forces brought cannon large enough to batter down what centuries of attackers had not.

Ancient tradition holds that a performer named Thespis, competing at a festival of Dionysus in Athens around 534 BCE, stepped out of the singing chorus to speak lines in the voice of a character, rather than narrating events in the third person as choruses had always done.

That single change, an individual addressing the audience as someone else, is the reason actors are still sometimes called thespians. The story survives only in later, secondhand accounts, and no text of what Thespis performed has survived, but ancient writers already treated him as the point where chorus became drama.

Crusader forces began besieging the port city of Acre in 1189, hoping to retake it from Saladin's garrison, but soon found themselves besieged in turn by a relieving Muslim army camped outside their own lines, fighting on two fronts at once through disease-ridden camps.

The stalemate lasted nearly two years until Richard the Lionheart and Philip II of France arrived with fresh forces in 1191, forcing the garrison's surrender within weeks. Richard's subsequent execution of roughly 2,700 captured defenders, after negotiations over ransom and prisoner exchange broke down, remains one of the more disputed episodes of the Third Crusade.

Ancient writers mentioned a port called Thonis where Helen and Paris supposedly landed en route to Troy, but no ruins matched it on any modern map, because the city was not on the coast anymore. Franck Goddio's team, surveying Abu Qir Bay near Alexandria with sonar and magnetometers, found it under several metres of silt and seawater in 2000.

Thonis and the Greek trading colony of Heracleion turned out to be the same place, known by two names to two peoples who had assumed they were separate. Slabs naming Pharaoh Nectanebo I, a giant temple to Amun-Gereb, and sunken ships still holding their cargo let archaeologists date the city's slow sinking, likely from earthquakes and rising sea levels, to around the eighth century AD.

Titan lost contact with its surface ship less than two hours into its descent on 18 June 2023, carrying tourists paying around 250,000 dollars each to view the Titanic wreck two and a half miles down. A multinational search located debris four days later on the seafloor, close to the wreck itself.

The five people killed were OceanGate's chief executive Stockton Rush, British explorer Hamish Harding, veteran Titanic diver Paul-Henri Nargeolet, and the father and son Shahzada and Suleman Dawood. Investigators traced the loss to the carbon fibre hull, a material never before used at that depth in a crewed submersible, which had shown signs of delamination on earlier dives.

Tomislav became duke of Croatia around 910 and spent the next years absorbing neighbouring Croatian duchies and holding off both Hungarian raids from the north and Bulgarian pressure from the east. By the mid 920s he controlled enough territory, and enough recognition from Rome, that later tradition credits him with taking the title of king.

No contemporary document records the coronation itself, and even the year, usually given as 924 or 925, rests on later chronicles rather than a surviving charter. What is firmer is that a synod under papal legates addressed him as king around that time, which is the documentary basis for treating him as the first king of a united Croatian realm.

Trajan needed a fixed crossing to move legions into Dacia rather than relying on boats, and his architect Apollodorus of Damascus built one on twenty masonry piers sunk into the Danube's bed, each pair carrying a timber arch about 38 metres across. The whole structure ran roughly 1,135 metres, the first bridge over the lower Danube.

It was finished in 105 CE after a build of about two years and was the longest arch bridge in the world, by both span and total length, for over a thousand years. Trajan's successor Hadrian removed its wooden superstructure and Aurelian later abandoned the province entirely, leaving only the stone piers that still stand in the riverbed.

The Mexican-American War had begun over a disputed strip of land along the Texas border, but by 1848 American forces had occupied Mexico City itself. Negotiator Nicholas Trist, defying orders to return home, signed terms at the Villa de Guadalupe Hidalgo that both sides could still accept.

Mexico ceded roughly half its territory, including present day California, Nevada, Utah and much of the wider Southwest, for a payment of fifteen million dollars and assumption of Mexican debts to American citizens. The new border, largely following the Rio Grande and the Gila River, has changed little since.

Three years of war around Sevastopol had killed hundreds of thousands, mostly to disease rather than combat, before Russia agreed terms in Paris in 1856. The treaty declared the Black Sea neutral, barring warships of any nation, Russian or otherwise, from its waters.

Russia also lost its claim to protect Orthodox Christians within the Ottoman Empire, a pretext it had used to justify the war. The neutrality clause proved short lived: Russia repudiated it in 1870 while Europe was distracted by the Franco-Prussian War, and nobody stopped it.

Edward IV had landed an English army in France threatening to revive the old claim to the French throne, but Louis XI preferred to buy him off rather than fight. The two kings met on a specially built bridge at Picquigny in August 1475, separated by a wooden lattice so neither monarch could be seized by the other's men.

Louis agreed a large lump sum and an annual pension to England in exchange for immediate withdrawal, and a marriage was proposed between the two royal houses. The Hundred Years' War never formally reopened after it, though English kings kept the title 'King of France' on paper for centuries afterward.

A human skull turned up with a section of bone deliberately removed by cutting, its edges smoothed and remodelled by new bone growth, evidence the patient survived the procedure and lived long enough afterward for the wound to heal substantially.

The find is the oldest solid evidence anywhere of a patient surviving cranial surgery, predating written medicine by thousands of years and showing that some form of surgical skill and aftercare existed in prehistoric societies. Why trepanation was performed, whether for injury, disease or ritual belief, remains debated.

Gaius Verres governed Sicily for three years in the 70s BCE and used the post to strip the province of art, statues and treasure, sometimes seizing pieces outright from temples and private owners who had no recourse against a sitting governor. When his term ended, Sicilian communities asked Cicero, then a rising advocate, to prosecute him.

Cicero's case against Verres in 70 BCE was so thoroughly documented, built on months of evidence gathered in Sicily itself, that Verres fled into exile before the trial concluded rather than face it. Cicero published his prepared speeches anyway, and the Verrine orations became a model for how Roman prosecutors built a case against provincial corruption.

Johannes Trithemius was a Benedictine abbot in Sponheim who spent his life defending himself against a rumour that his earlier book on angels was black magic. Polygraphiae, printed in 1518, two years after his death, was his answer: cryptography dressed as harmless devotional Latin, dedicated to Emperor Maximilian rather than hidden from him.

Its table assigns each letter of the alphabet its own column of code words, so enciphering a message and reading off the columns in order produces a string of Latin that looks like a prayer. A message hidden this way could pass as pious nonsense to anyone who intercepted it, which is why historians credit Trithemius as the first printed author on the subject rather than merely an early one.

Sandor Just and Franjo Hanaman filed their Hungarian patent for a tungsten filament bulb in December 1904, working in Budapest. Tungsten's appeal was its melting point, far higher than the carbon threads Edison had used, which meant the filament could run hotter and give off more light for the same electricity without burning through as quickly.

Making a usable filament was the hard part: tungsten's brittleness had to be worked around by extruding a paste of tungsten powder through a fine die and then baking off the binder in hydrogen. Commercial tungsten bulbs reached the market within a few years and displaced carbon-filament lamps almost entirely, the basic technology that lit homes until LED bulbs took over a century later.

Charles Parsons was not invited to the Royal Navy's fleet review for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee at Spithead on 26 June 1897. He brought his experimental steam turbine yacht Turbinia anyway, and ran her at speed through the lines of assembled warships in front of the assembled admiralty and foreign observers.

Naval picket boats sent to intercept her could not catch up. Turbinia reached around 34 knots that day, faster than any Royal Navy vessel afloat, and the demonstration converted sceptical naval officers almost overnight. Steam turbines replaced reciprocating engines in new warship designs within a few years of the stunt.

Drawn under Ramesses IV around 1150 BCE, the Turin Papyrus shows the gold and stone quarries of Wadi Hammamat in Egypt's Eastern Desert: coloured bands marking granite, black and pink rock, dry stream beds, and the huts and wells along the route.
