It is the oldest geological map known to survive from anywhere.

The papyrus was made for a practical purpose, guiding an expedition sent to haul stone for a royal statue, not for record's sake. It survives only in fragments, reassembled from pieces held in Turin, and its accuracy has let modern geologists match its rock colours to the wadi's actual strata.

The first bombe, named Victory, began running at Bletchley Park on 18 March 1940, built to Turing's design and refined with Gordon Welchman's addition of the diagonal board, which cut the search space dramatically. It was an electromechanical machine of spinning drums, each standing in for one of Enigma's rotors, testing thousands of possible settings against a guessed fragment of plaintext.

A working bombe did not read a message directly; it ruled out settings until only a handful remained plausible, which codebreakers then tested by hand. More than two hundred bombes were eventually built and run day and night by Wrens, recovering the German military's daily Enigma keys often within hours of the traffic being intercepted.

Alan Turing was twenty-three when his paper On Computable Numbers appeared in 1936, written to answer David Hilbert's question of whether a definite procedure could decide any mathematical statement's provability. Turing imagined a simple machine reading and writing symbols on an endless tape according to fixed rules, a device with no physical form that could still stand for any calculation a person could carry out by hand.

He proved that no such general procedure exists, because some questions about the machine's own behaviour, such as whether it will ever stop running, cannot be settled in advance for every case. The machine itself, an abstraction meant only to answer a question in logic, became the working blueprint for what a stored-program computer would later actually do.

Juanelo Turriano was Philip II's court clockmaker, credited with an elaborate water-lifting works at Toledo alongside his automata. According to the story attached to this one, Philip's son Don Carlos was badly injured and the king vowed a miracle in return for his recovery, then commissioned a moving likeness of the Franciscan friar Diego de Alcala once the boy survived.

The friar, about 38 centimetres tall and driven by a wound spring turning iron cams beneath its robe, walks a small square path, beats its chest with one arm, raises a cross and rosary with the other, turns its head and moves its lips as if praying. It survives at the Smithsonian, still able to run through its routine after more than four centuries, one of the oldest complex automata still working.

David Bushnell's Turtle was a one-man oak shell shaped like two turtle backs joined together, ballasted with water and driven by hand-cranked propellers. On the night of 6 September 1776, Sergeant Ezra Lee piloted it into New York harbour toward HMS Eagle, the anchored British flagship, meaning to screw a powder charge into her hull and swim clear before it exploded.

Lee reached the hull but could not drive the screw through it, most likely because he had struck an iron strap reinforcing the ship's bottom, and after repeated tries he gave up and turned for shore as daylight came on. The charge detonated harmlessly in the harbour. It was the first submarine attack on a warship in recorded history, even though it failed.

Ptolemy's planetary system worked well enough to predict positions, but it leaned on the equant, a point not at the centre of a circle from which motion was defined as uniform. Astronomers at the Maragha observatory in Persia treated that as a flaw in principle, not just a technical fix, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi set out to remove it entirely.

His solution, described in 1261, combined two circles: a small one rolling inside a larger one twice its size, so that a point on the small circle traces a straight line back and forth. Two such rotating circles could reproduce the oscillating motion the equant faked without one. Copernicus used the same device three centuries later, unattributed, in his own planetary models.

On 11 November 1572, Tycho Brahe noticed a point of light in Cassiopeia brighter than Venus, in a spot where no star belonged. Aristotelian cosmology held that everything beyond the Moon was fixed and unchanging, so a genuinely new light among the stars, rather than something nearer like a comet, was not supposed to be possible.

Tycho measured its position against neighbouring stars for months and found no parallax shift at all, proving it lay among the fixed stars rather than in the sublunar sphere where change was permitted. He published De Nova Stella in 1573, and what he had actually seen, unknown to him, was a supernova, the explosive death of a star, now catalogued as SN 1572 and still visible as a faint remnant to modern telescopes.

Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted for independence on 24 August 1991, days after a failed coup against Mikhail Gorbachev in Moscow exposed how weak the Soviet centre had become. The vote came suddenly, catching even some of its own deputies by surprise at how far events had moved.

The declaration still needed public backing to carry weight, and on 1 December 1991 a referendum returned over 90 percent in favour, with majorities in every region including Crimea and the mostly Russian-speaking east. A week later, leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed an agreement effectively dissolving the Soviet Union, which formally ceased to exist before the year was out.

George Devol patented a programmable mechanical arm in the 1950s and, with the engineer Joseph Engelberger, built it into a commercial machine called Unimate. General Motors installed the first one in 1961 at its die-casting plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, where the job was pulling red-hot metal castings from a die-casting machine and stacking them, a task too hot and repetitive for a human worker on every shift.

Unimate followed a sequence recorded onto a magnetic drum rather than sensing its surroundings, and it could not adapt if a part shifted out of place. Even so, it proved an arm could work unsupervised on a factory line without breaking down, and Engelberger's company Unimation went on to sell the design across the American auto industry through the following decade.

Prussia had just lost territory and prestige to Napoleon when the scholar and statesman Wilhelm von Humboldt set up a new university in Berlin in 1810, arguing that a defeated state needed to rebuild through education rather than arms.

Its guiding idea, that teaching should be inseparable from original research rather than the recitation of settled knowledge, became known as the Humboldtian model. It influenced how research universities were organised across Europe and, later, the United States.

Erling Kagge and Borge Ousland skied from Ellesmere Island to the North Pole in 1990, hauling their own food and fuel on sledges for the entire route without air resupply or dog teams. Earlier North Pole expeditions, including Ralph Plaisted's snowmobile party in 1968, had relied on air-dropped supplies, a support Kagge and Ousland deliberately refused.

The trek took fifty-eight days across drifting sea ice, terrain that shifts constantly underfoot and can carry a party backward overnight even while they sleep. Their arrival made them the first people confirmed to reach the pole entirely under their own power, a distinction polar explorers had specifically sought since Plaisted's earlier, supported success.

By early 1862 the Union's ability to pay for the Civil War was outrunning its gold reserves, and borrowing alone could not cover the bills. Congress responded with the Legal Tender Act, authorising the Treasury to print paper dollars, printed with green ink on the back, that were not redeemable in gold or silver on demand.

The bills, quickly nicknamed greenbacks, were declared legal tender for nearly all debts, forcing creditors to accept paper where they had previously expected coin. Their value floated against gold for years and dipped sharply when the war went badly for the Union, but the government never withdrew them, and the greenback established the precedent, still in force, that United States currency need not be backed by precious metal at all.

US President George W. Bush signed the Secure Fence Act in October 2006, authorising the construction of several hundred miles of additional fencing along the border with Mexico, along with new lighting, cameras and other surveillance infrastructure.

Congress passed the bill with broad bipartisan support during a period of intense debate over illegal immigration, though funding and construction lagged well behind the mileage the law had authorised. The act became a reference point in later, more expansive proposals to build a continuous border wall.

Earlier submarine designs struggled with propulsion: an engine that could breathe underwater needed to run on stored power, while a submerged battery alone lacked range on the surface. John Philip Holland's design solved it by pairing the two, a gasoline engine for surface running and an electric motor, charged by that engine, for submerged travel.

The US Navy commissioned USS Holland in 1900 as its first submarine, after Holland had spent decades building and testing earlier prototypes largely at his own expense. The dual-power arrangement she introduced, refined into diesel-electric propulsion, remained the standard submarine layout for the next half century.

The first leap second was inserted at midnight on 30 June 1972, the day Coordinated Universal Time switched from a stretched second to a fixed one matching the atomic caesium standard. Earth's spin is not perfectly steady, and clocks kept by atoms had begun drifting ahead of clocks kept by the planet's own rotation.

Rather than let the gap grow, the international timekeeping bodies agreed to freeze an extra second onto UTC whenever the difference approached a full second, keeping civil time within 0.9 seconds of solar time. More than two dozen leap seconds have followed since 1972, each announced months in advance and each capable of quietly breaking software that assumes a minute always has sixty of them.

Pedro de Valdivia marched south from Peru through desert that killed a large share of the indigenous porters forced to accompany his expedition, aiming to found a Spanish foothold beyond territory the Inca had already lost. In February 1541 he settled his party at the base of a rise the Mapuche called Huelen, with the Mapocho river curling around it, and founded Santiago there.

Valdivia's chosen site put the new town within reach of local Picunche communities whose resistance nearly destroyed it within months of founding, forcing settlers to survive largely on grain they had planted themselves. Santiago held on and grew into the capital of Chile, its street grid still centred on the same rise and river bend Valdivia picked.

Two burglars set a ladder against the museum's rear wall in Amsterdam in December 2002, climbed onto the roof, broke a window and grabbed two paintings, View of the Sea at Scheveningen and Congregation Leaving the Reformed Church at Nuenen, in under four minutes before a police response could arrive.

Both men were convicted and jailed within a few years, but the paintings themselves stayed missing for over a decade. In 2016 Italian police recovered them, undamaged despite crude storage, from a house linked to Camorra crime boss Raffaele Imperiale, who later handed himself in and returned the works to the museum.

Han van Meegeren was a Dutch painter whose own work had been dismissed by critics, and he spent years perfecting a technique for aging paint and canvas convincingly enough to pass as seventeenth-century work. In 1943, acting through an intermediary, he sold a painting he presented as a newly discovered Vermeer to Hermann Göring in exchange for a large sum and a group of paintings looted from Jewish collections.

After the war, Van Meegeren was arrested for collaborating with the Nazis by selling a Dutch national treasure, a charge that could carry the death penalty. To clear himself, he confessed the painting was his own forgery, and was made to paint another fake Vermeer under supervision to prove it, a demonstration that turned his trial into a sensation and reduced his charge to one of fraud.

Douzhen Xinfa, a text on smallpox from 1549, is the earliest surviving Chinese record of deliberately giving someone a mild case of the disease to prevent a severe one. Physicians dried scabs from smallpox pustules, ground them to powder and blew them up a healthy person's nose through a tube, aiming for an infection light enough to survive and leave lasting immunity.

The method was refined further around Huangshan in Anhui during the later Ming dynasty and stayed a regional, largely folk practice for generations rather than a state programme. It travelled outward slowly, reaching Russia, Central Asia and Japan over the following two centuries, well before variolation reached England and was adapted there into Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine.

The warship Vasa capsized and sank in Stockholm harbour on its maiden voyage in 1628, taking dozens of bronze cannons to the bottom with it. Bronze was valuable enough that Sweden hired Hans Albrekt von Treileben, a former army officer, and the German salvager Andreas Peckell to get the guns back rather than write them off.

Their tool was a diving bell, an open-bottomed chamber lowered on a rope that trapped a pocket of air a diver could breathe from while working blind in cold water with hooks and tongs. Over 1664 and 1665 they recovered 53 of the ship's 64 cannons, each weighing well over a tonne, a remarkable haul given the equipment. The hull itself, and its remaining guns, stayed on the harbour floor for another three centuries.

Matthew Vassar, an English-born brewer who had built a successful brewing business in Poughkeepsie, New York, chartered a college for women there in 1861, funding its entire endowment from his own personal fortune rather than public subscription.

He insisted it hold women to the same academic standard as men's colleges of the day, a deliberate stance at a time when women's education was widely dismissed as unnecessary or even harmful. Vassar became one of the earliest and most influential of the American women's colleges.

Jacques de Vaucanson unveiled his mechanical duck in Paris in 1739 alongside a flute player and a tambourine player, both genuine musical automata built to prove machines could reproduce living motion rather than just imitate a clock's tick. The duck was the crowd-pleaser: gilded copper, over four hundred moving parts in each wing, and a bill that took grain and appeared to pass it through a digestive tract.

The digestion was a trick. Grain vanished into a hidden reservoir while a separate stored paste, dyed to look like waste, came out the other end, a fact confirmed once later owners took the duck apart. Vaucanson never denied the deception outright, and the phrase Voltaire is said to have used, comparing him to a rival inventor, kept the duck famous long after it stopped working and was eventually lost.

Venice founded its state shipyard, the Arsenale, in the walled eastern district of the city in 1104, gathering rope makers, carpenters and caulkers who had previously worked scattered across smaller yards into one enclosed complex the Republic controlled directly.

By the time it reached its later peak, workers there could assemble a war galley from pre-cut, standardised parts stored along a canal, moving the hull past stations that fitted rigging and equipment in sequence, reportedly finishing a ship in under a day. The word arsenal, borrowed into most European languages, comes from this yard.

Gilbert Vernam, an engineer at AT&T, worked out his cipher in 1917 and received the patent, number 1,310,719, in 1919. It combined each letter of a teleprinter message with a letter from a key tape using an electrical add operation, so the output looked like noise unless the receiver held an identical tape.

Vernam had used a repeating key, which left a weakness a skilled cryptanalyst could exploit. Joseph Mauborgne of the Army Signal Corps saw that a truly random key, used only once and never repeated, closed that gap entirely. The combination, later called the one-time pad, is the only cipher ever proven mathematically unbreakable.

Victoria was eighteen and had been woken before dawn on 20 June 1837 to be told her uncle William IV had died overnight, making her queen. She had grown up sheltered under her mother's strict Kensington System, largely kept apart from the court, and her first act as monarch was reportedly to insist on seeing the Privy Council alone rather than with her mother present.

She was crowned the following year, on 28 June 1838, and went on to reign for 63 years, then the longest of any British monarch, a record only surpassed by Elizabeth II in 2015. The stretch of industrial and imperial expansion that filled those decades came to carry her name as the Victorian era.

The Geheime Kabinettskanzlei ran out of Vienna's main post office, where clerks worked before dawn. Sealed letters passing through were opened over steam, read, copied in a fair hand, resealed with forged wax impressions matched to the original seals, and sent on their way before the morning post left, so neither sender nor recipient ever knew.

Similar bureaux existed in Paris, Berlin and other capitals, but Vienna's black chamber ran longest and was studied as the model. Its decrypts went straight to the emperor and his ministers, giving Habsburg diplomacy a standing advantage over ambassadors who assumed their dispatches were private. The office survived into the nineteenth century before its methods became public knowledge.

The Angre family had ruled the fortress of Vijaydurg on India's Konkan coast for decades, taxing and raiding shipping that passed without paying tribute, European vessels included. In 1756 a joint British East India Company and Maratha force moved against Tulaji Angre's stronghold there.

Royal Navy ships bombarded the fort from the sea while Maratha troops closed off the land side, and Vijaydurg surrendered within days. Angre himself was handed over to the Marathas as a prisoner, and the raiding network his family had built along the coast did not survive the loss of its base.

A Viking fleet reportedly numbering in the hundreds of ships sailed up the Seine and surrounded Paris, then a fortified settlement confined mostly to the Ile de la Cite, in November 885. The Frankish count Odo led a small garrison in holding the bridges and walls against repeated assaults through the winter.

The siege dragged on for over a year without the Vikings breaking through, and it ended not with a Frankish victory but with the Carolingian emperor Charles the Fat paying tribute and allowing the raiders passage further upriver. Odo's defence, in contrast, boosted his own standing enough that he was later elected king of West Francia.

A Norse fleet under a chieftain named Reginheri, often identified with the legendary Ragnar, sailed up the Seine with well over a hundred ships in March 845. Parisians could offer little resistance, and the Vikings occupied and plundered the city over Easter.

King Charles the Bald, unable to dislodge the raiders by force, paid roughly 5,670 pounds of silver and gold to secure their withdrawal. It was an early instance of what became known as Danegeld, a payment strategy that bought short term peace but signalled to other Norse fleets that Frankish rivers were worth the trip.

Voyager was built almost entirely of lightweight composite materials, its wings so long and thin they drooped visibly under the weight of the fuel that made up most of its takeoff mass. Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager, who was not related to Chuck Yeager, packed themselves into a cabin barely large enough to lie down in for the entire flight.

They took off from Edwards Air Force Base on 14 December 1986 and landed there again on 23 December, having flown roughly 26,000 miles nonstop and without refuelling in just over nine days. Fuel ran so low near the end that one engine briefly failed; it was the first aircraft to circle the globe on a single tank.

Radiocarbon dating of the vellum places the Voynich manuscript's creation around 1420, well before the antiquarian Wilfrid Voynich who gave it his name bought it from a Jesuit college in 1912. Its roughly 240 surviving pages are filled with an unbroken invented script, alongside drawings of unidentifiable plants, nude women bathing in green liquid through tubes, and star charts that match no known constellation system.

Codebreakers who cracked German and Japanese military ciphers in the twentieth century have tried it and failed, as have statistical linguists comparing its letter patterns to real languages. The leading theories range between an unknown natural language, a deliberate hoax, and a genuine but unrecoverable cipher, and none has produced a translation that other specialists accept.

Albrecht von Wallenstein commanded the Habsburg armies through much of the Thirty Years' War, and his private diplomacy with Protestant enemies convinced Emperor Ferdinand II that he was negotiating a peace on his own account. Ferdinand stripped him of command in January 1634 and had a secret court convict him of treason without his knowledge.

On 25 February 1634 a group of Irish and Scottish officers in his own army, acting under Ferdinand's approval, killed Wallenstein and several companions at Eger. Colonel Walter Butler led the assassins; the garrison's commandant, John Gordon, and his deputy, Walter Leslie, had already been marked as willing. Ferdinand later rewarded them with property confiscated from Wallenstein's family.

Around 575 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt and expanded Babylon's fortifications into a double wall system, an inner and outer ring separated by a moat, faced with baked brick and wide enough, according to Greek accounts, for a chariot to turn on top.

Ancient writers ranked the walls among the wonders of the world, sometimes alongside the Hanging Gardens attributed to the same king. Excavated sections show gates decorated with glazed brick reliefs of dragons and bulls, and while later authors likely inflated the wall's height in the retelling, its scale was genuinely unmatched among cities of its time.

Beginning around 1400, the Edo people of the Benin Kingdom, in what is now southern Nigeria, built an enormous system of earthen ramparts and ditches around their capital, expanded in stages over generations rather than raised in a single campaign.

Aerial surveys have traced walls and moats extending well beyond the city itself into surrounding villages, a network some researchers have estimated totalled thousands of kilometres across the wider kingdom, making it among the largest man-made earthworks anywhere before the modern era. Much of it was destroyed when British forces burned Benin City in 1897.

Around 2700 BCE the Sumerian city of Uruk, already one of the largest settlements in the world, was enclosed by a defensive wall running for several miles, built of mudbrick along the Euphrates floodplain in what is now southern Iraq. Archaeological surveys have traced its circuit around the city's temple precincts and residential quarters.

Centuries later the wall was folklore, not just masonry: the Epic of Gilgamesh opens by inviting the listener to walk Uruk's ramparts and credits their building to the legendary king himself. The poem's boast that the wall's foundation was laid by seven sages reflects how thoroughly a real feat of engineering had passed into myth.

Wang Mang was regent for an infant emperor he had installed himself, and he had promised publicly to hand back the throne once the boy came of age. Instead, on 15 January in the year 9, he declared the promise void, deposed the child, and proclaimed his own Xin dynasty, ending two centuries of Han rule outright rather than merely dominating it from behind the throne.

His reign lasted only fourteen years before rebellion and a restored Han swept it away, but the manner of his rise, an approved regent simply keeping the crown, became a cautionary case study for later Chinese court politics. Historians afterward branded him the Usurper Emperor, a title meant to warn rather than merely describe.

German occupying forces began walling off a district of Warsaw in 1940, forcing the city's Jewish population, hundreds of thousands of people, into an area sealed by brick walls topped with broken glass and barbed wire. The wall ran for miles through the middle of a functioning city, cutting streets in two.

Conditions inside worsened through overcrowding, forced labour and deliberately restricted food, and the wall existed to make escape and smuggling difficult rather than to protect anyone within it. Most of the ghetto's population was later deported to death camps, and the wall itself was largely destroyed after the 1943 uprising and the German demolition that followed.

Workers were replacing frayed guy wires near the top of the Warsaw radio mast when a strong gust caught the temporarily unsupported section, buckling and snapping the structure in half. It fell in stages, and although the crew had left the immediate area, no one was killed.

The collapse handed the record for tallest human-made structure back to the KVLY-TV mast in North Dakota, which had briefly held it before Warsaw was built. Polish authorities considered rebuilding on the same site but abandoned the plan after local objections, and a shorter replacement was later erected elsewhere.

Built near the village of Konstantynow in central Poland, the guyed radio mast reached about 646 metres, intended to broadcast the state radio signal deep into Western Europe during the Cold War. On completion nothing built by human hands anywhere stood taller, surpassing North Dakota's KVLY-TV mast by a wide margin.

It held the record for seventeen years, the longest of any structure since the Woolworth Building, standing as an unmistakable landmark on the otherwise flat Mazovian plain. Its run ended abruptly in 1991, when the mast collapsed during routine maintenance work.

Construction on the obelisk honouring George Washington had stalled for over two decades after funds ran out and the Civil War intervened, leaving a visibly two-toned shaft where work later resumed with stone from a different quarry. Finished in 1884, it reached about 169 metres.

It became the tallest structure on Earth, overtaking Cologne Cathedral, and the first to hold that title without being a church. The record did not last: within thirty years the Eiffel Tower, then the Woolworth Building, surpassed it, though the monument remains the tallest predominantly stone structure ever built.

At Smithfield on 15 June 1381, the fourteen-year-old Richard II met the rebel leader Wat Tyler to negotiate an end to the Peasants' Revolt. Accounts differ on who moved first, but the Lord Mayor of London, William Walworth, drew a dagger and cut Tyler down in front of his own followers, who had gathered outside the city walls after burning the Savoy Palace and freeing prisoners days earlier.

Richard rode toward the stunned crowd and shouted that he himself would be their leader, buying time while armed men mustered. Tyler's head was displayed on London Bridge. The king's promises of freedom and lower rents were withdrawn within weeks, and Parliament reaffirmed serfdom, but the revolt had already forced the abandonment of the poll tax that provoked it.

Wild water buffalo ranged across South and Southeast Asia, and farmers there tamed them gradually for the heavy work of ploughing waterlogged rice paddies that cattle managed poorly. Their broad, splayed hooves and tolerance for standing in mud made them suited to exactly the terrain that rice farming needed worked.

Genetic evidence points to at least two separate domestication events, producing the river buffalo of South Asia and the swamp buffalo used across East and Southeast Asia, animals different enough that they rarely interbreed successfully today. Both lines remain central to rice agriculture and dairy production across the region.

Steam engines before 1788 needed a person watching the throttle constantly, because their speed climbed or sagged with every change in load. James Watt adapted a governor already used on windmills: two weighted arms spinning on a vertical shaft driven by the engine itself, flying outward as speed rose and dropping back as it fell.

The arms' movement was linked directly to the throttle valve, so a rising engine speed choked its own steam supply and a falling one opened it again, with no attendant needed to intervene. The device became a standard textbook example of feedback control long before that phrase existed, and its self-correcting logic underpins automatic regulators well beyond steam engines.

Congress established the United States Military Academy at West Point, New York, in 1802, on a bluff above the Hudson River that had already been a strategic fort guarding a chain stretched across the water during the Revolutionary War.

It was created to train American officers domestically rather than rely on foreign-trained commanders, filling a gap exposed during the Revolution. It grew into the country's oldest continuously operating military academy and a model for the service academies that followed.

Richard of Pudlicott, a wool merchant who had fallen into debt, spent months in 1303 quietly observing the royal treasury housed beneath Westminster Abbey while King Edward I was away campaigning in Scotland. He is said to have hidden in the abbey grounds and cultivated the monks who had access to the vault before making his move.

The theft made off with a large portion of the crown's accumulated wealth, gold, gems and coin gathered from taxes across the kingdom. Pudlicott was eventually caught and executed, and an old story claimed his flayed skin was nailed to the abbey door as a warning, though a modern examination of the door found the material to be animal hide, not human.

Robert Whitehead built his torpedo from a rough sketch handed to him by an Austrian naval officer, Giovanni Luppis, whose own version was a small unmanned boat steered by ropes from shore. Whitehead, an English engineer working in Fiume, threw out the boat and built a cigar-shaped hull driven by compressed air, tested on the Adriatic from 1866.

The device everyone wanted to copy was inside a sealed compartment called the balance chamber. A pendulum swinging fore and aft was linked to a spring-loaded valve reading water pressure, and together they drove the horizontal rudders that held the torpedo level at a set depth. Whitehead kept the mechanism secret for years, and navies paid to license it rather than reverse it.

Wicked opened on Broadway in October 2003, adapting Gregory Maguire's novel that retold The Wizard of Oz through the eyes of its two witches, tracing how the green-skinned Elphaba came to be branded wicked while her ambitious friend Glinda was cast as good.

Built around a friendship between two young women rather than a romance, the musical drew large audiences and became one of the highest-grossing shows in Broadway history. It has since spun off international productions and, decades later, a film adaptation released across two parts.

Wiley Post had already flown around the world once, in 1931, with a navigator beside him. Two years later he decided to do it alone, in the same Lockheed Vega he had named Winnie Mae, fitted with an early autopilot and a radio direction finder to make solo navigation possible without a second pair of hands.

He left New York on 15 July 1933 and returned on 22 July, having circled the globe in under eight days by flying long single-engine legs across the Atlantic, Soviet Union and Pacific with minimal sleep. Post, who had lost an eye in an oilfield accident years earlier, judged distance and drift largely by instinct once the autopilot took over the straight stretches.

William the Silent had led the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule for over a decade and survived at least one earlier attempt on his life. On 10 July 1584, Balthasar Gerard, posing as a Protestant refugee seeking a letter of introduction, shot him at close range on the stairs of his house in Delft.

Philip II of Spain had put a price on William's head, and Gerard had come specifically to collect it; he was captured, tortured and executed within days. William's death did not break the revolt he had led. His son Maurice took up the fight, and the northern provinces went on to secure their independence as the Dutch Republic.

The wokou crisis of the mid sixteenth century saw pirate bands, mostly Chinese smugglers operating under a Japanese label, raid deep into China's coastal provinces while Ming defences struggled to respond. In 1555 one such band, reportedly numbering only a few dozen men, penetrated far inland and briefly threatened Nanjing, one of the empire's great walled cities.

That a small raiding party could reach so close to a former imperial capital exposed how hollow China's coastal garrisons had become under years of underfunded defence. The alarm it caused pushed the Ming court toward the military reforms that would soon put commanders like Qi Jiguang in charge of rebuilding coastal defence from scratch.

Frank Woolworth paid cash for his headquarters tower, reportedly wanting it built without debt, and commissioned a Gothic-revival design so ornate it was nicknamed the Cathedral of Commerce. At its opening it reached 241 metres, the tallest building on Earth.

President Woodrow Wilson pressed a button in Washington to switch on its lights for the opening ceremony. The Woolworth Building held the record for seventeen years, longer than any other building of the twentieth century's early skyscraper race, before 40 Wall Street briefly overtook it in 1929.

The programme began in 1961 as a three-year experiment, approved by the UN General Assembly and the Food and Agriculture Organisation to test whether surplus food from wealthier countries could be redirected to emergencies and development projects elsewhere. Its first major operation, the following year, sent aid to victims of an earthquake in Iran and a hurricane in Thailand.

The experiment was made permanent in 1965 and grew into the largest humanitarian organisation addressing hunger, running logistics from ports and airstrips to remote distribution points in dozens of countries. It now sits alongside the Famine Early Warning Systems Network and national relief agencies as one of the standing responses to the kind of crisis British India's famine codes were first designed to manage.

Benny Binion invited a handful of the country's best-known professional gamblers to his Horseshoe Casino in downtown Las Vegas in May 1970, not for a structured tournament but for a run of cash games played over several days among a small, invited group, an event he was reviving after buying the rights to a similar Reno gathering.

There was no prize pool and no bracket. At the end, the assembled players simply voted on who among them had played the best, and Johnny Moss was named champion, receiving a silver cup rather than any cash. The following year's event switched to a freeze-out format that eliminated players by chip count, the structure the World Series of Poker has used ever since.

The North Tower's steel frame reached its full height in New York, surpassing the Empire State Building, which had held the title of tallest building in the world since 1931. The Twin Towers' developers had specifically pursued the record, adjusting the design during construction to stay ahead of a rival tower being built in Chicago.

The lead lasted barely two years before the Sears Tower in Chicago overtook it. Both New York towers stood until they were destroyed in the September 11 attacks in 2001, and the World Trade Center site was rebuilt around a new tower completed decades later.

Herodotus says the first attempt failed: a storm wrecked an earlier set of cables, and Xerxes had the strait itself whipped and branded for its insolence before ordering a second crossing built. Persian engineers anchored hundreds of ships bow to stern across the Hellespont, near modern Canakkale, and laid planking and packed earth over cables of flax and papyrus to carry the roadway.

Two parallel bridges carried the army over separately, one for troops and pack animals, the other kept clear so nothing held up the march. Herodotus put the crossing at seven days and nights without rest, an army large enough that ancient counts of a million or more are now treated as wild exaggeration rather than record.

A group of Congregationalist ministers, worried that Harvard was drifting from strict orthodoxy, met to pool their own personal book collections and chartered a Collegiate School in Connecticut in 1701 to train clergy in their own tradition.

It moved between towns for years before settling in New Haven, and in 1718 it was renamed for Elihu Yale, a merchant who had made his fortune with the East India Company and donated goods and books that helped keep the struggling school afloat.

The story comes from the Daoist text Liezi, written centuries after the supposed event: the artificer Yan Shi presented King Mu of Zhou, who is placed in the tenth century BCE, with a life-size figure of wood and leather that walked, tilted its head, and sang when its chin was touched.

The demonstration turned dangerous when the figure winked at the king's concubines, and Mu, taking it for a living rival, ordered Yan Shi executed on the spot. The craftsman tore the figure apart to show the king its jointed wood and painted leather held no life at all, saving himself and leaving one of the earliest robot stories on record.

Fertiliser producer Yara had been trucking product roughly 14 kilometres between its plant at Porsgrunn and its export port at Brevik in Norway, using around 40,000 diesel truck journeys a year, each one adding to road congestion and emissions along the route.

The ship built to replace that traffic, Yara Birkeland, launched in 2021 as the first fully electric, autonomous container vessel, running on batteries with no crew required aboard. It entered commercial service the following year, moving through a staged testing period before certification to sail fully unmanned.

Chuck Yeager broke two ribs falling from a horse two days before his scheduled flight and told almost no one, worried the Air Force would ground him and hand the attempt to someone else. He had a friend saw off a length of broom handle so he could lever the Bell X-1's hatch shut with his injured arm.

On 14 October 1947, dropped from a B-29 over the Mojave Desert, Yeager fired the X-1's rocket engine and reached Mach 1.06, roughly 700 miles per hour, at 45,000 feet. It was the first confirmed instance of a piloted aircraft exceeding the speed of sound, and it stayed classified for nearly a year before the Air Force made it public.

By 2018, a Saudi-led coalition blockade and continued fighting in Yemen's civil war had pushed the country's currency into collapse and cut off imports that supplied roughly ninety percent of its food. The port of Hodeidah, the main entry point for aid and commercial goods, became a repeated flashpoint in the fighting.

United Nations officials described the resulting crisis as the world's worst humanitarian emergency, with millions of Yemenis facing severe food insecurity and outbreaks of cholera compounding the strain on hospitals. A formal famine was never declared nationwide, but UN agencies warned repeatedly that parts of the country stood on the edge of one.

Alexandre Yersin arrived in Hong Kong in 1894 to a colonial epidemic and a rival already working the same wards: the Japanese bacteriologist Kitasato Shibasaburo, backed by better facilities and getting there first. Yersin, with a borrowed hut for a laboratory, took his samples from the buboes of the dead rather than the blood Kitasato favoured, and found a consistent rod-shaped bacterium the Japanese team had missed.

Yersin's bacterium was confirmed as the cause of bubonic plague and later named Yersinia pestis in his honour. The identification did not immediately explain how the disease spread; the role of fleas carried on rats was worked out separately over the following decade, but pinning the bacterium down gave researchers something to test treatments and diagnoses against.

The Yu Ji Tu, carved into stone in 1136, mapped China's rivers, coastline and mountain ranges over a regular square grid, each cell representing a fixed distance on the ground. That grid system for measuring scale on a map traced back centuries in Chinese cartography, to methods credited to the third century official Pei Xiu.

What struck later observers is how closely the coastline and river courses on the stone match a modern map, achieved without instruments for measuring longitude. The carving was meant for administrators governing the Song empire, a practical tool for a state that needed to know its own rivers and borders in exact proportion, not a decorative chart.

Zhang Heng held the post of Chief Astronomer at the Han court, a job that combined astronomy with calendar-keeping and omen reading for the emperor. His surviving writing on the subject, the Ling Xian, describes the moon as a ball that receives its light from the sun rather than glowing on its own.

From that he reasoned that a lunar eclipse happens when the moon passes through the cone of shadow the Earth casts opposite the sun. He also built a water-driven armillary sphere to model the sky's motion, work that put him a step ahead of most contemporaries anywhere in explaining eclipses as geometry rather than omen.

Zheng Yi Sao took command of her late husband's pirate confederation after his death in 1807 and built it into a force of tens of thousands of sailors and hundreds of ships along the South China coast, larger than the fleets of most navies of the day.

Rather than face a costly campaign to destroy it, Qing officials in 1810 negotiated directly with her for a mass amnesty. Most of her followers kept their loot and were allowed to return to ordinary life, and she herself retired to run a gambling house in Canton.

The Zodiac Killer sent the FBI a 340 character cryptogram in 1969, made of odd symbols substituting for letters, and unlike his earlier 408 character cipher it resisted every codebreaker for more than fifty years, including the FBI's own cryptanalysis unit and the NSA.

In December 2020, David Oranchak, a software developer, Sam Blake, an Australian mathematician, and Jarl Van Eycke, a Belgian programmer, cracked it using custom pattern-matching software the trio had built between them. The message contained no name and no confession, mostly a taunting claim about an afterlife, and the killer's identity remains unknown.

Fritz Zwicky measured the velocities of galaxies in the Coma cluster in 1933 and found them moving so fast that the cluster's visible stars could not possibly hold it together gravitationally; it should have flown apart long before. He proposed that some unseen form of matter, which he called dunkle Materie, made up most of the cluster's mass and kept it bound.

The idea was largely set aside for decades, partly because Zwicky's manner made him easy to dismiss and partly because the evidence was indirect. It was vindicated only in the 1970s, when Vera Rubin's studies of galaxy rotation found the same gap between visible mass and the gravity actually observed, turning Zwicky's inference into one of astronomy's central open problems.
